meta.devoTitle: Christ in All the Scriptures · A Reformed Covenantal Devotional · Volume 1: Genesis–Amos

devo.title: The Seed Who Will Crush the Serpent
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Genesis 1:26–31 — Humanity made in God’s image and blessed
  2. Genesis 3:8–15 — The fall, the curse, and the first gospel promise
  3. Genesis 12:1–3 — The call of Abram and the blessing for all nations
  4. Genesis 22:1–14 — The ram provided in place of the son

New Testament fulfillment: Galatians 3:7–9, 16; Romans 5:12–19

The Book and Its Themes

Genesis is the book of beginnings: of the world, of humanity, of sin, of death, of nations, and, most wonderfully, of grace. Its great themes are creation by the word of God, humanity as God’s image-bearer, the catastrophe of the fall, God’s judgment and patience (the flood), the scattering of the nations (Babel), and then, from chapter 12 onward, God’s free choice of one family through whom he will bless all the families of the earth. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph are not heroes of moral achievement. They lie, scheme, doubt, and quarrel. The constant hero of Genesis is the faithful God who keeps his promise despite them. The book closes with Joseph’s confession that God meant for good what his brothers meant for evil (50:20). That one sentence sums up the providence of the whole book.

Where Genesis Stands in the Covenant Story

Reformed covenant theology reads Genesis as the foundation of the whole Bible’s storyline. In Eden God freely bound himself to Adam. He gave life, a calling, and one command, with death threatened for disobedience (2:16–17). The Westminster Confession calls this arrangement the “covenant of works” (WCF 7.2). Reformed teachers have used different labels for it. John Murray, for example, preferred “Adamic administration,” but the substance is broadly shared. Adam stood as a representative head, and when he fell, he fell for all of us (Romans 5:12–19).

God did not abandon his ruined image-bearers. In Genesis 3:15 he promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head and that the serpent would bruise his heel. Historic Reformed readers have called this the protoevangelium, the first gospel. From there the covenant of grace unfolds: with Noah, preserving the world for redemption (Genesis 9), and with Abraham, promising land, offspring, and worldwide blessing, sealed by God passing alone between the pieces (Genesis 15) and signed with circumcision (Genesis 17).

How Genesis Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct promise: Paul says the gospel was “preached before” to Abraham (Galatians 3:8, KJV). He also says the promised “seed” is singular and is ultimately Christ (3:16). The serpent-crusher of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled in the one who, through death, destroyed the one who had the power of death (Hebrews 2:14; compare Romans 16:20).
  • Covenant headship: Adam is “the figure of him that was to come” (Romans 5:14, KJV). Where the first Adam disobeyed in a garden of plenty, the last Adam obeyed in a wilderness and a garden of agony. By his obedience many are made righteous (Romans 5:19).
  • Typology: On Mount Moriah, Abraham’s beloved son carried the wood up the mountain. God provided a ram in his place (22:13–14). The New Testament does not call Genesis 22 a prophecy in so many words, but Hebrews 11:17–19 reads it in light of resurrection, and Romans 8:32 echoes it: God “spared not his own Son.”
  • Thematic analogy: Joseph, rejected by his brothers and then exalted to save them, offers a pattern of humiliation followed by exaltation. That pattern finds its fullness in Jesus. It is a legitimate echo, but it should not be pressed into allegory of every detail.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin insisted that the covenant with the patriarchs “is so far from differing from ours in reality and substance, that it is altogether one and the same: still the administration differs” (Institutes 2.10.2). Abraham was saved exactly as we are, by trusting the promise of God, and his faith was “counted unto him for righteousness” (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3). J. I. Packer described covenant theology as a way of reading the whole Bible. He also called the promise “I will be your God” the promise that carries every other promise inside it.

Genesis 17 is also where Reformed friends begin to disagree. Calvin, the Westminster tradition, John Frame, and Doug Wilson see continuity between circumcision and baptism and so baptize the children of believers. Wayne Grudem, a Reformed Baptist in his soteriology, holds that baptism belongs to those who profess faith. All of them agree on the main point: the Abrahamic promise is fulfilled in Christ and received by faith.

For Today

Genesis tells you who you are: an image-bearer, a sinner in Adam, and, by faith, a child of Abraham in Christ. Your failures do not cancel God’s promise any more than Jacob’s did. Before you look at your own record today, look at the God who swore by himself (Hebrews 6:13–18). The God who said “Let there be light” has spoken a new-creation word over all who are in his Son (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Reflect

  1. Where are you tempted, like Adam, to treat God’s good command as a restriction instead of a gift?
  2. How does seeing Abraham’s flawed faith counted as righteousness free you from self-justification?

Pray

Father, Creator of all things, thank you that in the day of our ruin you promised a Deliverer. Thank you that in the fullness of time you sent your Son, the true Seed of Abraham, to crush the serpent and carry our curse. Make me a true child of Abraham by faith. Teach me to trust your promises when I cannot see how you will keep them. Through Jesus Christ our Lord, amen.

family.scriptureText: The next day John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!” The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus. Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, “What are you seeking?” And they said to him, “Rabbi… where are you staying?” He said to them, “Come and you will see.” So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day.
family.context: John the Baptist pointed away from himself to Jesus. Two listeners began following, and Jesus met them with a searching question—“What are you seeking?”—then an invitation: come close enough to see for yourselves. Faith often begins less with a speech and more with nearness. This is how discipleship often begins in a household too: not with a polished speech, but with a willingness to walk toward Jesus and stay long enough to know him. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is not a distant idea we admire from afar. He is the Lamb of God who welcomes seekers into his presence. Following him starts when curiosity becomes companionship. Tonight we answer his invitation to come near, not merely study about him. His question still searches us. We do not have to pretend we seek only noble things; we bring mixed motives, and he still says come. The Lamb of God is also the welcoming Rabbi. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Families can rush past the “why” of faith and jump to routines. Slow down. Before you talk or pray, pause and treat Jesus as present—someone who asks what you are seeking and then says, “Come and see.” Let tonight be coming near, not checking a box. You might even leave a chair empty for a moment as a small sign that Jesus is the guest of honor in the conversation.
family.talk: If Jesus asked our family tonight, “What are you seeking?” what honest answer would we give?
family.prayer: Jesus, thank you for inviting us to come and see who you are. We bring our questions and hopes. Draw our family close to you tonight. Amen.

quote.author: Sinclair B. Ferguson
quote.work: Grace Alone: How the Grace of God Amazes Me
quote.text: What Christ is doing in you is still incomplete. But in what Jesus Christ has done for you there is not a single tiny crack that the satanic arrows can penetrate.
quote.comment: On days when growth feels slow, our footing is not our progress but Christ's finished work, which has no gaps.

read.title: The Love of God
read.author: Sam Storms
read.note: Defines God's love as his free, self-giving disposition to bless his image-bearers, traces its different forms in Scripture, and shows it supremely in the gift of himself in Christ, a love meant to be felt, not just affirmed.

devo.title: The Lord Who Redeems and Dwells
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Exodus 3:1–15 — The burning bush and the revealed name
  2. Exodus 12:1–13 — The Passover lamb and the blood on the doorposts
  3. Exodus 19:3–6 — Redeemed to be a kingdom of priests
  4. Exodus 40:34–38 — The glory fills the tabernacle

New Testament fulfillment: 1 Corinthians 5:7; John 1:14

The Book and Its Themes

Exodus moves from slavery to worship. It opens with Israel crushed under Pharaoh and closes with the glory of the LORD filling a tent pitched among his people. In between come the revelation of God’s covenant name (3:14–15), the plagues as judgment on Egypt’s gods (12:12), the Passover, the crossing of the sea, the giving of the law at Sinai, the golden calf, Moses’ intercession, and the building of the tabernacle. Its major themes are redemption, the knowledge of the LORD (“ye shall know that I am the LORD,” 6:7, KJV), covenant law as the shape of a redeemed life, and God’s presence among sinners.

Notice the order. God says “I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt” (20:2, KJV) before he says “Thou shalt.” Grace comes before law, and the law is given to a people already redeemed.

Where Exodus Stands in the Covenant Story

Exodus begins with God remembering “his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob” (2:24). The exodus is God keeping the Abrahamic promise. At Sinai a new administration of the covenant is established. It includes priesthood, sacrifice, tabernacle, and detailed law, ratified with blood (24:8).

Reformed theologians have debated how to describe the Mosaic covenant. The Westminster Confession treats it as an administration of the one covenant of grace, “under the law” by “promises, prophecies, sacrifices… the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances… all foresignifying Christ to come” (WCF 7.5). Some Reformed scholars argue that Sinai also, in some sense, republished the works principle for Israel’s life in the land. This is a real intramural debate. What all agree on is that no Israelite was ever justified by law-keeping. The law exposed sin and pointed to the sacrifices, and the sacrifices pointed to Christ.

How Exodus Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: “Christ our passover is sacrificed for us” (1 Corinthians 5:7, KJV). Jesus deliberately went to his death at Passover. He took the bread and cup of that meal and declared the cup “the new testament in my blood” (Luke 22:20). Like the Passover lamb, not one of his bones was broken (Exodus 12:46; John 19:36).
  • Fulfillment of presence: John says the Word became flesh and “dwelt” among us (John 1:14). The Greek word means he “tabernacled” or pitched his tent, and John adds “we beheld his glory.” The glory cloud that filled the tent now shines in the face of Jesus Christ.
  • Typology: Moses as mediator foreshadows the greater Mediator. Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house; Christ is faithful as a Son over it (Hebrews 3:1–6). The manna in the wilderness points to Jesus, the true bread from heaven (John 6:32–35). The rock that gave water is identified by Paul with Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).
  • Thematic analogy: The exodus becomes the Bible’s master pattern for salvation. It is deliverance from bondage, through judgment, by blood, unto worship. Luke even calls Jesus’ coming death his “exodus” (Luke 9:31, Greek exodos; KJV “decease”).

Through Reformed Eyes

John Frame summarizes God’s covenant lordship in three words: control, authority, and presence. Exodus displays all three. God’s control is seen in the plagues and at the sea. His authority is seen in Sinai’s words. His presence is seen in the cloud, the fire, and the tabernacle. Calvin taught that the ceremonies of the law, though now abolished in use, still teach believers to look for Christ (Institutes 2.7.1–2, 16). The Reformed tradition also commonly uses the Ten Commandments as a rule of grateful obedience for believers. This is the so-called third use of the law. It is not a ladder to climb to God, but the family manners of those he has already brought out.

For Today

You were not saved in order to wander. You were saved in order to worship. Whatever “Egypt” still pulls at you, whether habits, fears, or idols, has been judged at the cross. The blood is on the doorposts, and judgment has passed over all who shelter under the Lamb. Obey today from gratitude, not for acceptance. Then remember that the God who dwelt in a tent now dwells in you by his Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Reflect

  1. In what area of life are you still acting like a slave rather than a redeemed child of God?
  2. How does “grace first, then law” (Exodus 20:2–3) change the way you approach God’s commands today?

Pray

LORD, I AM WHO I AM, you heard the groaning of your people and came down to save. Thank you for Jesus, my Passover Lamb, whose blood shelters me from judgment. Thank you for Jesus, the true tabernacle, in whom I behold your glory. Deliver me from every remaining bondage. Make my life a kingdom-of-priests offering of praise. In Christ’s name, amen.

family.scriptureText: Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” And immediately they left their nets and followed him. And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother… And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.
family.context: These men had ordinary work, family ties, and a familiar shoreline. Jesus interrupted that day with a clear call. Mark stresses their immediacy—not because following is always easy, but because Jesus’ word carries authority that rearranges priorities. Nets meant income, identity, and tomorrow’s plans. Leaving them did not erase responsibility overnight, but it did relocate who sets the agenda. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus does not only invite us to observe him; he calls us to belong to him. “Follow me” means he becomes the center of our direction. He also promises to reshape us—“I will make you”—so discipleship is his work in us, not a self-improvement project we invent. When Jesus says he will make us fishers of people, he claims both Lordship and craftsmanship—he forms messengers out of followers. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Think of one “net” that quietly competes with Jesus for first place at home—screens, schedules, image, or always needing the last word. Naming it together is often the first step of leaving it to walk after him. Talk honestly about cost without dramatizing it. Following Jesus in a family is usually a series of small rearrangements, not one cinematic exit. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: What everyday thing most often pulls our attention away from following Jesus together?
family.prayer: Lord Jesus, you called ordinary people and made them yours. Call us again tonight. Help us leave what distracts us and trust you to shape who we become. Amen.

quote.author: Wayne Grudem
quote.text: God is unchanging in his being, perfections, purposes, and promises, yet God does act and feel emotions, and he acts and feels differently in response to different situations.
quote.comment: The God who made his promises to you is the same God who keeps them: nothing in him wears out, drifts, or changes his mind about his people (Mal. 3:6).

read.title: Discourse VI: On the Immutability of God
read.author: Stephen Charnock
read.source: The Existence and Attributes of God (Puritan discourse, PDF via TGC)
read.note: A classic Puritan exposition of Psalm 102:26-27 arguing that God is unchangeable in essence, knowledge, will and promises, and drawing out the comfort that brings to believers.

devo.title: Holiness, Blood, and the Way Back to God
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Leviticus 1:1–9 — The burnt offering, accepted on the worshiper’s behalf
  2. Leviticus 16:6–22 — The Day of Atonement and the scapegoat
  3. Leviticus 17:11 — The life is in the blood
  4. Leviticus 19:1–2, 9–18 — “Ye shall be holy”: holiness in everyday love

New Testament fulfillment: Hebrews 9:11–14; 1 Peter 1:15–19

The Book and Its Themes

Many Bible-reading plans stall in Leviticus, but the book answers the question Exodus leaves hanging. Exodus ends with the glory filling the tabernacle, and even Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:35). Leviticus explains how sinful people can live near a holy God. Its themes are holiness, the five offerings, priesthood, clean and unclean, the Day of Atonement (chapter 16, the literary and theological center), and the holiness code (“Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy,” 19:2, KJV). The same chapter that commands ritual holiness also says “thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (19:18). Leviticus does not separate worship from ethics. Gleaning laws for the poor, fair wages, honest scales, and care for the disabled all belong to holiness.

Where Leviticus Stands in the Covenant Story

Leviticus is the worship manual of the Sinai covenant. It teaches by picture. Sin brings death, so life must be given in place of the sinner (17:11). The worshiper laid his hand on the animal (1:4), identifying with it and transferring guilt. On the Day of Atonement the high priest entered the Most Holy Place with blood, and a second goat carried the people’s sins away into the wilderness (16:21–22).

The Westminster Confession explains that these ordinances were “for that time, sufficient and efficacious, through the operation of the Spirit, to instruct and build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah” (WCF 7.5). Hebrews adds that the blood of bulls and goats could never take away sins (10:4). The sacrifices were real means of grace for Old Testament believers precisely because they pointed beyond themselves.

How Leviticus Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment (explicitly taught): Hebrews 9–10 reads Leviticus 16 as a script fulfilled by Jesus. He is both the high priest and the sacrifice. He entered “not… by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood” into heaven itself, “having obtained eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12, KJV). The torn veil at his death (Matthew 27:51) signaled that the way into the holiest is now open (Hebrews 10:19–22).
  • Substitution: The laying on of hands and the life-for-life principle lay the groundwork for penal substitution. Christ “his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24, KJV). J. I. Packer’s well-known essay “What Did the Cross Achieve? The Logic of Penal Substitution” (Tyndale Biblical Theology Lecture, 1973; published in Tyndale Bulletin 25, 1974) defends this as the heart of the gospel.
  • Typology: The scapegoat pictures sin removed “as far as the east is from the west” (Psalm 103:12). Jesus suffered “without the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), just as the sin-offering remains were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27).
  • Thematic analogy: The clean and unclean laws taught Israel that impurity spreads by contact. Jesus reverses the direction. When he touches the leper and the bleeding woman, he is not defiled. They are made clean (Mark 1:40–42; 5:25–34).

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed tradition, following Calvin (Institutes 2.7.16–17; 4.20.15), has commonly distinguished the moral, ceremonial, and civil (judicial) aspects of the law. The ceremonies are fulfilled and set aside in Christ. The moral law, summarized in love for God and neighbor, continues as the rule of life (WCF 19.3–5). Not every Reformed theologian draws these lines identically. Some Reformed writers caution that the three categories are useful but not always neatly separable in the text. Still, the shared conviction stands: we don’t offer animals, because the final offering has been made. We do pursue holiness, because the Holy One has made us his.

For Today

Holiness is not a grim religious atmosphere. It is belonging wholly to God. The God of Leviticus is not looking for a reason to keep you away. He designed an entire system to bring sinners near. Now that the blood of Christ has opened the way, you can come boldly (Hebrews 4:16). Let that confidence spill into Leviticus 19 holiness today: honest work, generosity to those in need, and love for your neighbor.

Reflect

  1. Do you think of holiness mainly as avoiding things, or as belonging to God and loving like him?
  2. What does it mean for your prayers today that the veil has been torn and the way is open?

Pray

Holy God, you are a consuming fire, and yet you have made a way for sinners to draw near. Thank you that Jesus, my great High Priest, has entered your presence with his own blood and obtained eternal redemption for me. Cleanse my conscience from dead works so that I may serve you. Make me holy in my worship, my work, and my love for my neighbor. For Jesus’ sake, amen.

family.scriptureText: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me. I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
family.context: On the night before the cross, Jesus used a vineyard picture his disciples knew. Fruit does not come from straining branches; it comes from staying connected to the vine. Separation can look independent for a while, then withers. Branches do not lecture themselves into grapes. They remain attached through seasons of pruning and waiting. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is our life-source, not merely our example. Union with him—“abide in me, and I in you”—is how love, patience, and faithfulness grow in a household. Apart from him, even good intentions run dry. With him, fruit overflows from belonging. Jesus’ “apart from me you can do nothing” is not insult; it is mercy that frees us from pretending we are our own source. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Pick one simple way to stay connected to Jesus this week: a short shared reading, a whispered prayer before a hard conversation, or naming gratitude tied to his care. Connection is usually small and repeated, not dramatic. If tonight feels dry, treat that as a signal to reconnect, not a verdict that you have failed permanently. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: When do we most feel “apart from Jesus”—rushed, empty, or on our own—and what helps us reconnect?
family.prayer: Jesus, you are the vine. Keep us close to you. Let your life flow into our words and choices so that anything good in us comes from you. Amen.

quote.author: Thomas Watson
quote.work: A Body of Divinity, "The Mercy of God"
quote.text: God is more inclinable to mercy than wrath. Mercy is his darling attribute, which he most delights in.
quote.comment: When you come to God burdened by sin, you are not dragging mercy out of a reluctant Judge; you are asking for the very thing he most loves to give (Mic. 7:18).

read.title: The Never-Failing, Never-Changing, All-Surpassing Goodness of God
read.author: Kevin DeYoung
read.note: Working from Exodus 33-34, DeYoung argues that God's goodness is the sum of his glory: he is good in himself, good to all he has made, and supremely good to his people in Christ, so we can trust him in hard times.

devo.title: Wilderness Wanderers and the Lifted-Up Savior
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Numbers 6:22–27 — The priestly blessing
  2. Numbers 14:1–24 — Unbelief at the border and Moses’ intercession
  3. Numbers 21:4–9 — The bronze serpent lifted up
  4. Numbers 24:15–19 — Balaam’s oracle: a Star out of Jacob

New Testament fulfillment: John 3:14–15; 1 Corinthians 10:1–13

The Book and Its Themes

Numbers gets its English name from its two censuses (chapters 1 and 26), but the Hebrew title, “In the Wilderness,” fits it better. It tells how an eleven-day journey (Deuteronomy 1:2) became forty years. Its themes include the ordered camp around God’s presence, grumbling and unbelief, rebellion against God-appointed leaders (Korah, chapter 16), judgment, and the stubborn faithfulness of God. A whole generation dies in the desert because they would not believe God could give them the land (14:11). Yet their children reach the plains of Moab, and even a hired pagan prophet, Balaam, cannot curse those whom God has blessed (23:8, 20).

Where Numbers Stands in the Covenant Story

Numbers shows the covenant community as a mixed multitude. All passed through the sea, all ate the manna, and all were under the cloud, “but with many of them God was not well pleased” (1 Corinthians 10:5). The sign and the privileges were real, yet unbelief kept many from entering the rest. Moses’ intercession in chapter 14 is grounded not in Israel’s merit but in God’s own revealed name: “longsuffering, and of great mercy, forgiving iniquity” (14:18, KJV, echoing Exodus 34:6–7).

This is also where one of the more sensitive conversations among the authors you appreciate surfaces. Doug Wilson, in Reformed Is Not Enough (2002), stresses the “objectivity of the covenant.” On his view, the baptized are truly covenant members who will be either faithful or unfaithful, much as wilderness Israel was. Many confessional Presbyterians sympathize with his concern against bare individualism. However, the Presbyterian Church in America’s 2007 study report rejected several Federal Vision formulations associated with this movement, particularly any view in which covenant membership includes a losable justification or election. Calvin, Packer, Frame, and Grudem would all say plainly that a true member of the covenant may lose outward privileges, but that those whom God justifies he also glorifies (Romans 8:30). The wilderness warning is real, and so is the promise that Christ loses none whom the Father gives him (John 6:39).

How Numbers Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment (Jesus’ own words): “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish” (John 3:14–15, KJV). The cure in Numbers 21 was strange. Israel was healed by looking at an image of the very curse that was killing them. In the same way, Christ was “made a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), and sinners are healed by looking to him in faith.
  • Messianic prophecy: Balaam’s “Star out of Jacob” and “Sceptre… out of Israel” (24:17) point first to David and ultimately to the royal Messiah. That is why later Jewish and Christian readers alike saw a messianic king here (compare Revelation 22:16, “the bright and morning star”).
  • Typology: Paul explicitly calls the wilderness events “types” (typoi) written “for our admonition” (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). The rock that followed them “was Christ” (10:4).
  • Thematic analogy: The Aaronic blessing (6:24–26), with its threefold “the LORD,” finds its fullest Christian sound in the apostolic benediction of Father, Son, and Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:14). This is a fitting echo rather than a proof text for the Trinity.

For Today

Most of the Christian life is lived “in the wilderness”: between redemption accomplished and inheritance received. Grumbling is unbelief with a loud voice. Numbers warns us not to presume on outward privileges, but its deepest word is gospel: look and live. When your conscience bites like a serpent today, don’t stare at the wound. Look to the One lifted up.

Reflect

  1. Where has complaint quietly replaced trust in your heart this week?
  2. How do you hold together the real warnings of 1 Corinthians 10 and the sure promises of John 6:37–40?

Pray

LORD, bless me and keep me. Make your face shine on me and give me peace. Forgive my grumbling and unbelief in the wilderness places of my life. Thank you that Jesus was lifted up for me, so that by looking to him I live. Keep me trusting you all the way to the promised rest. In his name, amen.

family.scriptureText: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you? Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them… is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it… But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation…”
family.context: Jesus ends a stretch of teaching with a mirror. Calling him Lord is not the same as building life on his words. Storms expose foundations. Hearing without doing leaves a house looking fine until pressure arrives. Floods in Jesus’ picture are not rare disasters only; they are the pressures that reveal whether our faith is decorative or structural. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is Lord—worthy of obedience—because he is the wise foundation and the Savior who later bears judgment for us. Obeying him is not earning his love; it is living in the security of the One who already speaks truth for our good. Because Jesus is the rock, obedience is how we live on what he has already secured, not how we pile sandbags of self-effort. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Choose one clear word of Jesus you already know—forgive, tell the truth, serve—and name one concrete way your household can practice it this week when irritation or hurry hits. Write the practice on a note where you will see it when the flood usually hits. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: Where is our family good at hearing Jesus’ words, and where do we struggle to put them into practice?
family.prayer: Lord Jesus, we call you Lord. Help us dig deeper than talk. Build our home on your words, and hold us steady when pressure comes. Amen.

devo.title: Love the Lord: The Covenant Renewed on the Border
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Deuteronomy 6:4–9 — The Shema: love the LORD with all your heart
  2. Deuteronomy 8:1–6 — Man does not live by bread alone
  3. Deuteronomy 18:15–19 — A prophet like Moses
  4. Deuteronomy 30:1–14 — The promise of a circumcised heart

New Testament fulfillment: Matthew 4:1–11; Romans 10:5–13

The Book and Its Themes

Deuteronomy (“second law”) is Moses’ farewell preaching to the new generation on the plains of Moab. It is a covenant renewal document, and its shape closely resembles ancient Near Eastern treaties. It contains a historical prologue (chapters 1–4), stipulations (5–26), blessings and curses (27–28), and witnesses and succession (29–34). Its great themes are the oneness and exclusive lordship of God (6:4), love as the heart of obedience, remembering God’s past grace, the danger of forgetting him in prosperity (8:11–18), one central place of worship, care for the poor and the stranger, and the choice between life and death (30:19). Jesus quoted Deuteronomy more than almost any other book. He answered every temptation in the wilderness from Deuteronomy 6–8 and named 6:5 the first and great commandment (Matthew 22:37–38).

Where Deuteronomy Stands in the Covenant Story

Deuteronomy is honest about Israel’s heart. Moses says plainly that the LORD had not yet given them “an heart to perceive” (29:4). He foresees exile (chapters 28–30) and then promises that God himself will “circumcise thine heart… to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart” (30:6, KJV). That promise anticipates the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36.

The Westminster tradition reads the law in Deuteronomy as having more than one use. It reveals God’s holy will, convicts sinners of their inability, and drives them to Christ (Galatians 3:24). For believers, it serves as a guide for grateful life (WCF 19.6). Deuteronomy itself refuses to make love and law enemies: “this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments” (1 John 5:3).

How Deuteronomy Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct prophecy: “The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet… like unto me” (18:15, KJV). Peter (Acts 3:22–26) and Stephen (Acts 7:37) identify Jesus as this Prophet. At the transfiguration the Father adds, “hear ye him” (Matthew 17:5), echoing 18:15.
  • Obedient Son: Israel was God’s son tested forty years in the wilderness and failed (8:2–5). Jesus, the true Son, tested forty days in the wilderness, quoted Deuteronomy and obeyed (Matthew 4:1–11). He kept the Shema perfectly, and his obedience is counted to those who trust him (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9).
  • Curse-bearing: “He that is hanged is accursed of God” (21:23). Paul quotes this to show that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The curses of Deuteronomy 27–28 fell on him.
  • Word of faith: Paul applies Deuteronomy 30:12–14 to the gospel. We need not ascend to heaven or descend to the deep, because Christ has come down and risen. “The word is nigh thee” (Romans 10:6–8). This is apostolic interpretation, and it shows that the gracious heart of Deuteronomy was always about God doing for his people what they could not do.

Through Reformed Eyes

John Frame’s “normative perspective” asks what God’s authoritative word requires. Deuteronomy is the normative perspective in sermon form. Yet Frame also insists that God’s authority is never separated from his presence and control, and Deuteronomy agrees: the law is given by the God who is “nigh” (4:7). Calvin taught that the law shows us what we owe and cannot pay, so that we flee to grace (Institutes 2.7.6–9). He also taught that the law exhorts believers, much as a whip urges on a sluggish animal (2.7.12). Wayne Grudem, writing in a more Baptist key, affirms the same three themes: the moral law reflects God’s character, it convicts us, and it guides the Christian life. (See his chapters on the covenants and on sanctification in Systematic Theology.)

For Today

Deuteronomy calls you to remember and to love. Prosperity is the season of greatest danger, when full stomachs forget the Giver (8:10–14). Rehearse God’s grace in Christ today as deliberately as Israel rehearsed the exodus at the table and on the doorposts (6:7–9). And take heart: the God who demanded a circumcised heart has promised to give one.

Reflect

  1. What blessings in your life are most likely to make you forget God (Deuteronomy 8:11–14)?
  2. How can you speak of God’s works “when thou sittest in thine house” this week, with your family or friends?

Pray

Hear, O my soul: the LORD our God is one LORD. Father, I have not loved you with all my heart, soul, and strength. I thank you that Jesus did, in my place, and bore the curse I deserved. Circumcise my heart by your Spirit, so that I may love you and keep your word with joy. Help me remember your redemption every day. In Jesus’ name, amen.

family.scriptureText: And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons.
family.context: Before Jesus sent the Twelve to do anything public, he appointed them “so that they might be with him.” Mission flowed from companionship. Presence came before performance. Many of us default to usefulness as proof of love. Jesus reverses the order: withness first, then sentness. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus desires people, not only workers. Being with him is the heart of Christian life—through his Word, prayer, and the Spirit’s nearness. From that closeness he still sends us into ordinary places with his authority to speak life and resist darkness. His desire for companions shows the heart of God—he wants nearness, then entrusts authority that flows from relationship. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: Protect a few unhurried minutes with Jesus before rushing into tasks for him—or for everyone else. Family rhythms that always produce but never linger with him slowly empty out. Even five unhurried minutes before a busy evening can reset the order: presence, then tasks. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: Do we more often treat faith as “being with Jesus” or as “getting things done”? What would a small change look like?
family.prayer: Jesus, thank you for wanting us with you. Teach our family to enjoy your presence first, then to go where you send us with courage. Amen.

devo.title: The Greater Joshua and the Promised Rest
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Joshua 1:1–9 — “Be strong and of a good courage”
  2. Joshua 2:8–21 — Rahab’s faith and the scarlet cord
  3. Joshua 5:13–15 — The Commander of the LORD’s army
  4. Joshua 21:43–45 — Not one good promise failed

New Testament fulfillment: Hebrews 4:1–11; Hebrews 11:30–31

The Book and Its Themes

Joshua tells how God brought Israel into the land promised to Abraham. Its main movements are entering (crossing the Jordan, chapters 1–5), conquering (6–12), dividing the inheritance (13–21), and renewing the covenant (22–24). Its themes are God’s faithfulness to his promises (21:45), courage grounded in God’s presence (1:9), holy war as God’s judgment on Canaanite wickedness (compare Genesis 15:16), the danger of hidden sin (Achan, chapter 7), and the call to choose whom you will serve (24:15). The conquest passages are hard reading. Scripture presents them as a unique, divinely commanded judgment in redemptive history, not a model for Christian warfare. The church’s weapons are “not carnal” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Where Joshua Stands in the Covenant Story

Joshua is the fulfillment of one strand of the Abrahamic promise: land. Yet Hebrews tells us it was not the final rest: “if Jesus [Joshua] had given them rest, then would he not afterward have spoken of another day” (Hebrews 4:8, KJV). The land was a real gift and also a down payment pointing to a better country (Hebrews 11:16). Even Abraham “looked for a city which hath foundations” (11:10). Paul widens the promise from Canaan to the whole world (Romans 4:13), and Jesus promises that the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5).

Rahab is a striking covenant surprise. She was a Canaanite and a prostitute, yet she was saved by faith and grafted into Israel. She appears in Jesus’ genealogy (Matthew 1:5), and both Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 commend her. The covenant has always been entered by grace through faith, not by bloodline.

How Joshua Leads Us to Christ

  • The name: “Joshua” (Yehoshua, “the LORD saves”) is the same name as “Jesus” in Greek (Iēsous). Hebrews 4:8 uses it for Joshua. The angel told Joseph to call Mary’s son Jesus, “for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).
  • Typology of rest: Joshua led Israel into a temporary rest. Jesus leads his people into the sabbath-rest of God, entered by faith now and enjoyed fully in the new creation (Hebrews 4:9–11; Matthew 11:28–30).
  • Theophany: Many Reformed interpreters (and church fathers before them) have understood the Commander of the LORD’s army (5:13–15), who receives worship and makes the ground holy, as a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son. Scripture does not state this explicitly, so hold it as a reasonable and widely held interpretation rather than a certainty.
  • Thematic analogy: The scarlet cord that marked Rahab’s house for rescue (2:18–21) echoes the Passover blood. Christian readers have long connected it with the blood of Christ. It is a fitting echo, but the New Testament itself emphasizes her faith rather than the cord.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin read the promise of Canaan as a mirror. In it Israel saw an earthly inheritance, but through it the faithful looked to a heavenly one (Institutes 2.11.1–2). This is a key Reformed way of honoring both the literal history and its typological depth. On the future shape of the inheritance, your teachers differ. Grudem expects a future earthly millennium after Christ’s return. Wilson is an optimistic postmillennialist who expects the gospel to transform the nations before Christ returns. Calvin rejected the chiliasts’ thousand-year kingdom (Institutes 3.25.5). All of them agree that the final inheritance is a renewed creation under King Jesus.

For Today

Joshua’s courage did not come from self-confidence. It came from a promise: “the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” (1:9, KJV). Christ makes the same promise to you: “I am with you alway” (Matthew 28:20). Whatever giants loom today, you are already standing on promised ground. And the One who leads you has never failed in one good word.

Reflect

  1. Is there an “Achan’s tent,” some hidden compromise, that is weakening your walk with God?
  2. How does Rahab’s story change the way you think about who can be welcomed into God’s people?

Pray

LORD who saves, thank you that not one of your good promises has ever failed. Thank you for Jesus, the greater Joshua, who leads me into your rest. Give me courage rooted in your presence, not in myself. Like Rahab, help me cling to you in faith. Like Joshua, help me choose to serve you, with my whole household. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.”
family.context: Jesus had just said he would suffer, be rejected, and be raised. Then he invited anyone into daily self-denial—not a once-a-year sacrifice, but willingness to put his way above self-protection. Daily cross-bearing is rarely glamorous. It is the repeated choice to let Jesus’ way outrank self-protection. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: We take up a cross because Jesus first carried the cross for us. He lost his life and gained ours. Following him means trusting that the life we “lose” for his sake—pride, comfort, the need to win—is the life he truly saves and restores. The paradox stands because Jesus pioneered it: losing life for his sake is how true life is found in him. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Name one small daily cross: apologizing first, sharing attention, choosing honesty when a shortcut would be easier. Self-denial at home often looks like laying down the right to be first. Celebrate small surrenders. They train a household for larger faithfulness. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: What would “losing our life for Jesus’ sake” look like in one ordinary moment tomorrow?
family.prayer: Jesus, you gave yourself for us. Give us courage to deny selfish ways today, trust your better life, and follow you with open hands. Amen.

devo.title: Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Judges 2:11–19 — The cycle: sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance
  2. Judges 6:11–16 — Gideon: “The LORD is with thee”
  3. Judges 16:23–30 — Samson’s death and victory
  4. Judges 21:25 — No king in Israel

New Testament fulfillment: Hebrews 11:32–34; 1 Corinthians 1:26–31

The Book and Its Themes

Judges is one of the darkest books in Scripture, and it is honest on purpose. After Joshua’s generation dies, “there arose another generation… which knew not the LORD” (2:10, KJV). What follows is a downward spiral repeated about seven times: Israel sins, God hands them to oppressors, they cry out, God raises a deliverer (a “judge”), and the land rests. Then the cycle starts again, worse each time. The judges themselves decline, from faithful Othniel to fearful Gideon, to rash Jephthah, to Samson, who is driven by appetite. The book ends in idolatry, sexual violence, and civil war (chapters 17–21). Its refrain explains why: “In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (21:25, KJV). Its themes are the depravity of the human heart, the patience of God, deliverance by weak instruments, and the need for a righteous king.

Where Judges Stands in the Covenant Story

Judges shows the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 coming into effect. It also shows the stubborn mercy of the covenant of grace: “it repented the LORD because of their groanings” (2:18, KJV). In the shape of the canon, Judges prepares for kingship. Ruth and 1–2 Samuel answer its cry for a king with David, and David himself points beyond to a greater Son. The book teaches total depravity in narrative form. It does not mean every person is as bad as possible. It means sin infects every part of us, and left to ourselves, we always spiral downward.

How Judges Leads Us to Christ

  • Thematic fulfillment (the need for a king): Judges’ closing refrain is a longing that Jesus answers as the righteous King who rules hearts, not merely territory (Luke 1:32–33). Where every man did what was right in his own eyes, Christ teaches us to pray, “Thy will be done.”
  • Typology of the deliverer: The judges were Spirit-empowered saviors (3:10; 6:34; 14:6), raised up when God’s people could not save themselves. Jesus is the Spirit-anointed Deliverer par excellence (Luke 4:18). Unlike them, he has no fatal flaw. He delivers once for all, and the rest he brings does not end.
  • Typology in Samson: Samson’s greatest victory came in his death, arms outstretched between two pillars (16:29–30). The parallel to the cross is real, and readers through the centuries have noticed it. But Samson died for his own vengeance and failures, while Jesus died sinless for others. The type works by both likeness and contrast.
  • New Testament reading: Hebrews 11:32 lists Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among the faithful. That is grace. Paul explains God’s pattern: he chooses “the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin’s doctrine of total depravity (Institutes 2.1–3) is not pessimism for its own sake. It clears the ground so that grace can be seen as grace. A conviction that runs through much of Doug Wilson’s cultural writing, and that he shares with older Reformed thinkers, is that a people’s culture flows out of its worship. Judges illustrates this vividly. When Israel’s worship collapses, its families, cities, and justice collapse with it. J. I. Packer’s Knowing God has a chapter on “the goodness and severity of God” (compare Romans 11:22) that fits Judges well. God’s patience is not indifference, and he disciplines his people precisely because he will not let them go.

For Today

Judges invites honest self-examination. Where are you doing what is right in your own eyes? But it does not leave you there. The answer to the chaos of the human heart is not trying harder. It is the true King. Bow to Jesus’ rule in the specific places you have kept for yourself. And if you feel weak, like Gideon threshing wheat in hiding, remember that God delights to use weak people so that he receives the glory.

Reflect

  1. What “cycle” of sin and repentance keeps repeating in your life, and what would it look like to bring it under King Jesus’ rule rather than merely feeling sorry again?
  2. How does God’s use of flawed judges encourage you in your own weakness?

Pray

King of kings, I confess that I so often do what is right in my own eyes. Thank you for your patience with your people through generation after generation. Thank you for Jesus, the Deliverer without flaw, who conquered through his death. Rule my heart, my home, and my choices today. Use my weakness to show your strength. Amen.

family.scriptureText: As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love. These things I have spoken to you that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
family.context: Jesus roots obedience in already-given love. The Father loves the Son; the Son loves his people the same way. Staying in that love produces joy, and joy overflows as mutual love that mirrors his. Joy here is not hype; it is Jesus’ own joy shared with those who stay in his love. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus loves us with the same steadfast love the Father has for him—secure, not fragile. Our love for one another is not invented from thin air; it is a response patterned after how he has already loved us, even to the cross. Commandment-keeping, in this frame, is relational loyalty to the One who loved first—patterned after the Son’s obedience to the Father. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Practice love “as I have loved you”: patient listening, covering an offense without keeping score, serving without announcing it. Let joy, not guilt, set the mood of obedience tonight. Let the discussion stay warm. Love as he loved is learned in tone as much as in tasks. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: Where have we felt Jesus’ love recently, and how could that shape how we treat each other this weekend?
family.prayer: Jesus, thank you for loving us as the Father loves you. Keep us in your love. Fill our home with your joy, and teach us to love one another as you have loved us. Amen.

devo.title: The Kinsman-Redeemer Under Whose Wings We Rest
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Ruth 1:15–18 — “Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God”
  2. Ruth 2:8–13 — Boaz’s kindness and the shelter of God’s wings
  3. Ruth 3:7–13 — Ruth asks Boaz to redeem
  4. Ruth 4:13–22 — The redeemer, the son, and the line of David

New Testament fulfillment: Matthew 1:1–6; Ephesians 1:7

The Book and Its Themes

Ruth is set “in the days when the judges ruled” (1:1), but it reads like a breath of fresh air after Judges. It is a short, beautifully crafted story of loss and restoration. Naomi goes out “full” and returns “empty” (1:21). Through the steadfast love of a Moabite daughter-in-law and a godly Israelite landowner, she ends with a grandson on her lap. The key Hebrew word is hesed: loyal, covenant love (1:8; 2:20; 3:10). Other themes are God’s hidden providence (Ruth “happened” upon Boaz’s field, 2:3), the kinsman-redeemer (go’el) law (Leviticus 25:25; Deuteronomy 25:5–10), the inclusion of a Gentile, and the coming of King David (4:17–22).

Where Ruth Stands in the Covenant Story

Ruth answers Judges’ cry for a king by quietly tracing the line of David. In the middle of national chaos, God was working through ordinary faithfulness at harvest time. Ruth also displays the covenant’s worldwide reach. A Moabite, from a nation restricted from Israel’s assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), is welcomed by faith under “the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust” (2:12, KJV). The promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed is visible in miniature.

How Ruth Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct genealogical fulfillment: Matthew names Ruth in Jesus’ genealogy (Matthew 1:5). The son born to Ruth and Boaz is the grandfather of David, and from David comes the Christ. This is not allegory. It is history moving toward the Messiah.
  • Typology of the redeemer: The go’el had to be a near kinsman, able to pay, and willing to redeem. The nearer kinsman in chapter 4 was able but unwilling. Boaz was both. Christ took our flesh to become our near Kinsman (Hebrews 2:11–17). He was able, being sinless and divine. He was willing, giving himself (Galatians 2:20). He paid with his own blood (Ephesians 1:7; 1 Peter 1:18–19).
  • Thematic analogy: Ruth’s request, “spread therefore thy skirt [wing] over thine handmaid” (3:9, KJV), uses the same word as Boaz’s blessing about God’s “wings” (2:12). Boaz becomes the answer to his own prayer. Scripture elsewhere pictures the LORD spreading his covering over his bride (Ezekiel 16:8), and Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem “as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings” (Matthew 23:37). Christ is the Bridegroom-Redeemer who covers his people.
  • Gentile inclusion: Ruth anticipates Ephesians 2:12–13. Those who were “strangers from the covenants of promise” are brought near by the blood of Christ.

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed doctrine of providence (WCF 5; Calvin, Institutes 1.16–17) shines in Ruth. God is mentioned mostly in the characters’ blessings and prayers, and yet he orders every “chance” meeting. John Frame’s emphasis on God’s control as covenant Lord fits well here. God’s control is not cold machinery but the loving rule of a Father who works all things for his people’s good. Ruth also shows covenant faithfulness lived out in family obligations, field work, and fair dealing at the city gate, which is the kind of whole-life covenant piety Packer commended.

For Today

You may feel more like Naomi, empty and bitter, than like Ruth. The book of Ruth was written for such seasons. God’s hand is often hidden, but it is never absent. Your Redeemer has already paid the price, spread his covering over you, and given you a name and an inheritance. Show hesed today in an ordinary place, in your work, your family, or toward a stranger. God builds his kingdom through faithful ordinary days.

Reflect

  1. Where do you need to trust God’s hidden providence in a season that feels empty?
  2. To whom can you show steadfast, covenant kindness this week, especially someone on the outside?

Pray

Lord God of Israel, under whose wings I have come to trust, thank you for your steadfast love. Thank you that Jesus became my Kinsman, able and willing to redeem me at the cost of his blood. When my life feels empty, help me trust your quiet providence. Make me loyal in love, as Ruth and Boaz were. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.”
family.context: Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount by blessing people the world rarely applauds: the spiritually needy, the grieving, the gentle, those aching for what is right. The kingdom begins with empty hands, not impressive résumés. Jesus blesses hunger, not self-sufficiency. That alone overturns many family myths about strength. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus himself lived this way—meek, mourning over sin, hungry for the Father’s will—and he fulfills righteousness for us. In him, poverty of spirit is not despair; it is the doorway into his kingdom grace. He comforts mourners because he is the Man of Sorrows who also rose; kingdom comfort is personal. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Tonight, resist the urge to impress God or each other. Admit one need honestly. Families that can say “we need Jesus” stay soft enough for his blessing to land. Admitting need together can be the most blessed moment of the week. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: Where do we feel spiritually “poor” or hungry right now, and how might that be a place Jesus wants to meet us?
family.prayer: Jesus, we come with empty hands. Comfort our mourning, teach us meekness, and satisfy our hunger for what is right in you. Amen.

devo.title: The LORD Looks on the Heart: The Rise of the Anointed King
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 1 Samuel 2:1–10 — Hannah’s song: the LORD exalts his anointed
  2. 1 Samuel 8:4–9 — “Make us a king… like all the nations”
  3. 1 Samuel 16:1–13 — David anointed: the LORD looks on the heart
  4. 1 Samuel 17:41–51 — David and Goliath: the battle is the LORD’s

New Testament fulfillment: Luke 1:46–55; Acts 13:21–23

The Book and Its Themes

1 Samuel covers the transition from judges to kings. It follows three central figures: Samuel, the last judge and a prophet; Saul, the people’s king; and David, God’s chosen king. Its themes are the reversal of fortunes (the barren woman sings, the proud fall, 2:4–8), the word of the LORD being rare and then restored (3:1, 19–21), the danger of wanting a king “like all the nations,” the difference between outward appearance and the heart (16:7), obedience over sacrifice (15:22), and the patient, suffering path by which the anointed one comes to the throne.

Where 1 Samuel Stands in the Covenant Story

Kingship itself was not the problem. Deuteronomy 17:14–20 anticipated a king, and Genesis 49:10 promised a scepter in Judah. The problem was Israel’s motive: they rejected the LORD as king and wanted security like their neighbors (8:7, 20). God gives them Saul, tall, impressive, and from Benjamin, and Saul fails through partial obedience and fear of people. Then God chooses a shepherd boy from Judah, “a man after his own heart” (13:14; Acts 13:22).

The word “anointed” (mashiach, “messiah”; Greek christos) becomes central. Hannah’s song ends with the first explicit mention in Scripture of the LORD’s “anointed” king: “he shall… exalt the horn of his anointed” (2:10, KJV). She sang it before Israel even had a king.

How 1 Samuel Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct prophetic echo: Mary’s Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55) deliberately echoes Hannah’s song. God lifts the lowly, fills the hungry, and remembers his mercy. What God began with Samuel’s birth, he completes with Jesus’ birth.
  • Typology of the anointed king: David is anointed with oil and the Spirit comes upon him (16:13). Jesus is anointed with the Spirit at his baptism (Luke 3:21–22; Acts 10:38). Like David, he was anointed long before he was enthroned and walked a road of rejection and suffering before his exaltation.
  • Typology of the representative champion: In chapter 17 one man fights for the whole people, and his victory becomes theirs. This is covenant representation. Christ is the champion who defeated our enemies, sin, death, and the devil, when we could only tremble (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15). Applying the story mainly as “defeat your own giants” misses its main thrust. We are the frightened Israelites, not David.
  • Contrast: Saul, the king who looks impressive, shows what a king like the nations becomes. Jesus had “no form nor comeliness” (Isaiah 53:2), and he is the true king after God’s heart.

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed tradition speaks of Christ’s threefold office as prophet, priest, and king (Calvin, Institutes 2.15; Westminster Shorter Catechism 23–26). 1 Samuel shows all three offices in tension. Samuel is a prophet who also offers sacrifice. Saul is a king who sins by grasping the priest’s role (13:8–14). Only in Christ do the three offices come together in one sinless person. Wayne Grudem’s Systematic Theology presents the same threefold office in a widely accessible way, showing that this teaching unites Presbyterian and Baptist Reformed writers alike.

For Today

“The LORD seeth not as man seeth” (16:7, KJV). God is not impressed by the height of your achievements, and he is not limited by the smallness of your position. Like Saul, we are often tempted toward partial obedience, doing most of what God says and keeping the “best of the sheep.” Bring to God the whole of your obedience today. And rest in your Champion, who has already won the battle that you could not fight.

Reflect

  1. Where are you tempted to want security “like all the nations” rather than trusting God as King?
  2. Do you tend to read David and Goliath as a story about your courage or about Christ’s victory? Why does it matter?

Pray

LORD, you bring low and lift up. You raise the poor from the dust. Thank you for your Anointed One, Jesus, who fought the battle I could not fight and won. Search my heart, which you see clearly. Root out my partial obedience and my fear of people. Make me wholly yours, under the rule of your King. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.”
family.context: Jesus tells his disciples they already are salt and light—not that they must invent a public brand. Salt preserves and seasons; light reveals. Hiding either wastes the gift. Salt that stays in the jar and light under a basket both fail their purpose. Jesus assumes his people will season and illuminate ordinary rooms. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the true light of the world (John 8:12). Our shining is borrowed brightness—good works that point past us to the Father. We do not shine to earn glory but because we belong to him who is light. Because he is the light, our works are meant to redirect glory to the Father, never to build a family brand of goodness. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Ask where your household’s “lamp” tends to go under a basket—kindness at home that never reaches a neighbor, faith that stays private out of fear. Choose one simple, visible good that quietly points to God this week. Keep the good deed small enough to finish and clear enough to be noticed without a speech. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What is one way our family could “give light to all in the house”—and beyond it—without showing off?
family.prayer: Father, thank you for Jesus, our light. Make us salty with grace and bright with good works that give you glory, not us. Amen.

devo.title: A House, a Throne, and a Son Forever
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 2 Samuel 7:8–17 — The Davidic covenant: a house and a throne forever
  2. 2 Samuel 11:1–5, 14–17; 12:1–13 — David’s sin, Nathan’s rebuke, David’s confession
  3. 2 Samuel 9:1–13 — Kindness to Mephibosheth for Jonathan’s sake
  4. 2 Samuel 23:1–5 — David’s last words: an everlasting covenant

New Testament fulfillment: Luke 1:30–33; Acts 2:29–36; Hebrews 1:5

The Book and Its Themes

2 Samuel tells David’s reign, its glory and its ruin. The first half (chapters 1–10) shows God establishing David, uniting the tribes, taking Jerusalem, bringing up the ark, and receiving the covenant promise. The second half (11–24) shows the consequences of David’s adultery and murder: violence and rebellion within his own household, Absalom’s revolt, and a kingdom torn. The themes are God’s sovereign grace in covenant, the reality of forgiveness and the reality of consequences, the king as representative of the people, and the hope of a greater Son.

Where 2 Samuel Stands in the Covenant Story

Chapter 7 is one of the mountain peaks of the Old Testament. David wanted to build God a house (a temple). God answered that he would build David a house (a dynasty). God promised to raise up David’s offspring, establish his kingdom forever, and be a Father to him: “I will be his father, and he shall be my son” (7:14, KJV). The Davidic covenant narrows the Abrahamic promise of a “seed” to a royal line and adds an everlasting throne. Psalm 89 and Psalm 132 sing of it. When the line of kings later collapses into exile, the prophets cling to this promise (Isaiah 9:6–7; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Amos 9:11).

How 2 Samuel Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: Gabriel tells Mary that God will give her son “the throne of his father David… and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1:32–33, KJV), almost a quotation of 2 Samuel 7:13–16. Hebrews 1:5 applies “I will be to him a Father” directly to Jesus. Peter argues at Pentecost that David, being a prophet and knowing God’s oath, foresaw the resurrection of the Christ to sit on his throne (Acts 2:30–31).
  • Fulfillment beyond the type: 7:14 also says that if the son commits iniquity, God will discipline him. Solomon and his heirs did sin. Jesus did not, yet he bore “the stripes of the children of men” for others (Isaiah 53:5). The type fails where the Antitype triumphs.
  • Thematic analogy: David’s kindness to lame Mephibosheth “for Jonathan’s sake” (9:1, 7) beautifully pictures grace shown for the sake of another. We are seated at the King’s table for Christ’s sake, though we bring nothing. This is a legitimate echo, though the text does not present it as a direct type.
  • Repentance and forgiveness: David’s confession, “I have sinned against the LORD,” and Nathan’s answer, “The LORD also hath put away thy sin” (12:13, KJV), together with Psalm 51 written in response, show justification by grace alone. David’s sin is forgiven. Its consequences remain. Romans 4:6–8 cites David as an example of the blessed man to whom God imputes righteousness without works.

Through Reformed Eyes

The Davidic promise is a focal point for discussing the future, and here the thinkers you value differ graciously. Wayne Grudem’s historic premillennialism expects Christ to reign on earth for a thousand years after his return. Doug Wilson’s postmillennialism expects the Son of David’s present reign from heaven to subdue the nations through the gospel before he returns. Calvin’s view, and much of the confessional tradition, sees Christ’s reign as present now at the Father’s right hand and consummated at his single return (Calvin rejected the chiliasts, Institutes 3.25.5). All agree that Jesus is already the enthroned Son of David (Acts 2:36) and that his kingdom will have no end.

For Today

David’s story warns that a man after God’s heart can fall terribly, especially in idle, privileged moments (11:1). But it also proclaims that no sin is beyond covenant mercy for the repentant. If you have sinned, do not hide like David at first. Confess like David at last. And take your seat at the King’s table, not because you are worthy, but for the sake of the Son.

Reflect

  1. Where might ease or idleness be setting you up for temptation, as it did David?
  2. What does it mean for your daily life that Jesus is already reigning on David’s throne?

Pray

Faithful God, you made an everlasting covenant with David, ordered in all things and sure. Thank you that Jesus, David’s greater Son, reigns now, and his kingdom will never end. Have mercy on me according to your steadfast love, and blot out my transgressions. Keep me watchful against sin. Thank you for bringing me to your table for Jesus’ sake. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment… So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.”
family.context: Jesus digs beneath the outward act of murder to the heart of contempt and unresolved anger. Worship that ignores a broken relationship is incomplete. He prioritizes reconciliation even over a religious gift already in hand. Jesus treats contempt as spiritually serious because it corrodes the image of God in our neighbor and hardens worship into theater. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the reconciler who makes peace by his blood (Colossians 1:20). He does not merely ban murder; he forms peacemakers who refuse to nurse contempt. Coming to him means letting him interrupt our worship until we seek peace. He is able to heal anger because he absorbed hostility at the cross without returning curse for curse. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: If someone in the room—or someone you will see soon—has something against you, do not wait for the “perfect moment.” Take a first step toward repair: an apology, a clarifying question, a softened tone. If reconciliation needs time, still take the first honest step tonight rather than waiting for perfect feelings. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: Is there a tension in our home or circle that Jesus would tell us to address before we move on tonight?
family.prayer: Jesus, you make peace by your cross. Soften angry hearts in us. Help us seek reconciliation quickly and honestly. Amen.

devo.title: Wisdom, Temple, and a Divided Heart
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 1 Kings 3:5–14 — Solomon asks for wisdom
  2. 1 Kings 8:22–30 — Solomon’s prayer at the temple dedication
  3. 1 Kings 11:1–13 — Solomon’s heart turned away
  4. 1 Kings 18:30–39 — Elijah on Carmel: “The LORD, he is the God”

New Testament fulfillment: Matthew 12:42; John 2:19–21

The Book and Its Themes

1 Kings begins in golden splendor and ends in division and apostasy. Solomon receives wisdom, builds the temple, and rules over peace and prosperity (chapters 1–10). Yet he multiplies wives, horses, and gold, which is exactly what Deuteronomy 17:16–17 forbade, and his heart turns to other gods (chapter 11). The kingdom splits under Rehoboam (chapter 12). Jeroboam sets up golden calves in the north, and the books measure every later king against David and against “the sin of Jeroboam.” Then comes Elijah, the prophet of fire, confronting Ahab, Jezebel, and Baal (chapters 17–22). Themes include wisdom, temple and presence, covenant faithfulness of the king as the measure of national blessing, idolatry, and the prophetic word that judges and preserves.

Where 1 Kings Stands in the Covenant Story

Under Solomon, the Abrahamic promises appear almost fulfilled. Israel is “as the sand which is by the sea in multitude” (4:20, KJV), the land reaches its widest borders, and nations come to hear wisdom (4:34; 10:1–9). The temple realizes the promise of God’s dwelling. Yet Solomon himself confesses that “the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house” (8:27, KJV). The golden age collapses because no son of David so far has kept covenant faithfully. The Davidic promise survives “for David my servant’s sake” (11:12–13). Grace preserves a lamp in Jerusalem even when the king fails.

How 1 Kings Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct claim of Jesus: “A greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). Jesus is the wise Son of David who “is made unto us wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:30) and in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom (Colossians 2:3). Unlike Solomon, his heart never turned.
  • Temple fulfillment: Solomon’s prayer asks God to hear when sinners pray “toward this place” (8:29–30). Jesus speaks of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21). He is now the meeting place of God and humanity. We pray in his name, and God hears.
  • Typology of the prophet: Elijah’s ministry is picked up in the New Testament in two ways. John the Baptist comes “in the spirit and power of Elias” (Luke 1:17). Jesus’ own ministry echoes Elijah’s, for example in raising a widow’s son (1 Kings 17:17–24; Luke 7:11–17). On Carmel, fire falls on the sacrifice instead of on the people. At Calvary, the judgment of God fell on the Sacrifice so that the people could live.
  • Contrast: Solomon’s many marriages pulled his heart to idols. Christ has one bride, the church, and he sanctifies her (Ephesians 5:25–27).

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin’s well-known observation that the human heart is a perpetual “forge” or “factory” of idols (Institutes 1.11.8; the wording differs by translation) is vividly illustrated in Solomon and Jeroboam. Even wisdom and blessing can become idols if they are loved more than the Giver. John Frame’s work on the second commandment, in The Doctrine of the Christian Life, stresses that God alone has the right to define how he is worshiped. Jeroboam’s calves were “worship” designed for political convenience. Elijah’s question, “How long halt ye between two opinions?” (18:21, KJV), still presses every heart.

For Today

Solomon began by asking for wisdom and ended with a divided heart. Gifts, success, and even spiritual privileges can draw your affection away from God. Long faithfulness matters more than a brilliant start. Ask today for the wisdom of the One greater than Solomon, and for an undivided heart (Psalm 86:11). Pray toward the true temple: Jesus Christ, in whom you are always heard.

Reflect

  1. What good gift in your life most threatens to become a rival to God?
  2. Where do you need to stop “halting between two opinions” and choose the Lord wholeheartedly?

Pray

LORD, the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, and yet you have come near in Jesus Christ. Thank you for the One greater than Solomon, who is my wisdom, righteousness, and redemption. Unite my heart to fear your name. Burn up every idol I have set beside you. Keep me faithful to the end, not only at the beginning. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.”
family.context: Jesus overturns the instinct to reserve love for allies. He ties enemy-love to the Father’s generous character—sun and rain given without favoritism—and to the family resemblance of those who belong to him. Enemy-love is one of Jesus’ most distinctive teachings. It reveals the Father’s generous character more than our natural instincts ever will. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus practiced this to the end, praying for those who crucified him. Loving enemies is possible because we have first been loved as former rebels reconciled by his grace. We pray for opponents as children reflecting our Father. We can pray for difficult people because Jesus intercedes for us and has already loved us at our worst. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: “Enemy” at home may mean a difficult coworker, a harsh relative, or someone who embarrassed you. Pray for them by name tonight—not a performance, a release of bitterness into Jesus’ care. Keep the prayer short and sincere. Bitterness loosens when we place a name in the Father’s care. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: Who is hard for us to love right now, and what would praying for them sound like in one sentence?
family.prayer: Father, your sun rises on us by mercy. Through Jesus, teach us to love those who oppose us and to pray for them with honest hearts. Amen.

devo.title: Exile and a Lamp That Does Not Go Out
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 2 Kings 2:9–15 — Elijah taken up and Elisha receiving the Spirit
  2. 2 Kings 5:1–14 — Naaman the Syrian cleansed
  3. 2 Kings 17:7–18 — Why Israel went into exile
  4. 2 Kings 25:27–30 — Jehoiachin lifted up in Babylon

New Testament fulfillment: Luke 4:24–27; Luke 7:11–17

The Book and Its Themes

2 Kings continues the history from Elisha’s ministry to the fall of both kingdoms. The northern kingdom (Israel) falls to Assyria in 722 BC (chapter 17). The southern kingdom (Judah) has reforms under Hezekiah and Josiah, but falls to Babylon in 586 BC. The temple is burned and the people are exiled (chapter 25). The themes are the power of the prophetic word, God’s grace reaching outsiders (Naaman, the Shunammite woman), the long patience of God, the certainty of judgment when warnings are rejected, and the stubborn survival of David’s line.

Where 2 Kings Stands in the Covenant Story

Chapter 17 is a theological sermon explaining the exile. Israel “would not hear, but hardened their necks” (17:14, KJV), and the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 came to pass. Yet the book ends with a quiet ray of hope. Jehoiachin, the exiled son of David, is lifted out of prison and eats at the king’s table “all the days of his life” (25:29–30). The lamp of David has not gone out. The covenant promise of 2 Samuel 7 hangs by a thread, but it is God’s thread.

How 2 Kings Leads Us to Christ

  • Jesus’ own use: In his first sermon at Nazareth, Jesus cited Elisha’s healing of Naaman, a Gentile, as a sign of grace flowing beyond Israel (Luke 4:27). This enraged his hearers. Naaman had to humble himself and wash in the Jordan, as he was told. He had to come with empty hands, and his flesh became “like unto the flesh of a little child” (5:14, KJV).
  • Typology of resurrection and miracles: Elisha raised the Shunammite’s son (4:32–37), multiplied bread for a hundred men with some left over (4:42–44), and his very bones revived a dead man (13:21). Jesus raised the widow’s son at Nain, very near Shunem (Luke 7:11–17), fed thousands with leftovers to spare, and himself rose from the dead. Elisha points forward. Jesus fulfills.
  • Spirit transfer: Elijah ascends, and Elisha receives a double portion of his spirit (2:9–15). Jesus ascends and pours out the Holy Spirit on his church (Acts 1:9; 2:33). This is a thematic parallel that Luke seems to shape deliberately, though the New Testament does not label it as a type.
  • Hope of the King: The exiled king eating at the table points ahead to the restoration of David’s house in the Messiah (Amos 9:11; Acts 15:16).
