  2. What does it mean to you today that God says, “I will remember their sin no more”?

Pray

Fountain of living waters, forgive me for forsaking you and digging broken cisterns. Thank you for the new covenant in Jesus’ blood. Write your law on my heart. Let me know you truly. Thank you that you remember my sins no more. Jesus, the LORD our Righteousness, clothe me in your righteousness today. Amen.

family.scriptureText: For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
family.context: Paul argues that faith unites diverse people into one family. Baptism language—“put on Christ”—pictures being wrapped in Jesus’ identity so old status ladders lose their power to divide. Putting on Christ relativizes every hierarchy that divides the family of faith. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the clothing of our true self. Oneness in him does not erase difference; it relativizes rankings that fracture community. Faith in Christ makes us God’s children together. Oneness in Jesus is a gift to protect, especially where personality or preference usually wins. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Notice ranking habits at home: who “matters more,” who must always yield, who always wins. Practice treating each person as equally clothed with Christ—equal dignity, shared belonging. Compliment a difference in someone at home as a gift to the body, not a threat to sameness. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: How can remembering we have “put on Christ” change the way we talk to and about each other?
family.prayer: Jesus, we put you on by faith. Make us one in you. Strip away rankings that divide, and dress our home in your grace. Amen.

devo.title: Great Is Thy Faithfulness in the Ruins
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Lamentations 1:1–12 — The desolate city: “Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by?”
  2. Lamentations 3:19–33 — “His compassions fail not… great is thy faithfulness”
  3. Lamentations 3:40–58 — “Let us search and try our ways”
  4. Lamentations 5:15–22 — “Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD”

New Testament fulfillment: Luke 19:41–44; 2 Corinthians 1:3–5

The Book and Its Themes

Lamentations is five poems of grief over Jerusalem’s destruction by Babylon in 586 BC. Tradition attributes them to Jeremiah. Four of the poems are acrostics, with each verse or stanza beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapter 3 triples it. The form itself expresses grief “from A to Z,” ordered and complete. The themes are the horror of judgment (the city is like a widow, children starve, the temple is defiled), the honest acknowledgment that God is righteous and the people have sinned (1:18), raw lament addressed to God, and at the very center of the book a rising confession of hope: “It is of the LORD’S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness” (3:22–23, KJV).

Where Lamentations Stands in the Covenant Story

Lamentations is the covenant curse experienced. What Deuteronomy 28 threatened has happened. Yet Lamentations does not abandon the covenant. It appeals to it. The hope of chapter 3 rests on God’s hesed (steadfast covenant love) and his faithfulness. Even the final, unresolved prayer, “Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned” (5:21, KJV), anticipates the new-covenant gift of a heart turned by grace. Reformed theology calls this sovereign, effectual grace: God must turn us before we can turn.

How Lamentations Leads Us to Christ

  • Thematic fulfillment (the Weeper): Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold its destruction in A.D. 70 (Luke 19:41–44). He is the compassionate Lord whose heart breaks over his people’s ruin.
  • Typology of the afflicted man: Chapter 3 begins, “I am the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath” (3:1, KJV). The speaker represents the suffering community. Christian readers have long heard in this an anticipation of Christ, who bore the rod of God’s wrath, not for his own sin, but for ours (Isaiah 53:4–6). In chapter 3 the poet speaks of bitterness, wormwood, and gall (3:15, 19), and his enemies “hiss” and mock (2:15–16). These echoes resonate with the passion, but they are typological and thematic rather than explicit prophecy.
  • Devotional application of 1:12: “Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow” (KJV). Originally these are the words of Jerusalem personified. The church has long sung them on Good Friday as an echo of Christ’s sufferings. This is a fitting devotional application, but not the verse’s original meaning, and the New Testament does not quote it this way.
  • Morning mercies: The compassion that does not fail is secured at the cross. Because the full wrath fell on Christ, God’s mercy toward those in him is new every morning (Romans 8:1, 32).

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed tradition, sometimes caricatured as cold, has deep resources for lament. Calvin’s commentaries on Jeremiah and Lamentations treat affliction as the fatherly discipline of God for his children (compare Institutes 3.8 on bearing the cross). J. I. Packer, in Knowing God, writes about God’s goodness and his severity, and about the comfort of God’s unchanging character. That is the theology of Lamentations 3. The hymn “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” (Thomas Chisholm, 1923) brought these verses into the church’s worship.

For Today

You are allowed to lament. Scripture gives you five chapters of it. Bring your grief to God in ordered, honest words. Then, in the middle of the ruins, recall: “This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope” (3:21, KJV). The mercies of God did not run out yesterday. They are new this morning, because Christ has drunk the cup of wrath to the dregs.

Reflect

  1. What loss or grief do you need to bring to God in honest lament rather than hiding it?
  2. What specific truths about God’s character can you “recall to mind” when hope feels thin?

Pray

LORD, your compassions fail not. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness. I bring you the ruins in my life and in the world, and I confess my sin where it has contributed. Thank you that Jesus bore the rod of your wrath so that I might know only fatherly mercy. Turn me to yourself, and I will be turned. Amen.

family.scriptureText: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
family.context: Paul roots daily mindset in resurrection union: raised with Christ, dead to the old self, life hidden securely with him until glory appears. Identity is both present and not yet fully revealed. Hidden life with Christ is security when public life feels unstable or unseen. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Christ is our life—not an accessory to life. Hidden with him means safety and destiny are locked in God’s keeping. Seeking “things above” means orienting desire toward the risen Jesus who reigns. Seeking things above is desire directed toward the reigning Jesus, not escape from earth’s responsibilities. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: When image, achievement, or online comparison feel like your real life, remember: your life is hidden with Christ. Choose one earthly fixation to loosen your grip on tonight. Loosen one earthly fixation by naming Christ’s life as your deeper identity. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: What earthly thing most easily becomes our “life,” and how does Jesus being our life free us?
family.prayer: Risen Jesus, you are our life. Lift our minds to where you are. Keep us hidden with you in God until we appear with you in glory. Amen.

devo.title: The Glory Departs and Returns: Hearts of Flesh and Dry Bones Alive
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Ezekiel 1:26–28 — The likeness of the glory of the LORD
  2. Ezekiel 34:11–24 — “I myself will search for my sheep”; one Shepherd, my servant David
  3. Ezekiel 36:24–28 — A new heart and a new spirit
  4. Ezekiel 37:1–14 — The valley of dry bones

New Testament fulfillment: John 10:11–16; John 3:3–8

The Book and Its Themes

Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in the first deportation (597 BC). There, by the river Chebar, he saw visions of God’s glory on a throne-chariot (chapter 1). He was commissioned as a watchman (3:17; 33:7) and performed strange sign-acts: lying on his side, eating siege bread, and shaving his head. He saw the glory of the LORD depart from the defiled temple (chapters 8–11) before Jerusalem’s fall. After the fall (chapter 33) his message turned to hope: a true Shepherd, a new heart, dry bones raised, a reunited people, victory over Gog, and a visionary new temple from which a river of life flows (chapters 40–48). The book ends, “The LORD is there” (48:35, KJV). Its themes are God’s glory and holiness, the purpose that nations “shall know that I am the LORD” (repeated over 60 times), individual responsibility (chapter 18), judgment, and resurrection-renewal by the Spirit.

Where Ezekiel Stands in the Covenant Story

Ezekiel explains the exile theologically. God’s presence cannot remain amid idolatry, so the glory leaves (10:18–19; 11:22–23). But God is not finished. He promises to act “for mine holy name’s sake” (36:22). He will cleanse his people, give them a new heart and his Spirit, cause them to walk in his statutes, and be their God (36:25–28). This is the same new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31, now with explicit emphasis on the Spirit. He will make “a covenant of peace… an everlasting covenant” and set his sanctuary among them forever (37:26–27).

How Ezekiel Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment (the Shepherd): God says, “I, even I, will both search my sheep,” and also, “I will set up one shepherd over them… my servant David” (34:11, 23, KJV). Both are fulfilled when Jesus says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). He is the LORD himself coming to seek the lost (Luke 19:10), and the Son of David ruling his flock.
  • Fulfillment by the Spirit: Jesus told Nicodemus, “Ye must be born again… of water and of the Spirit” (John 3:5–7, KJV). As “a master of Israel” (3:10), Nicodemus should have known Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises to sprinkle clean water and put his Spirit within. Regeneration is Ezekiel’s promise fulfilled in Christ’s ministry.
  • Resurrection: The dry bones (37:1–14) primarily depict the national restoration of exiled Israel (“these bones are the whole house of Israel,” 37:11). They also reveal a God who raises the dead by his word and Spirit. That anticipates both spiritual regeneration (Ephesians 2:1–5) and the bodily resurrection secured by Christ (John 5:25–29).
  • The glory and the temple: The glory that departed returns in Ezekiel’s vision (43:1–5). In the New Testament it returns in Jesus (John 1:14), dwells in the church by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16), and fills the new creation, which has no temple “for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it” (Revelation 21:22, KJV). The river of Ezekiel 47 flows again in Revelation 22:1–2.

Through Reformed Eyes

Ezekiel 36–37 is one of the clearest Old Testament pictures of what Reformed theology calls monergistic regeneration: God alone gives life to the spiritually dead (WCF 10.1–2; Calvin, Institutes 2.3.6–10; Grudem’s chapter on regeneration). Interpretation of Ezekiel 40–48 divides readers. Most confessional Reformed interpreters read the visionary temple as symbolically fulfilled in Christ, the church, and the new creation. (Calvin’s own Ezekiel lectures ended at chapter 20 when he died.) Dispensational readers expect a literal future temple. Historic premillennialists like Grudem differ from dispensationalists on many points, so don’t assume every premillennialist reads Ezekiel 40–48 the same way. All Reformed readers affirm that Christ’s sacrifice is final (Hebrews 10:12–14).

For Today

Perhaps parts of your life feel like a valley of dry bones: a cold heart, a dead relationship, a church in decline. The question is still, “Can these bones live?” The answer is still, “O Lord GOD, thou knowest” (37:3, KJV). Speak God’s word over the dry places and pray for the breath of the Spirit. The Good Shepherd is searching for his sheep, and the One who raised Jesus from the dead gives life.

Reflect

  1. Where do you most need the Spirit to give you a “heart of flesh” in place of stone?
  2. Who is a “lost sheep” you can pray for and seek in the name of the Good Shepherd this week?

Pray

Sovereign LORD, for the sake of your holy name, cleanse me from all my idols. Take away my heart of stone and give me a heart of flesh. Put your Spirit within me and cause me to walk in your ways. Good Shepherd, search for your scattered sheep. Breathe on the dry bones of your church. Amen.

family.scriptureText: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law. And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
family.context: Fruit grows; it is not a costume. Paul lists what the Spirit produces in people who belong to Christ, then calls them to keep in step—active cooperation with the life already given. Fruit lists are not ladders; they are harvest descriptions of Spirit-life in those who belong to Jesus. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with him. The Spirit applies Jesus’ victory, growing his character in us. Fruit is evidence of union, not a ladder to reach him. Keeping in step implies rhythm—daily cooperation with the Spirit who applies Christ’s victory. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Pick one fruit your household especially needs this week—patience or gentleness, for example. Ask the Spirit for help in a specific recurring moment (bedtime, transitions, disagreements). Choose the recurring flashpoint and ask for one fruit by name before you enter it tomorrow. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: Which fruit of the Spirit do we most need to keep in step with right now, and where will it be tested?
family.prayer: Holy Spirit, we belong to Christ Jesus. Grow your fruit in us. Help us keep in step with you in the ordinary pressures of our days. Amen.

devo.title: The Kingdom That Shall Never Be Destroyed
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Daniel 2:31–45 — The statue and the stone that becomes a mountain
  2. Daniel 3:16–28 — The fiery furnace: a fourth man in the fire
  3. Daniel 6:10–23 — Daniel prays; the lions’ mouths are shut
  4. Daniel 7:9–14 — The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man

New Testament fulfillment: Mark 14:61–62; Matthew 28:18–20

The Book and Its Themes

Daniel was carried to Babylon as a youth (605 BC) and served in pagan courts through the rise of Persia. Chapters 1–6 are court stories of faithful exiles: Daniel’s diet, Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, the fiery furnace, the king’s humbling madness, the writing on the wall, and the lions’ den. Chapters 7–12 are apocalyptic visions of beasts, kingdoms, the Son of Man, seventy weeks, and final resurrection. The book is written partly in Aramaic (2:4–7:28) and partly in Hebrew. The key theme is that “the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men” (4:17, KJV). Other themes include faithfulness in a hostile culture, prayer, the rise and fall of empires, suffering before vindication, and the everlasting kingdom of God.

Where Daniel Stands in the Covenant Story

Daniel prays in exile on the basis of covenant promise. His great prayer in chapter 9 appeals to the God “keeping the covenant and mercy” (9:4, KJV) and to Jeremiah’s seventy years (9:2). The answer opens a much longer horizon. Restoration and the full end of sin will come through an “anointed one” in God’s timing (9:24–27). The interpretation of the seventy weeks is notoriously debated, and wise readers hold the details humbly. The big picture is clear: Babylon, Persia, Greece, and their successors rise and fall, but God will set up a kingdom “which shall never be destroyed” (2:44).

How Daniel Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct self-identification by Jesus: “Son of Man” was Jesus’ favorite self-designation. Before the high priest he combined Psalm 110 and Daniel 7:13. He said they would see “the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62, KJV). The high priest called it blasphemy, because Jesus was claiming the divine-human figure who receives everlasting dominion from the Ancient of Days.
  • Fulfillment of the kingdom: The stone “cut out without hands” that strikes the statue and becomes a mountain filling the earth (2:34–35, 44–45) is the kingdom of God, inaugurated by Christ. After his resurrection Jesus said, “All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth” (Matthew 28:18). That is Daniel 7:14 language, and the Great Commission is the mountain growing.
  • Typology of the faithful exile: Daniel was faithful under pressure, falsely accused, condemned to death by an irrevocable law, placed in a pit sealed with a stone, and brought out alive at dawn. The parallels to Jesus’ passion and resurrection are striking. They are best read as typological echoes rather than intended prophecy.
  • Christ in the fire: Nebuchadnezzar saw a fourth figure “like the Son of God” (3:25, KJV; others “a son of the gods”). Many Christian interpreters see a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ here. Others see an angel (3:28). Either way, the passage reveals a God who is present with his people in the fire (Isaiah 43:2), and that presence is fulfilled in Immanuel.

Through Reformed Eyes

Daniel is a frequent battleground for millennial views, and your favorite teachers diverge here. Wilson’s postmillennialism reads the stone filling the earth (Daniel 2) as the gradual, gospel-driven triumph of Christ’s kingdom in history. Grudem’s historic premillennialism expects the kingdom to be visibly consummated in a thousand-year reign after Christ’s return. Calvin’s approach, which most closely resembles what is now called amillennialism, sees the kingdom as present in Christ’s heavenly reign and the church, consummated at his single return. All share the conviction of 4:34–35: God’s dominion is everlasting, and none can stay his hand. Frame’s lordship emphasis captures the book’s heart. God controls history, speaks with authority through his prophets, and is present with his people in exile.

For Today

You live as an exile in a culture that does not share your King. Daniel shows how: serve faithfully, refuse idolatry, pray openly and regularly (“three times a day… as he did aforetime,” 6:10, KJV), and trust God with the outcome. “If not,” the faithful still will not bow (3:18). The Son of Man already has all authority. Your faithfulness today belongs to an unshakable kingdom.

Reflect

  1. What “Babylonian” pressures in your workplace or culture press you to compromise, and where must you quietly refuse to bow?
  2. How does the vision of the Son of Man’s everlasting dominion steady you when the news is troubling?

Pray

Most High God, you rule in the kingdom of men and give it to whom you will. Your kingdom is everlasting. Thank you for Jesus, the Son of Man, who has received all authority. Give me Daniel’s faithfulness in prayer and his courage under pressure. Be with me in every fire. Let the stone of your kingdom grow until it fills the earth. Amen.

family.scriptureText: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body… and all were made to drink of one Spirit. For the body does not consist of one member but of many… Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.
family.context: Paul corrects a divided church by pointing to the body: diversity of members, unity of life. The Spirit immerses believers into Christ’s body; no one is self-sufficient, and no gift is the whole story. Paul’s body metaphor protects both unity and diversity. Christ is not reduced to one gifted personality. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: The church is “so… with Christ”—joined to him as head and life. Belonging to Jesus means belonging to his people. Individual faith is real, yet never isolated from his body. Drinking of one Spirit means shared life from Jesus, not forced identical roles. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Affirm one another’s different strengths without ranking them. Ask how your household can honor the wider body of Christ—praying for your church, serving, welcoming someone who feels on the margins. Pray for your church as Christ’s body, not as a vendor of religious goods. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: How do we need each other’s different gifts at home and in church, the way a body needs many members?
family.prayer: Jesus, we are members of your body by one Spirit. Teach us to honor every part and to live as one in you. Amen.

devo.title: The Faithful Husband of an Unfaithful Bride
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Hosea 1:2–11 — Hosea’s marriage and the children’s names
  2. Hosea 2:14–23 — “I will betroth thee unto me for ever”
  3. Hosea 11:1–9 — “When Israel was a child, then I loved him”
  4. Hosea 14:1–9 — “O Israel, return unto the LORD”

New Testament fulfillment: Matthew 2:13–15; Romans 9:25–26; 1 Peter 2:10

The Book and Its Themes

Hosea prophesied to the northern kingdom in its last prosperous, corrupt decades before Assyria destroyed it in 722 BC. God commanded him to marry Gomer, who proved unfaithful. Their children’s names announced judgment: Jezreel (God scatters), Lo-ruhamah (no mercy), Lo-ammi (not my people). Later God told Hosea to buy back his adulterous wife and love her again (3:1–3). The marriage became a living sermon. Israel had played the harlot with Baal, but God would allure her back, and the names would be reversed: “I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people” (2:23, KJV). The themes are God’s covenant love (hesed), spiritual adultery, the lack of “knowledge of God” (4:1, 6), empty religion (“I desired mercy, and not sacrifice,” 6:6), judgment, and God’s anguished, unstoppable compassion (11:8–9).

Where Hosea Stands in the Covenant Story

Hosea portrays the covenant as a marriage. Israel’s sin is adultery, not just lawbreaking. It is a broken relationship. Hosea 6:7 says, “they like men [Adam] have transgressed the covenant” (KJV, with margin). The verse is debated, but many Reformed theologians, including Grudem in his chapter on the covenants, cite it in support of an Adamic covenant. God’s response to the broken covenant is not merely to enforce its penalties, but to woo his bride back and betroth her “in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies… in faithfulness” (2:19–20, KJV).

Hosea also speaks to the question of covenant membership raised earlier in Numbers. Israel was in covenant and was unfaithful, and God judged real covenant breakers. Doug Wilson’s “objective covenant” emphasis draws heavily on this kind of marriage imagery, as his own illustration of an adulterous husband who remains a husband shows. Critics, including the PCA’s 2007 report, have urged that this emphasis not blur the distinction between outward covenant membership and the elect’s saving union with Christ, which cannot be lost. Both sides would agree that Hosea’s main point is God’s astonishing faithfulness to an unfaithful people.

How Hosea Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct apostolic fulfillment: Matthew quotes Hosea 11:1, “Out of Egypt have I called my son,” as fulfilled when the infant Jesus returns from Egypt (Matthew 2:15). This is typological fulfillment. Israel, God’s son, was called out of Egypt and then failed. Jesus, the true Son, recapitulates Israel’s story and succeeds.
  • Gentile inclusion: Paul and Peter apply the reversal of “not my people” to Gentiles brought into God’s people through Christ (Romans 9:25–26; 1 Peter 2:10). Hosea’s mercy reaches further than Hosea saw.
  • Typology of the redeeming husband: Hosea bought back his wife for silver and barley (3:2). Christ bought his bride “not with corruptible things, as silver and gold… But with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19, KJV). He loved the church and gave himself for her (Ephesians 5:25).
  • Resurrection hope: “After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up” (6:2, KJV). Some interpreters hear an echo of the third-day resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:4, “according to the scriptures”). Others are more cautious. It is an echo worth hearing, not a proof text. Hosea 13:14 (“O death, I will be thy plagues”) is directly echoed in 1 Corinthians 15:55.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin wrote a full commentary on Hosea. The Reformed tradition has found in Hosea a vivid portrait of the “perseverance of the saints,” which is grounded in the perseverance of God: “How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?” (11:8, KJV). Packer’s emphasis on God’s covenant love as personal commitment (“I will be your God”) is enacted here in a marriage. Jesus twice quoted Hosea 6:6 against religious formalism (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). It is a warning for any tradition, including the Reformed, that values right doctrine but neglects mercy.

For Today

You are Gomer before you are Hosea. Name your idols honestly: comfort, approval, control, or money. Then hear God speak “comfortably” to you in the wilderness (2:14). He has paid the price to bring you home. Return to him today with words: “Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously” (14:2, KJV). His love is not tired of you.

Reflect

  1. In what ways have you been unfaithful to God, giving your heart to lesser lovers?
  2. How does God’s anguished love in Hosea 11:8–9 change your picture of how he feels toward you when you have strayed?

Pray

Faithful God, I have been an unfaithful bride, and still you pursue me. Thank you that Jesus bought me back, not with silver, but with his precious blood. Speak tenderly to me, betroth me to yourself in faithfulness, and let me know you, the LORD. Heal my backsliding, and love me freely. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
family.context: Ambassadors speak for another’s kingdom. Paul’s message is urgent reconciliation. The basis is stunning: the sinless Christ made sin for us, that we might become God’s righteousness in him. Ambassadors do not invent the message; they carry the King’s appeal. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is both the content and the king of the appeal. He knew no sin, yet was treated as sin for our sake. In him we receive righteousness we could never manufacture—and then we speak his peace to others. The great exchange—Christ made sin, we become righteousness in him—is the heart of reconciliation. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Think of one relationship still needing reconciliation—with God or another person. Let Christ’s exchange (our sin for his righteousness) humble pride and fuel a gentle appeal, not a lecture. Let humility from that exchange shape how you invite someone toward peace. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: As ambassadors for Christ, what appeal of reconciliation is God making through our family right now?
family.prayer: God, you made Christ sin for our sake that we might become your righteousness in him. Make your appeal through us—reconcile us and send us as peacemakers. Amen.

devo.title: The Day of the LORD and the Outpoured Spirit
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Joel 1:1–4, 13–15 — The locust plague and the call to lament
  2. Joel 2:12–14 — “Rend your heart, and not your garments”
  3. Joel 2:25–32 — Years restored; the Spirit poured out on all flesh
  4. Joel 3:14–18 — The valley of decision; the LORD dwelling in Zion

New Testament fulfillment: Acts 2:14–21, 38–39; Romans 10:12–13

The Book and Its Themes

Joel is short and urgent. Its date is uncertain. A devastating locust plague has stripped the land (chapter 1). Joel reads it as a warning sign of “the day of the LORD,” the day of God’s decisive intervention in judgment and salvation. He calls priests and people to fast, weep, and return to God, who is “gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness” (2:13, KJV, echoing Exodus 34:6). God answers with promises: he will restore “the years that the locust hath eaten” (2:25), pour out his Spirit on all flesh (2:28–29), save all who call on his name (2:32), judge the nations (chapter 3), and dwell in Zion with his people forever (3:17–21). The themes are judgment as a call to repentance, true inward repentance, the abundant restoration of grace, the Spirit, and the day of the LORD.

Where Joel Stands in the Covenant Story

Joel stands in the Mosaic covenant pattern: disaster, repentance, restoration (Deuteronomy 28–30; 2 Chronicles 7:13–14). But he stretches beyond it. Moses had wished “that all the LORD’S people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them!” (Numbers 11:29, KJV). Joel promises exactly that for “all flesh,” including sons and daughters, old and young, and male and female servants. The Spirit, once given to select leaders, will be poured out on the whole covenant community. This is a hallmark of the new covenant (Ezekiel 36:27; Jeremiah 31:34).

How Joel Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct apostolic fulfillment: At Pentecost, Peter declared, “this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16, KJV) and quoted Joel 2:28–32. The risen and exalted Christ received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:33). Joel’s “last days” began with Christ’s resurrection and ascension.
  • Salvation by calling on the name: “Whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered” (2:32, KJV). Peter applies this to calling on Jesus (Acts 2:21, 36–38). Paul applies it to confessing Jesus as Lord, for both Jew and Gentile (Romans 10:9–13). The “LORD” (Yahweh) of Joel is identified with Jesus, which is a powerful New Testament witness to Christ’s deity.
  • The day of the LORD: The darkened sun (2:31) echoes in the darkness at the cross (Luke 23:44–45) and in Jesus’ teaching on his return (Matthew 24:29). The day of the LORD fell on Christ at Calvary in judgment, so that those who call on him might be saved in the final day.
  • Thematic analogy: “Restore… the years that the locust hath eaten” (2:25) is an Old Testament promise to Judah of agricultural restoration. Christians legitimately take comfort from it as an expression of God’s restoring character, fulfilled ultimately in the new creation, where every loss is made good (Revelation 21:4–5).

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin taught that the Holy Spirit is the bond by which Christ effectually unites us to himself (Institutes 3.1.1). Joel’s promise is the Old Testament root of this. The Spirit poured out by Christ is how we receive Christ. Your favorite teachers do differ about the Spirit’s gifts today. Wayne Grudem is a well-known continuationist who argues that gifts like prophecy continue (see his The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today, rev. ed. 2000). Many confessional Reformed theologians are cessationist, or at least cautious, about the miraculous gifts. Packer took a nuanced position in Keep in Step with the Spirit (1984). They share the essentials: the Spirit is poured out on all believers, regenerates, unites to Christ, sanctifies, and empowers witness.

For Today

“Rend your heart, and not your garments” (2:13). God is not impressed by religious display. He looks for real repentance, and he is quick to meet it with grace. Whatever “locust years” lie behind you, years wasted by sin or stolen by suffering, call on the name of the Lord Jesus today. The Spirit he has poured out is at work in you, and he restores.

Reflect

  1. Where are you tempted to “rend your garments,” to look repentant, without truly rending your heart?
  2. How might the Spirit’s outpouring on “all flesh” (young, old, men, women, servants) shape how you value every believer in your church?

Pray

LORD, you are gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. I return to you with my whole heart. Thank you that Jesus, exalted at your right hand, has poured out your Spirit on all who call on his name. Fill me with your Spirit. Restore the years the locusts have eaten. Make me ready for the day of the Lord. Amen.

family.scriptureText: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit. And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. And his delight shall be in the fear of the Lord.
family.context: Isaiah speaks into a season when David’s royal line looked like a cut-down stump. Hope would not be human optimism; it would be a shoot God causes to grow—a king uniquely filled with the Spirit. Stump imagery tells the truth about devastation; shoot imagery tells the truth about God’s future. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is that shoot from Jesse—David’s greater Son, anointed with the Spirit at his baptism, delighting to honor the Father. Advent hope is personal: not a vague light, but Jesus himself growing God’s promise into fruit. Jesus’ Spirit-anointed life is the fruit Isaiah foresaw—wisdom, counsel, might, holy fear. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Where something in your life feels like a stump—tired plans, strained relationships—ask God to grow hope through Jesus, not through denial. Name the stump and the shoot together in prayer. Hope is allowed to be small at first, like a shoot, as long as it is rooted in him. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What feels cut down in our world or home, and how does Jesus as the Spirit-anointed King give us real hope?
family.prayer: Father, from Jesse’s stump you brought forth Jesus. Rest your Spirit’s wisdom on our waiting. Grow hope in us that bears fruit in him. Amen.

devo.title: Let Justice Roll Down, and David's Tent Be Raised
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Amos 3:1–8 — “You only have I known… therefore I will punish you”
  2. Amos 5:4–15, 21–24 — “Seek me, and ye shall live”; “let judgment run down as waters”
  3. Amos 8:4–12 — A famine of hearing the words of the LORD
  4. Amos 9:11–15 — The fallen tabernacle of David raised up

New Testament fulfillment: Acts 15:13–18; Matthew 23:23

The Book and Its Themes

Amos was “among the herdmen of Tekoa” (1:1, KJV) and a dresser of sycamore figs. He was not a professional prophet (7:14). God sent him from Judah to the prosperous northern kingdom of Israel about 760 BC, during the reign of Jeroboam II. Israel was wealthy, religious, and confident, but the rich lived in ivory houses while they “sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes” (2:6, KJV). Amos begins with oracles against the surrounding nations, which surely drew applause, and then turns the same judgment on Judah and Israel (chapters 1–2). His themes are God’s sovereignty over all nations, the greater responsibility of the privileged (“You only have I known,” 3:2), social justice as covenant faithfulness, the emptiness of worship without righteousness (5:21–24), the day of the LORD as darkness for the complacent (5:18–20), and, at the very end, the restoration of David’s fallen house.

Where Amos Stands in the Covenant Story

Amos is a covenant lawsuit. Israel’s oppression of the poor violated the Mosaic laws (Exodus 22:21–27; Deuteronomy 24:10–22). Their feasts and offerings, commanded in Leviticus, had become hateful to God because they were separated from justice and mercy. Covenant privilege does not grant immunity. It increases accountability (3:2; compare Luke 12:48). Yet the book does not end in judgment. God will “raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen” (9:11), restore his people, and include “all the heathen, which are called by my name” (9:12, KJV).

How Amos Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct apostolic fulfillment: At the Jerusalem Council, James quoted Amos 9:11–12 to explain why Gentiles were coming to faith without circumcision. God was rebuilding David’s fallen tent so that “the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles” (Acts 15:16–17, KJV, following the Greek Old Testament). The risen Son of David is that rebuilt house, and the multiethnic church is its fruit.
  • Fulfillment of justice: Jesus came “to preach the gospel to the poor” (Luke 4:18). He rebuked those who tithed mint “and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” (Matthew 23:23, KJV). That is pure Amos. At the cross, God’s justice and mercy met. Sin was truly punished, and sinners were truly forgiven (Romans 3:25–26).
  • The famine of the word: Amos warned of a famine “of hearing the words of the LORD” (8:11). After centuries of prophetic silence, the Word himself became flesh (John 1:14). Christ is the bread that ends the famine (John 6:35).
  • Thematic analogy: Darkness at noon (8:9) is a picture of judgment. It finds a striking echo at the crucifixion, when darkness covered the land from the sixth to the ninth hour (Mark 15:33). Judgment fell on Christ at midday so that the light might dawn for us.

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed tradition holds that true faith produces works of love and justice. The Westminster Confession says that good works are “the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith” (WCF 16.2). Calvin preached and wrote with deep concern for the poor, and Geneva’s deacons organized relief for refugees. John Frame’s ethics (The Doctrine of the Christian Life, 2008) applies the commandments to economics and justice. Wayne Grudem has written at length on economics and poverty from a free-market perspective (for example, The Poverty of Nations, with Barry Asmus, 2013). Doug Wilson has also written on economics and culture from a strongly Reformed, often contrarian standpoint. These teachers differ in their political and economic conclusions, but all of them would say with Amos that God hates worship that ignores justice. They would also say that the final answer to injustice is the reign of the Son of David.

For Today

This completes the first thirty books, Genesis through Amos. Across them, you have watched one covenant story unfold. God promised a Seed, called a people, gave his law, dwelt among them, raised up kings and prophets, judged and restored, and kept pointing forward to Jesus. Amos asks whether your worship and your life match. Seek the Lord and live. Let justice and mercy flow from you like a river, in your business, your family, and your community. Do it not to earn God’s favor, but because the Son of David has raised you up and made you his.

Reflect

  1. Is there a gap between your Sunday worship and your weekday treatment of people, especially the poor and powerless?
  2. Looking back over these thirty days, what single truth about Christ in the Old Testament has most changed how you read your Bible?

Pray

LORD God of hosts, you are the one who forms the mountains and declares to man his thoughts. Forgive me for worship that is empty of justice and mercy. Thank you for Jesus, the Son of David, whose fallen tent you have raised. You are gathering people from every nation into it. Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream, in my life and in your church. Amen.

family.scriptureText: She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us).
family.context: Joseph hears two names that interpret each other: Jesus (the Lord saves) and Immanuel (God with us). Salvation is not God shouting advice from a distance; it is God drawing near in a Son. Joseph’s obedience receives a Son whose names explain the mission: save, and be God-with-us. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus saves from sins by coming as God-with-us—living our life, dying our death, rising for our life. Advent is about presence: the holy God making a home among sinners to redeem them. Immanuel means the holy God refuses to redeem from a safe distance; he enters. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: When loneliness or shame whispers that God is far, answer with Immanuel. Practice “with-ness” in your home as a small echo—staying present with each other instead of withdrawing. Practice presence with someone who feels unseen—an echo of God’s with-ness in Jesus. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: Where do we most need to remember that Jesus is God with us this week?
family.prayer: Jesus, you are Immanuel—God with us—and you save from sins. Draw near to our family. Save us and stay with us. Amen.

devo.title: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Obadiah 1–4 — “The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee”
  2. Obadiah 10–16 — “As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee”
  3. Obadiah 17–21 — “Upon mount Zion shall be deliverance”; “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s”

New Testament fulfillment: Revelation 11:15; Luke 1:51–53

The Book and Its Themes

Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament, twenty-one verses aimed at one nation. Edom was descended from Esau, Jacob’s twin, and lived in the rocky heights south and east of the Dead Sea. When Jerusalem fell, most likely to Babylon in 587 BC, the Edomites cheered, looted the city, blocked the roads, and handed fleeing refugees over to the enemy (verses 11–14). Obadiah announces that God has seen it. Edom thought itself safe “in the clefts of the rock” (verse 3, KJV), but the LORD says, “thence will I bring thee down” (verse 4). His themes are the pride that deceives, the sin of gloating over a brother’s ruin, the day of the LORD on “all the heathen” (verse 15), and, at the end, deliverance and holiness on Mount Zion and a kingdom that belongs to God.

Where Obadiah Stands in the Covenant Story

The quarrel between Edom and Israel began in the womb (Genesis 25:22–23). God chose Jacob over Esau before either had done good or evil, and Paul uses that choice to show that God’s purpose “according to election” stands by grace (Romans 9:10–13). Edom’s hatred ran through the whole history: refusing passage to Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 20:14–21), wars with Saul and David, and finally the treachery of 587 BC. Obadiah reads that last betrayal in covenant terms. Edom attacked the people to whom God had bound himself, so Edom had attacked God’s own promise to Abraham: “I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee” (Genesis 12:3). The book closes not with Israel’s revenge but with God’s rule. Exiles return, Zion is holy again, and “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (verse 21).

How Obadiah Leads Us to Christ

  • Typology: Obadiah promises that “saviours shall come up on mount Zion” (verse 21). In their first sense these are deliverers like the judges of old. Calvin reads the verse that way, and then adds that God’s deliverance of the church comes to its height in Christ, so that “Christ is to be distinguished from all others, and that others are saviors under his authority” (Commentary on Obadiah 21).
  • Direct fulfillment: The closing line, “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s,” is the theme of the whole Bible. In Revelation the seventh trumpet sounds and loud voices say, “The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever” (Revelation 11:15, KJV). Calvin draws the same line: “God himself really rules in the person of Christ” (Commentary on Obadiah 21).
  • Thematic analogy: Edom’s sin was pride and gloating over a brother’s fall. Mary sings that God “hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree” (Luke 1:52, KJV). The proud mountain-dwellers are brought low, and the humble Son of David is lifted up. The eternal Son came down from the heights so that brothers who deserve judgment could be made his brothers.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin’s comment on verse 17 is full of pastoral comfort for a church in ruins: “Whenever then God inflicts wounds on his Church, prepared at the same time is the remedy” (Commentary on Obadiah 17). D. A. Carson asks why the prophets spend so much space on little Edom. His answer is that the book is about God’s justice, that Edom stands as a model for all nations, and that “the hope of the world lies in Judah’s future, not Edom’s—and that kingdom is the Lord’s” (For the Love of God, vol. 2, November 21). John Frame would remind us that the LORD is the covenant Lord over the nations as well as over Israel, and that his control reaches even to the high places of Edom.

Obadiah also touches a point where Reformed believers differ in emphasis. Paul’s use of Jacob and Esau (Romans 9) is central to the Reformed doctrine of unconditional election, which Calvin, Packer, Grudem, Frame, and Wilson all hold. Interpreters debate how much Romans 9 concerns individuals and how much it concerns the two nations. The Reformed tradition answers that Paul’s argument covers both, and that God’s choosing is the root of all grace.

For Today

It is easy to read Obadiah and nod along against Edom. It is harder to see Edom in yourself. Gloating over someone else’s fall, standing “on the other side” (verse 11) when a brother is in trouble, and trusting the heights you have built for yourself are the sins of this book. God brings down the proud. He also keeps a remnant, plants holiness on Mount Zion, and gives the kingdom to his Son. If you belong to Christ, your security is not your rock but his.

Reflect

  1. Where are you tempted to take quiet pleasure in someone else’s failure, whether a rival, a neighbor, or a family member?
  2. How does the promise “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” change the way you look at the news this week?

Pray

Sovereign LORD, you bring down the proud and lift up the humble. Forgive me for the pride that deceives me and for the times I have stood aside while others suffered. Thank you that deliverance and holiness are found on Mount Zion, in your Son, our only Savior. Let your kingdom come in my heart, my home, and the nations, until the kingdoms of this world become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low… and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’”
family.context: John’s ministry clears roadblocks for the Lord’s arrival. Repentance is not self-hate; it is turning so the King has a straight path. Valleys and mountains picture the leveling needed for God’s salvation to be seen. John’s wilderness voice still matters in crowded Decembers: prepare by turning. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: John prepares for Jesus. Seeing “the salvation of God” means seeing Christ. Advent repentance clears clutter—pride, distraction, hidden sin—so we can welcome the Savior who already comes with forgiveness. Repentance prepares for Jesus because salvation is a Person to welcome, not a mood to manufacture. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Identify one “crooked path” in your household rhythms—rush that crowds out prayer, sarcasm that blocks kindness. Make one straightening change this week as preparation for Jesus’ nearness. Straightening one crooked habit is Advent worship. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: What needs leveling or clearing in us so we can more clearly see Jesus, God’s salvation?
family.prayer: Lord Jesus, we prepare room for you. Straighten what is crooked in us. Let our family see your salvation with fresh eyes. Amen.

devo.title: Salvation Is of the LORD
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Jonah 1:1–17 — The runaway prophet and the great storm
  2. Jonah 2:1–10 — “Salvation is of the LORD”
  3. Jonah 3:1–10 — Nineveh repents: “Who can tell if God will turn and repent”
  4. Jonah 4:1–11 — “Should not I spare Nineveh, that great city?”

New Testament fulfillment: Matthew 12:38–41; Luke 24:44–47

The Book and Its Themes

Jonah son of Amittai prophesied in the northern kingdom during the reign of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), in the eighth century BC. God sent him to Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, the cruellest empire of the age. Jonah ran the other way, toward Tarshish. The book is short and dramatic: a storm, pagan sailors who pray harder than the prophet, a great fish, a city-wide repentance, and a sulking prophet under a withered plant. Its themes are God’s sovereignty over sea, fish, plant, and worm; his mercy toward the nations; the call to repentance; and the ugly gap between a prophet who enjoys grace and a prophet who wants it withheld from others. As D. A. Carson notes, the fish occupies only three verses of the book.

Where Jonah Stands in the Covenant Story

God’s promise to Abraham was that in him “shall all families of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). Israel was meant to be a light to the nations, but by Jonah’s day it had turned the covenant into a fence. Jonah’s own confession shows that he knew better. He was a Hebrew who feared “the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land” (1:9, KJV). His complaint in chapter 4 quotes the great covenant description of God from Exodus 34:6: “I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness” (4:2). The book ends with a question that God never lets Jonah answer, and it is left for every reader in the covenant community to answer.

How Jonah Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: Jesus named Jonah as the one sign he would give that generation: “For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40, KJV). Calvin is careful about what the type is: “Jonah was not a type of Christ, because he was sent away unto the Gentiles, but because he returned to life again” (Commentary on Jonah 1:1–2).
  • Contrast: Jesus also said, “a greater than Jonas is here” (Matthew 12:41). Jonah ran from God’s mission and was thrown overboard for his own sin. Christ came willingly, and he was cast into death for the sins of others so that the storm of God’s wrath would be stilled for us.
  • Thematic analogy: Jonah’s prayer from the deep ends, “Salvation is of the LORD” (2:9). That line could stand over the whole gospel. The risen Christ opened the Scriptures and said that “repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations” (Luke 24:47, KJV). Nineveh’s repentance is a preview of Gentiles turning to God through the preaching of the greater Jonah.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin’s comment on Jonah 2:8–9 is a warning against invented religion. Those who chase “lying vanities” forsake their own mercy, he explains, because “God alone possesses in himself all fullness of blessings” (Commentary on Jonah 2:8–9). The Westminster Shorter Catechism defines what Nineveh showed: “Repentance unto life is a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God” (WSC Q. 87).

John Frame’s teaching on God as covenant Lord fits this book closely. Under control, Frame writes, “The Lord is one who is in total control of the world” (“Introduction to the Reformed Faith”). Storm, lots, fish, plant, worm, and east wind all obey him. Frame also lists Jonah 2:7 among the texts that show the LORD near to his people. Carson calls the God of Jonah “the missionary God—far more committed to reaching toward ‘outsiders’ than his people are” (For the Love of God, vol. 2, November 22). He also observes that when the prophets want mercy for themselves, they appeal to God’s character, but when Jonah does not want mercy for others, “he portrays the same attributes of God as fatal weaknesses” (November 25). Doug Wilson puts Jonah’s motive bluntly: “Jonah ran because he knew how gracious God was to the utterly undeserving” (“Race, Grace, and the Crimes of Nineveh,” 2018).

The Reformed tradition has generally read Jonah as real history. Jesus treats the men of Nineveh as real people who “shall rise in judgment” (Matthew 12:41). Some scholars outside this tradition read the book as a parable. Calvin’s commentary treats it throughout as history.

For Today

You may not be running to Tarshish, but most of us have a Nineveh: a person, group, or place we would rather God judged than saved. Jonah teaches that we did not earn mercy any more than they did. It was mercy that pulled Jonah out of the deep, and mercy that spared the city. Say with Jonah, “Salvation is of the LORD,” and then let it change how you pray for your enemies.

Reflect

  1. Who is your “Nineveh,” the person or group you find it hardest to want God to bless?
  2. Jonah was angry over a plant and indifferent to a city. What small comforts do you care about more than people’s souls?

Pray

Gracious and merciful God, slow to anger and of great kindness, I confess that I have often run from what you asked of me. Thank you for Jesus, the greater Jonah, who went down into death and rose again on the third day. Since salvation is of the LORD, give me a heart like yours for the lost, for my neighbors, and even for my enemies. Make me glad when you show mercy. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.”
family.context: Mary’s song answers astonishing news with worship. She calls God “my Savior,” locates herself as humble, and praises the Mighty One for great things already begun. Joy and humility hold hands. Mary’s humility does not cancel her joy; it hosts it. She knows she needs a Savior. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Mary rejoices in God her Savior because the child she carries is the Savior for her too. Advent praise centers on Jesus—the holy God doing great things by giving his Son through a humble servant. Magnifying the Lord means our problems shrink to true size next to Jesus’ greatness. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Practice magnification: spend a minute making God “larger” in conversation than problems. Rejoice specifically in Jesus as Savior, not only in seasonal cheer. Rejoice out loud—even briefly—so praise sets the emotional weather of the room. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: What great thing has God done for us in Jesus that our souls could magnify tonight?
family.prayer: Mighty God, holy is your name. With Mary we rejoice in you, our Savior. You have looked on us with mercy through Jesus. We magnify you. Amen.

devo.title: Out of Bethlehem: The Shepherd Who Pardons
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Micah 4:1–5 — “They shall beat their swords into plowshares”
  2. Micah 5:2–5 — “But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah… out of thee shall he come forth”
  3. Micah 6:1–8 — “What doth the LORD require of thee?”
  4. Micah 7:18–20 — “Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity?”

New Testament fulfillment: Matthew 2:1–6; John 10:11–16

The Book and Its Themes

Micah came from Moresheth, a country town in the lowlands of Judah, and prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (1:1), in the late eighth century BC. He was a younger contemporary of Isaiah, and Micah 4:1–3 runs almost word for word with Isaiah 2:2–4. Assyria was rising. Samaria would fall in 722 BC, and Jerusalem would be threatened in 701. Micah speaks to both kingdoms. He condemns land-grabbing, bribed judges, hired prophets, and priests who teach for money (2:1–2; 3:11). The book moves back and forth between judgment and hope three times. His themes are covenant justice, the coming ruler from Bethlehem, a remnant gathered by a shepherd-king, the nations streaming to Zion, and the God who delights in mercy. His name means Who is like the LORD?, and the book ends by asking that very question (7:18).

Where Micah Stands in the Covenant Story

In chapter 6 God takes Israel to court, with the mountains as witnesses: “O my people, what have I done unto thee?” (6:3, KJV). He reminds them of the exodus, of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, and of Balaam’s failed curse. The people ask what offering would satisfy him, even “my firstborn for my transgression” (6:7). The answer is not a bigger sacrifice but a changed heart: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (6:8). That verse is not a way to earn salvation. It is the life of a people already redeemed. The book closes by resting the whole future on God’s oath to the patriarchs: “Thou wilt perform the truth to Jacob, and the mercy to Abraham, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old” (7:20).

How Micah Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: When the wise men came asking for the newborn King, the chief priests and scribes answered from Micah 5:2: the Christ would be born in Bethlehem of Judea (Matthew 2:4–6). Carson notes that God arranged the affairs of an empire so that Jesus was born in David’s town rather than in Nazareth: “It was almost as if Almighty God was going a second mile” (For the Love of God, vol. 2, November 30).
  • Typology: The ruler from Bethlehem “shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD” (5:4). He is a new David, the shepherd-king. Jesus says, “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (John 10:11, KJV). Calvin comments that “Christ then rules not in his Church as a dreaded tyrant, who distresses his subjects with fear; but he is a Shepherd who gently deals with his flock.” He adds, “no less safety is to be expected from Christ, than there is of power in God” (Commentary on Micah 5:4).
  • Thematic analogy: God will “cast all their sins into the depths of the sea” (7:19). At the cross, the Lamb of God carried our sins away, so that God remembers them no more (Hebrews 8:12).

Through Reformed Eyes

Micah 5:2 says the ruler’s “goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.” Interpreters differ on how much to make of this. Many in the Reformed tradition have seen in it a hint of Christ’s eternal origin. Carson thinks the wording points mainly back to the ancient line of David, while noting that it does not deny the Messiah’s preexistence. Either way, the New Testament is clear that the child of Bethlehem is the eternal Word made flesh (John 1:1, 14).

Calvin’s comment on 7:19 is pure comfort: “whenever we flee to God for mercy, pardon is ever ready for us” (Commentary on Micah 7:19). Calvin goes on to say that this is no license to sin but an open door for confession.

Micah 4 is also a place where these teachers differ on the millennium. Doug Wilson, who is postmillennial, preached that this vision of nations streaming to the Lord and learning war no more is fulfilled through the Messiah’s reign in history, and that “God is up to something, and what He is up to is the coming of the Christ” (“The Prophecy of Micah [6],” 2021). Wayne Grudem, a historic premillennialist, holds that some Old Testament prophecies of a world under the Messiah’s rule, in which sin and death still remain, point to a future earthly kingdom after Christ returns. Calvin read the prophets’ pictures of the kingdom chiefly as the spiritual reign of Christ through the gospel. All agree that the peace of Micah 4 comes only through the ruler of Micah 5.

For Today

Micah 6:8 is often quoted and seldom lived. It asks for justice in how we trade and treat people, mercy that loves to forgive, and a humble walk with God. None of us does this well. That is why the book ends with the God who pardons and delights in mercy. Come to the Shepherd from Bethlehem with your sin and your failure. He will not crush you. He will feed you in the strength of the LORD.

Reflect

  1. Which part of Micah 6:8 (justice, mercy, or humility) is hardest for you right now, and why?
  2. Micah’s name asks, Who is like the LORD? What about God’s pardoning mercy in 7:18–20 most moves you to worship today?

Pray

Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression? You do not keep your anger forever, because you delight in mercy. Thank you for sending your Son, born in little Bethlehem, to be our Shepherd and our peace. Teach me to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with you. Cast my sins into the depths of the sea, and keep me in your flock. Amen.

family.scriptureText: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone… For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
family.context: Isaiah pairs deep darkness with a great light, then names the light as a child given—a ruler with titles that stretch beyond any ordinary king. Hope arrives as a person who governs with peace. Darkness in Isaiah is historical and spiritual; light is a given Son with government on his shoulder. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the child born, the Son given—Wonderful Counselor and Prince of Peace—who claims, “I am the light of the world.” Darkness does not get the last word where he reigns. Jesus’ titles are not poetry only; they are how he cares for a family under pressure—counsel, might, peace. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Name a darkness you feel—news, conflict, inner gloom. Do not pretend it away. Hold it next to Jesus’ names and ask him to shine as Counselor and Prince of Peace in that exact place. Pray one title over the darkness you named. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: Which of Jesus’ titles in this passage do we most need tonight, and why?
family.prayer: Jesus, light of the world, child born and Son given—be our Wonderful Counselor and Prince of Peace. Shine on our darkness. Amen.

devo.title: The LORD Is Good, a Strong Hold in the Day of Trouble
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Nahum 1:1–8 — “God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth”; “The LORD is good, a strong hold”
  2. Nahum 1:12–15 — “Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings”
  3. Nahum 3:1–7, 18–19 — “Woe to the bloody city!”

New Testament fulfillment: Romans 10:14–15; Romans 12:19; 2 Thessalonians 1:6–8

The Book and Its Themes

Nahum is the sequel to Jonah. About a century after Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching, Assyria had returned to its cruelty. It had destroyed Samaria in 722 BC, ravaged Judah, and was famous for torturing captives. Nahum, whose name means “comfort,” announces that Nineveh will fall, and it did in 612 BC. Nahum 3:8 mentions the fall of Thebes (“No,” KJV) in 663 BC as already past, so the book was written between those dates. The message was not delivered to Nineveh but to Judah. Its themes are God’s jealous holiness, his patience and his power, his goodness as a refuge for those who trust him, the certain end of tyrants, and good news of peace for an oppressed people.

Where Nahum Stands in the Covenant Story

Nahum’s opening hymn draws on God’s self-description to Moses. Exodus 34:6–7 says the LORD is merciful and slow to anger, yet “will by no means clear the guilty.” Nahum takes up both halves: “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked” (1:3, KJV). Jonah had used the first half to complain about God’s mercy. Nahum uses the second half to comfort God’s people. The same God who spared Nineveh when it repented now judges it when it returns to bloodshed. For Judah, this was covenant faithfulness. God had used Assyria as “the rod of mine anger” (Isaiah 10:5), but he had not forgotten his promise to Abraham’s children.

How Nahum Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: “Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!” (1:15). Isaiah uses almost the same words (Isaiah 52:7), and Paul quotes Isaiah’s version for the preaching of the gospel: “How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace” (Romans 10:15, KJV). The fall of Nineveh was good news for Judah. The defeat of sin, death, and the devil at the cross is good news for the world.
  • Typology: The oppressor is “utterly cut off” (1:15). Nineveh’s fall is a picture of the final overthrow of every power that sets itself against God. Christ “spoiled principalities and powers” and triumphed over them in the cross (Colossians 2:15), and he will return “in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God” (2 Thessalonians 1:8, KJV).
  • Thematic analogy: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble” (1:7). God’s wrath and God’s refuge meet at the cross. Jesus bore the storm of judgment that we deserved, so that he is now our strong hold.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin will not let readers set God’s wrath against his goodness: “There is indeed nothing more peculiar to God than goodness.” He adds, “How much soever then God may subject his people to the cross and to troubles, he still succors them in their distress” (Commentary on Nahum 1:7).

J. I. Packer wrote about the jealousy of God in Knowing God (1973). In its chapter on God’s jealousy, as quoted by others, he explains that God’s jealousy “is not a compound of frustration, envy and spite, as human jealousy so often is, but appears instead as a praiseworthy zeal to preserve something supremely precious.” God’s jealousy is the zeal of a faithful husband for his covenant bride. Carson draws out why Nahum strengthened persecuted believers. It tells them that “God is just, and will hold the violent oppressors accountable, regardless of their political stance, religious affiliation, race, economics, or public image” (For the Love of God, vol. 2, December 3).

Nahum also teaches how to read a book of judgment as a Christian. Paul says, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Romans 12:19). Believers do not take revenge. We leave room for God’s justice, pray for our enemies, and preach the good news that even the worst sinners may still flee to the strong hold.

For Today

Nahum is a hard book to read and a comforting one to believe. Some of you carry real wounds from cruel people. God sees. He is slow to anger, but he is not indifferent, and he will not acquit the wicked. You do not have to carry the work of vengeance. You can hand it to him and run to him as your strong hold. Remember, too, that you were once among God’s enemies, and Christ took the wrath you deserved.

Reflect

  1. Where do you need to trust that God is just, rather than trying to settle a score yourself?
  2. Nahum 1:7 says the LORD “knoweth them that trust in him.” What does it mean for you today that God knows you?

Pray

LORD, you are slow to anger and great in power. You will not acquit the wicked, yet you are good and a strong hold in the day of trouble. I bring you the injustices I have suffered and the bitterness I have nursed. I leave vengeance with you. Thank you that Jesus bore your wrath for me, so that I may hide in you. Make my feet beautiful with the good news of peace. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”
family.context: Fear meets favor. The angel’s “do not be afraid” rests on God’s grace and on the identity of the child: Jesus, Son of the Most High, forever King on David’s throne. The announcement is bigger than Mary’s nerves. Favor from God is the opposite of earning your way out of fear. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus’ greatness and endless kingdom are the reason fear can loosen its grip. Favor with God comes through him. Advent courage is not bravado; it is trust that his reign has no end. Jesus’ endless kingdom means no rival fear gets final authority in your story. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Speak “do not be afraid” over a real fear in your household—then ground it in Jesus’ forever kingdom, not in empty pep talk. Favor is God’s stance toward you in Christ. Speak the angel’s comfort over tonight’s real dread, then rest in the King’s forever reign. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What fear needs to hear that Jesus’ kingdom has no end?
family.prayer: Son of the Most High, Jesus, you reign forever. We receive the word “do not be afraid” because of your favor and your endless kingdom. Rule our fears. Amen.

devo.title: The Just Shall Live by His Faith
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Habakkuk 1:1–4, 12–13 — “O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!”
  2. Habakkuk 2:1–4 — “Though it tarry, wait for it”; “the just shall live by his faith”
  3. Habakkuk 2:14, 20 — “The earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD”
  4. Habakkuk 3:2, 17–19 — “In wrath remember mercy”; “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD”

New Testament fulfillment: Romans 1:16–17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:35–39

The Book and Its Themes

Habakkuk prophesied in Judah shortly before the Babylonian invasions, probably late in the seventh century BC. Unlike most prophets, he does not speak to the people for God. He speaks to God about the people, and the book records the conversation. First he complains that violence and injustice go unpunished in Judah (1:2–4). God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans (Babylonians) to judge Judah (1:5–11). That answer makes things worse. How can a holy God, “of purer eyes than to behold evil” (1:13, KJV), use a nation more wicked than Judah? Habakkuk climbs his watchtower to wait (2:1). God replies with a vision that will surely come, a declaration that “the just shall live by his faith” (2:4), and five woes on Babylon. The book ends in a prayer that turns into a song. Its themes are honest lament, God’s sovereignty over nations, patient faith, and joy in God himself when everything else is gone.

Where Habakkuk Stands in the Covenant Story

Habakkuk lives at the edge of exile. The covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28, including invasion, siege, and failed harvests, are about to fall. Habakkuk does not deny that Judah deserves judgment. His prayer is, “in wrath remember mercy” (3:2). He also looks back to the exodus and the conquest, when God “wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed” (3:13). The God who saved before will save again. Until then, the righteous live by trusting his promise. That is how Abraham lived (Genesis 15:6), and it is how all God’s people have always lived.

How Habakkuk Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted three times in the New Testament. Paul uses it to show that the gospel reveals a righteousness from God received by faith (Romans 1:17) and that no one is justified by the law (Galatians 3:11). Hebrews uses it to urge believers not to shrink back while they wait for Christ’s return (Hebrews 10:37–38).
  • Typology: Habakkuk 3:13 speaks of salvation “with thine anointed.” Carson notes that “anointed one” there apparently refers to the whole people of God and not only to the king (For the Love of God, vol. 2, December 8). Calvin hears in it the line of David’s kingdom pointing to the Messiah (Commentary on Habakkuk 3:13). The full answer to Habakkuk’s prayer is God’s Anointed, Jesus, in whom wrath and mercy meet.
  • Thematic analogy: “Though it tarry, wait for it” (2:3). Hebrews applies this waiting to the second coming: “For yet a little while, and he that shall come will come, and will not tarry” (Hebrews 10:37, KJV).

Through Reformed Eyes

This is a Reformation text. Calvin reads 2:4 exactly as Paul does: “But we obtain righteousness by faith alone for this reason, because God finds nothing in us which he can approve, or what may avail to obtain righteousness” (Commentary on Habakkuk 2:4). The Shorter Catechism says that justification is “an act of God’s free grace, wherein he pardoneth all our sins, and accepteth us as righteous in his sight, only for the righteousness of Christ imputed to us, and received by faith alone” (WSC Q. 33). R. C. Sproul stressed that this faith waits: “Waiting for God is at the heart of living by faith” (“Waiting on God,” Ligonier, 2021). Carson adds that the Hebrew word can mean “faith” or “faithfulness,” and that a good case can be made for keeping both in view, since true faith depends on God and is never puffed up (December 7).

Habakkuk 2:14 shows a difference in emphasis. Doug Wilson, who is postmillennial, reads the promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of God’s glory alongside Isaiah 11:9 as the advance of Christ’s kingdom through history: “The story of redemption is a long story, encompassing all of human history.” He also notes that Calvin read the verse first as the news of Babylon’s fall filling the world (“That He Who Runs May Read 2,” 2019). In fact Calvin adds that he does not object if the verse is extended to the coming of Christ (Commentary on Habakkuk 2:14). Amillennial and premillennial readers expect the full answer chiefly at Christ’s return. All agree that God’s glory will fill the earth.

For Today

Today is the Lord’s Day, and Habakkuk is a good companion for worship. He shows that you may bring your honest questions to God. He also shows where faith lands. Carson puts it well: “That kind of faith can live without knowing; it can triumph when there is no revival; it can rejoice in God even when the culture is in decline” (December 8). The fig tree may not blossom this year. If Christ is yours, you can still say, “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation” (3:18).

Reflect

  1. What “How long, O LORD?” question are you carrying? Have you brought it to him honestly in prayer?
  2. If the “fig tree” in your life failed, whether income, health, or plans, what would remain for you to rejoice in?

Pray

O LORD, I have heard of your work, and I fear. Revive your work in the midst of the years. In wrath remember mercy. Thank you that I am justified by faith alone, in Christ alone, and that you find in me nothing to approve except the righteousness of your Son. Teach me to wait for you. Though the fig tree does not blossom, I will rejoice in you, the God of my salvation. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And again Isaiah says, “The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope.” May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.
family.context: Paul braids Isaiah’s promise of Jesse’s root with a blessing: God of hope fills believers with joy and peace as they trust, and the Spirit makes hope overflow—especially among the nations welcomed in. Hope abounds by the Spirit, not by denying winter. Paul blesses joy and peace in believing. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the root of Jesse in whom the nations hope. Joy and peace come “in believing”—trusting him—not in perfect circumstances. The Spirit’s power makes hope abound as Advent waiting continues. Jesus, Jesse’s root, gathers nations into hope—including households that feel small on the map. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
