family.application: Practice believing that produces joy and peace: thank God for one promise kept in Jesus, then ask the Spirit to make hope abound beyond your natural optimism. Ask the Spirit for hope that outlasts your natural personality. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: How is hoping in Jesus different from ordinary wishing—and where do we need Spirit-powered hope?
family.prayer: God of hope, fill us with joy and peace in believing Jesus, the root of Jesse. By your Spirit, make us abound in hope. Amen.

devo.title: The Day of Wrath and the God Who Sings
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Zephaniah 1:7, 12–18 — “The great day of the LORD is near”
  2. Zephaniah 2:1–3 — “Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth”
  3. Zephaniah 3:8–13 — “A pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD”
  4. Zephaniah 3:14–20 — “He will rejoice over thee with joy… he will joy over thee with singing”

New Testament fulfillment: Acts 2:1–11, 21; Romans 5:9; Luke 15:4–7

The Book and Its Themes

Zephaniah prophesied “in the days of Josiah” (1:1), about 640 to 609 BC, probably before or early in Josiah’s reforms. His family line goes back four generations to a Hezekiah, possibly the king. Judah was full of Baal worship, star worship, and people who swore by the LORD and by Molech at the same time (1:4–5). Worse still was the practical unbelief of men “settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil” (1:12, KJV). Zephaniah’s great theme is the day of the LORD. It is “a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress” (1:15), the passage behind the medieval hymn Dies irae. It reaches the nations around Judah and Jerusalem itself. Then, in chapter 3, the book turns to a purified people from many nations and to a God who rejoices over his people with singing.

Where Zephaniah Stands in the Covenant Story

Zephaniah’s opening echoes the flood: “I will utterly consume all things from off the land” (1:2). The judgment on Judah is covenant curse, the result of breaking the law given at Sinai. But God has always kept a remnant: “an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD” (3:12). The promise of 3:9, a “pure language” so that peoples “may all call upon the name of the LORD,” reverses the scattering of Babel (Genesis 11). The end of the book is a picture of the new covenant. The king of Israel, “even the LORD, is in the midst of thee” (3:15). Judgments are taken away and enemies are cast out.

How Zephaniah Leads Us to Christ

  • Typology: At Pentecost, people “out of every nation under heaven” heard the apostles speak of “the wonderful works of God” in their own languages (Acts 2:5, 11, KJV), and Peter announced that “whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts 2:21). Babel’s curse began to be undone, just as Zephaniah 3:9 pictured.
  • Direct fulfillment: The LORD as “king of Israel… in the midst of thee” (3:15) is fulfilled when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). Nathanael confessed Jesus as “the King of Israel” (John 1:49).
  • Thematic analogy: The day of wrath in chapter 1 fell on Christ at the cross. Because he bore it, “we shall be saved from wrath through him” (Romans 5:9, KJV). And the God who sings over his people in 3:17 is the God of Jesus’ parables, where heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7).

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin is struck by the tenderness of 3:17. He grants that such feelings are ascribed to God by accommodation to our weakness, yet he insists on what they mean: “God is most highly pleased when he can show himself kind to his Church” (Commentary on Zephaniah 3:16–17). John Frame’s account of God’s covenant presence shows both sides of this book. He writes that “God’s presence is a means of blessing, but it can also be a means of curse, when the people break the covenant,” and that “later he draws near in Jesus Christ, and in the Spirit” (“Introduction to the Reformed Faith”).

Carson uses 1:12 to warn about a quiet kind of unbelief that confesses God’s rule on paper but expects nothing from him: “But the worst is rarely systematic or intentional. It simply ignores God” (For the Love of God, vol. 2, December 9). Doug Wilson applies 3:17 to Christian parents. God’s strength, he writes, is used for his people’s good: “But His might is deployed for the good of His people, for their salvation, and not for their suffocation” (“Why Children Matter,” 2013). Parents imitate the God who saves and sings.

Christians differ on how to read the restoration in 3:19–20, which promises to gather the outcast and bring them home. Many Reformed interpreters see its fullest fulfillment in the gathering of Jews and Gentiles into one church. Others, including many premillennialists, also expect a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ, a hope many Reformed teachers find in Romans 11 as well.

For Today

You are probably not bowing to Baal. You may still be like the men “settled on their lees,” living as if God will do neither good nor evil in your life. Zephaniah calls you to seek the LORD and to take his holiness seriously. He also gives you the most surprising verse in the prophets. If you are in Christ, God is not merely putting up with you. He rejoices over you with joy, rests in his love, and joys over you with singing. Four days before Christmas, remember that the King came into our midst to make that song possible.

Reflect

  1. In what area of life do you act as if God “will not do good, neither will he do evil”?
  2. How would it change your day to believe that God rejoices over you in Christ?

Pray

Holy LORD, the great day of your wrath is near, and none can stand before it except those hidden in your Son. Thank you that Jesus bore that day for us. Purify my lips to call on your name, and make me humble and trusting. You are mighty in our midst. You save, you rejoice over your people, and you sing over them. Quiet my anxious heart with your love. Amen.

family.scriptureText: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
family.context: John opens at creation’s dawn, then shocks us: the eternal Word pitched his tent in human flesh. Glory is no longer only on a mountain; it is seeable in the Son—grace and truth embodied. “Dwelt among us” echoes God tenting with Israel—now permanently in the Son’s flesh. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is God the Word made flesh. Incarnation means God did not send a mere messenger; he came. Grace and truth are not slogans; they are a Person who lived among us. Grace and truth are not balanced slogans; they are Jesus’ character toward sinners who need both. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Let wonder slow you down. Say out loud: the God who made us moved in among us. Let that reshape how you treat embodied life at home—meals, rest, care for weary bodies—as places Jesus has honored by taking flesh. Honor bodies and ordinary life tonight as places the Word has dignified by incarnation. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: What does it mean for our family that grace and truth came as a real person, not only as ideas?
family.prayer: Eternal Word, Jesus, you became flesh and dwelt among us. We worship your glory—full of grace and truth. Make our home a place that honors your nearness. Amen.

devo.title: Consider Your Ways: The Glory of the Latter House
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Haggai 1:1–15 — “Consider your ways”; “I am with you, saith the LORD”
  2. Haggai 2:1–9 — “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former”
  3. Haggai 2:20–23 — Zerubbabel, “my servant… as a signet”

New Testament fulfillment: John 2:19–21; Hebrews 12:26–29; Matthew 1:12–16

The Book and Its Themes

Haggai is the first of the three prophets after the exile, and his messages are dated precisely. All four came within about four months in 520 BC, the second year of Darius king of Persia. The exiles had come home from Babylon about eighteen years before, under Cyrus’s decree (Ezra 1). They had laid the temple’s foundation, met opposition, and stopped (Ezra 4:24). Meanwhile they built their own homes. Haggai asks, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (1:4, KJV). Their harvests had failed and their wages leaked away, like money put “into a bag with holes” (1:6). Within weeks of Haggai’s first sermon, the leaders and the people obeyed and started to build (1:12–15). His themes are putting God first, the presence of God with his people, the shaking of the nations, the coming glory of God’s house, and a chosen son of David.

Where Haggai Stands in the Covenant Story

Haggai speaks to the remnant of the covenant people, living under the leadership of Zerubbabel the governor, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, and Joshua the high priest. Older people who remembered Solomon’s temple wept that this one seemed “as nothing” (2:3). God’s answer reaches back to Sinai: “According to the word that I covenanted with you when ye came out of Egypt, so my spirit remaineth among you: fear ye not” (2:5). The covenant had not been cancelled by the exile. And the curse on Jehoiachin, whose line was compared to a signet ring pulled off God’s hand (Jeremiah 22:24), is reversed when God makes Zerubbabel “as a signet” (Haggai 2:23).

How Haggai Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: Hebrews quotes Haggai 2:6, “Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven” (Hebrews 12:26, KJV), and applies it to the new covenant. God is shaking everything that can be shaken so that “we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved” may worship him with reverence (Hebrews 12:28).
  • Typology: The greater glory of “this latter house” (2:9) was not gold. That temple never matched Solomon’s in splendour. Its glory came when the Lord himself walked into its courts. Jesus spoke of his own body as the temple (John 2:19–21). Calvin applies the promise “to the excellency of those spiritual blessings which appeared when Christ was revealed” (Commentary on Haggai 2:6–9).
  • Typology: Zerubbabel, the chosen “servant” and “signet” (2:23), appears in both genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27). Carson writes that he sets a pattern that “points to the ultimate Zerubbabel, the ultimate David—King Jesus” (For the Love of God, vol. 2, December 13).

Through Reformed Eyes

Haggai 2:7 is a well-known puzzle. The KJV reads, “the desire of all nations shall come,” and many Christians, including Doug Wilson, take this as a title of Christ. Wilson writes, “When all nations are shaken, they will come to the Desire of All Nations, who is the Lord Jesus Christ” (“Reverence and Godly Awe,” 2006). In the same sermon he argues from Hebrews 12 for a high view of new covenant sanctions and links his view to “federal vision advocates.” This volume’s introduction notes that the Federal Vision is disputed and is not treated here as the shared Reformed position. Carson points out that the Hebrew is plural, “the desired things,” that is, the treasures of the nations. Calvin grants that “Christ was the expectation of the whole world,” yet he judges that “the more simple meaning is that which I first stated–that the nations would come, bringing with them all their riches” (Commentary on Haggai 2:6–9). Both readings end in Christ, because the nations’ treasures come to the house only because the Lord of the house has come.

Calvin also sees the work of grace in the “shaking”: “men come not to Christ except through the wonderful agency of God” (Commentary on Haggai 2:6–9). John Frame’s three lordship attributes are all present in Haggai. God controls the harvests, his word has authority (“Consider your ways”), and his presence is the heart of the promise: “I am with you, saith the LORD” (1:13).

For Today

Haggai still asks, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses?” It is easy to pour time, money, and energy into our own houses while the work of God’s house, his church, waits. This is not a call to neglect your family or business. It is a call to put first things first, in your giving, your Sundays, and your service. Seek first the kingdom (Matthew 6:33). The God who said “I am with you” to a small, discouraged remnant says it to his church today, because Christ has come into his temple.

Reflect

  1. Haggai says twice, “Consider your ways.” What would honest consideration show about where your time and money actually go?
  2. When God’s work looks small, as the second temple did, how does the promise of Christ’s coming glory encourage you?

Pray

LORD of hosts, forgive me for building my own house while yours waits. Stir up my spirit, as you stirred up Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people. Thank you that your Spirit remains among us, and that the glory of your house has come in Jesus Christ, the true temple and the true son of David. Shake from my life what cannot last, and give me a kingdom that cannot be moved. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And the angel said to them, “Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord. And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”
family.context: Shepherds on night shift receive heaven’s headline: good news, great joy, for all the people. The Savior-Christ-Lord is found not in a palace but in a manger—glory wrapped in humility. Shepherds receive the headline first—a hint of the gospel’s reach to unlikely people. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is Savior, Messiah, and Lord in one infant. Joy is “great” because salvation is real; it is “for all the people” because his reach is wide. The sign of the manger shows how he saves—by stooping. Savior, Christ, and Lord in a manger redefine power as nearness and humility. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Share joy that is gospel-shaped: not only festive feeling, but “unto you a Savior.” Tell someone outside your usual circle a simple line of this good news this week. Share the good news simply with one person who needs joy that is more than seasonal. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: How can our celebration make room for “great joy… for all the people,” not only for those already comfortable?
family.prayer: Christ the Lord, born Savior for us—thank you for good news of great joy. Cast out fear, and let joy in you spill beyond our walls. Amen.

devo.title: Thy King Cometh: The Branch, the Pierced One, and the Opened Fountain
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Zechariah 3:1–10; 6:12–13 — Joshua’s filthy garments; “my servant the BRANCH”; a priest upon his throne
  2. Zechariah 9:9–11 — “Behold, thy King cometh unto thee… lowly, and riding upon an ass”
  3. Zechariah 12:10–13:1, 7 — “They shall look upon me whom they have pierced”; “a fountain opened”; “smite the shepherd”
  4. Zechariah 14:8–9, 20–21 — “The LORD shall be king over all the earth”

New Testament fulfillment: Matthew 21:1–11; Matthew 26:31; John 19:34–37; Revelation 1:7

The Book and Its Themes

Zechariah, a priest’s son and Haggai’s younger colleague, began to prophesy in 520 BC (1:1). His call was the same as every prophet’s: “Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you” (1:3, KJV). Chapters 1–6 record eight night visions: horsemen patrolling the earth, horns and smiths, a measuring line, the high priest cleansed, a lampstand fed by olive trees, a flying scroll, a woman in a basket, and four chariots. Their message is that God is jealous for Jerusalem, will judge the nations, cleanse his people, and finish his temple “not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” (4:6). Chapters 7–8 answer a question about fasting with a call to justice and a promise of joy. Chapters 9–14 contain two later oracles about the coming king, the rejected shepherd, the pierced one, and the day when the LORD is king over all the earth. The Gospels return to Zechariah again and again in telling the story of Jesus’ last week.

Where Zechariah Stands in the Covenant Story

Zechariah gathers up the earlier promises. The covenant formula, “they shall be my people, and I will be their God” (8:8), is renewed for the returned remnant. J. I. Packer called this repeated promise “the pantechnicon promise, inasmuch as every particular promise that God makes is packed into it” (“Introduction: On Covenant Theology”). The Branch from Jeremiah 23:5 reappears as God’s servant (3:8). Priest and king, kept apart under Moses, are joined in one person who “shall be a priest upon his throne” (6:13). The blood of the covenant sets prisoners free (9:11), and the nations take hold of a Jew’s garment, saying, “We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you” (8:23).

How Zechariah Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: “Behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass” (9:9). Matthew and John cite it for Palm Sunday (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15). Calvin comments that “the hope of the ancient people, as our hope, was founded on Christ” (Commentary on Zechariah 9:9). The thirty pieces of silver cast to the potter (11:12–13) are recalled in Matthew 27:9–10.
  • Direct fulfillment: “Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered” (13:7). Jesus applied this to himself on the night he was betrayed (Matthew 26:31). “They shall look upon me whom they have pierced” (12:10) is quoted by John at the cross (John 19:37) and at Christ’s return (Revelation 1:7). The fountain “for sin and for uncleanness” (13:1) is opened by his blood. Calvin writes that “true ablution is by the blood which he shed for us” (Commentary on Zechariah 13:1).
  • Typology: Joshua the high priest, stripped of filthy garments and clothed in clean ones (3:3–5), is a picture of justification. God says, “I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day” (3:9), and Christ did so on the day he died. The Branch who is both priest and king (6:12–13) is the Mediator whom the Shorter Catechism describes as prophet, priest, and king (WSC Q. 23–26).

Through Reformed Eyes

Good Reformed interpreters do not always agree on these verses. Calvin takes the piercing of 12:10 in its first sense as Israel’s provocation of God: “this piercing is to be taken metaphorically for continual provocation.” He also widens the shepherd of 13:7 to the whole order of shepherds, while granting that the text “was fulfilled in Christ” (Commentary on Zechariah 12:10; 13:7). D. A. Carson reads both texts more directly. He says the most natural reading of 12:10 is that it is the LORD himself who is pierced, and that John points to “a more literal fulfillment, a more literal piercing” (For the Love of God, vol. 2, December 25). He also notes that the shepherd of 13:7 is “the man who is close to me” (December 26).

Zechariah 14 is a key text in the millennium debate. Wayne Grudem argues for historic premillennialism partly from this chapter. He is quoted as writing that its description “does not fit the present age, for the Lord is King over all the earth in this situation. But it does not fit the eternal state either, because of the disobedience and rebellion against the Lord that is clearly present” (Systematic Theology, 1994, as quoted by Michael Vlach). Amillennial interpreters, closer to Calvin, read the chapter as a prophetic picture of the gospel age and its consummation. Postmillennialists such as Doug Wilson expect Christ’s kingdom to grow through the gospel until the nations are discipled before he returns. Carson observes that the Gospels quote Zechariah 9:9 but not 9:10, because “unqualified disarmament and unqualified peace among the nations (9:10) await the consummation” (December 22).

For Today

Two days before Christmas, Zechariah shows us who came to Bethlehem. He is the lowly King on a donkey, the Shepherd struck for his sheep, the one they pierced, and the fountain that washes away sin. One day “HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD” will be written even on the bells of the horses (14:20), and every ordinary thing will belong to God. Start today with the ordinary things in your hands.

Reflect

  1. Zechariah 3 pictures filthy garments exchanged for clean robes. What sins do you need to confess and leave at the fountain today?
  2. How does seeing Jesus as both the lowly King and the pierced Shepherd shape the way you celebrate Christmas?

Pray

LORD of hosts, you are jealous for your people with great jealousy. Thank you for your servant the Branch, our Priest upon his throne, who came to us lowly and having salvation. Pour on us the spirit of grace and of supplications, so that we look on him whom we pierced and mourn for our sin. Wash us in the fountain opened for sin and for uncleanness, and write holiness to the LORD on all our days. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
family.context: Paul holds up Jesus’ mindset as the pattern for Christian community: not grasping status, but self-emptying service down to the cross. Christmas and the cross belong to one descent of love. Paul insists the mindset of Christ become the mindset among believers—community shaped by descent. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus’ incarnation is voluntary humility—God the Son taking servant form. He connects us to God by coming down, then calls us into his mind: shared life marked by laying down privilege for love. Incarnation leads to cross; Christmas love is self-giving all the way down. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Ask where grasping shows up at home—credit, control, comfort. Practice one self-emptying act that mirrors Jesus: serving without being asked, yielding a preference, apologizing without defending. Choose the stooping act that costs a little pride; that is where his mind becomes yours. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: Where do we need the mind of Christ Jesus—the willingness to stoop—most clearly this week?
family.prayer: Jesus, you emptied yourself and obeyed to the cross. Give us your mind. Make our family humble in love as you have loved us. Amen.

devo.title: The Messenger of the Covenant and the Sun of Righteousness
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Malachi 1:1–5, 11 — “I have loved you, saith the LORD”; “my name shall be great among the Gentiles”
  2. Malachi 2:13–16 — “Let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth”
  3. Malachi 3:1–7, 16–18 — “The messenger of the covenant”; “I am the LORD, I change not”
  4. Malachi 4:1–6 — “The Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings”; Elijah the prophet

New Testament fulfillment: Matthew 11:7–15; Mark 1:1–4; Luke 1:13–17, 76–79

The Book and Its Themes

Malachi (“my messenger”) is the last book of the Old Testament in our English order. He prophesied in the middle of the fifth century BC, around the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. The temple had been rebuilt, but the glory had not come, and the people had grown tired and cynical. Malachi is written as a series of disputes. God makes a statement, the people answer back (“Wherein?”), and God replies. “I have loved you, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us?” (1:2, KJV). The priests offered blind and lame animals. Men divorced the wives of their youth and married women who worshipped other gods. The people robbed God in tithes and offerings and said it was vain to serve him. Malachi’s themes are God’s electing love, true worship, the covenant of marriage, the coming of the Lord to his temple, refining judgment, the book of remembrance for those who fear him, and the promise of Elijah before the great day.

Where Malachi Stands in the Covenant Story

Malachi ends the prophetic voice of the Old Testament with a summary of the whole story. God’s love for Jacob over Esau (1:2–3) recalls the election of grace that we saw in Obadiah. The covenant with Levi (2:4–7) shows what a faithful priest should be. Marriage is a covenant made before God, who seeks “a godly seed” (2:15). The command to “remember ye the law of Moses my servant” (4:4) and the promise of Elijah (4:5) join the Law and the Prophets together. Then come four hundred years of silence. The next prophet to speak is a man dressed like Elijah at the Jordan River.

How Malachi Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: “Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me” (3:1). Jesus said of John the Baptist, “This is he, of whom it is written, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face” (Matthew 11:10, KJV). The angel told Zacharias that John would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children” (Luke 1:17). Jesus said plainly, “this is Elias, which was for to come” (Matthew 11:14).
  • Direct fulfillment: The Lord whom they sought, “even the messenger of the covenant” (3:1), came suddenly to his temple when Jesus came. Calvin writes that “the office of Christ consists in confirming and sealing to us the covenant of God, not only by his doctrine, but also by his blood and the sacrifice of his cross” (Commentary on Malachi 3:1). Packer describes “the one messenger and mediator of the covenant, Jesus Christ the God-man, prophet and king, priest and sacrifice, the Messiah of Old Testament prophecy and New Testament proclamation” (“Introduction: On Covenant Theology”).
  • Typology: “Unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings” (4:2). Calvin says, “There is indeed no doubt but that Malachi calls Christ the Sun of righteousness.” The fathers, he adds, “were content with the dawn only, or with the moon and stars” (Commentary on Malachi 4:2). Zacharias sang of “the dayspring from on high” who visits us (Luke 1:78).

Through Reformed Eyes

Malachi 3:6, “I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed,” is a classic text for God’s unchangeableness. Calvin, Packer, Frame, and Grudem all teach it, and Frame lists the verse among his texts on God’s covenant presence. Carson sums up the chapter: “People may be faithless, but the Lord does not change” (For the Love of God, vol. 2, December 30).

Doug Wilson applies Malachi 4:6 to fathers and children: “The call to repentance is the entryway into grace.” Where hearts are turned, he writes, “There is reconciliation where there was estrangement. This is what the gospel does. This is why Jesus came” (“Repentance and Fatherhood,” 2012). Here the traditions differ in how they apply the covenant to children. Wilson, Frame, Calvin, and the Westminster tradition baptize the children of believers as members of the covenant community. Grudem and Reformed Baptists, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, baptize only those who profess faith. Both sides call fathers to bring their children up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4).

Malachi 3:8–10 on tithes is another point where Christians differ. Some hold that the tithe still binds believers, and others see it as a principle of generous giving now fulfilled in Christ. All agree that robbing God of honor and firstfruits is sin.

For Today

It is Christmas Eve. Malachi closes the Old Testament with the people waiting in the dark, longing for the Lord to come to his temple. Tonight we remember that he came. The Sun of righteousness rose in Bethlehem, and the Messenger of the covenant sealed it with his blood. This also finishes Volume 2, the last nine books of the Old Testament. From Obadiah to Malachi you have watched God bring down the proud, spare Nineveh, raise a shepherd from Bethlehem, shake the nations, and promise a King on a donkey and a pierced Shepherd. Volume 3 turns to the New Testament, where the promised one is named.

Reflect

  1. Malachi’s hearers asked, “Wherein hast thou loved us?” Where have you doubted God’s love, and how does Christmas answer you?
  2. Is there a relationship in your family where hearts need to be turned toward one another again?

Pray

LORD, you do not change, and so we are not consumed. Thank you for sending your messenger to prepare the way, and for coming yourself as the Messenger of the covenant. On this holy night, let the Sun of righteousness rise on our home with healing in his wings. Turn the hearts of fathers to their children and children to their fathers. Write our names in your book of remembrance, and make us your treasured possession in Christ. Amen.

family.scriptureText: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
family.context: History hits “fullness of time.” God sends his Son into real human birth and real legal obligation to redeem and adopt. Then God sends the Spirit of his Son so the cry of family rises in our hearts. Fullness of time means God is never late in redemption history, even when we feel delayed. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus’ birth is mission: born to redeem and to bring adoption. Christmas leads to “Abba.” The Spirit of the Son makes the Son’s intimacy with the Father echo in us—heirs, not slaves. The double sending—Son and Spirit—brings redemption and the cry of adoption into one gift. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Trade slave-language (“I have to earn belonging”) for adoption-language (“we are heirs through God”). Let Christmas fuel identity, not only nostalgia. Replace “prove yourself” talk with “you belong in Jesus” talk at least once today. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: How does knowing Jesus was born to redeem and adopt us change the pressure we put on ourselves this season?
family.prayer: Father, in the fullness of time you sent your Son, and you send his Spirit into our hearts. We cry Abba. Thank you that we are heirs through Jesus. Amen.

devo.title: The King Born to Fulfill All the Scriptures
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Matthew 1:18–25 — The virgin’s son, named Jesus and called Immanuel
  2. Matthew 2:1–12 — The wise men worship the King born in Bethlehem
  3. Matthew 5:17–20 — “I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them”
  4. Matthew 28:16–20 — All authority given, and the nations discipled

Old Testament background: Isaiah 7:14; Micah 5:2; Daniel 7:13–14

The Book and Its Themes

Matthew is the bridge between the Testaments, and it is built to be crossed. Its first words are “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (1:1). That one line gathers up the promise to Abraham (a blessing for the nations) and the promise to David (a son on his throne forever). Matthew writes as a Jewish believer for readers who know their Bibles, and he keeps saying “this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet” (1:22). Jesus is the true King of Israel, the new and greater Moses who teaches from a mountain (chapters 5–7), the Son of Man who receives all authority, and Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23). The book is arranged around five great blocks of teaching, and it ends with the risen King sending his disciples to all nations with the promise that he will be with them “always, to the end of the age” (28:20). God with us at the beginning, and Christ with us at the end.

Where Matthew Stands in the Covenant Story

The Old Testament closed with a promise and a long silence. Israel had returned from exile, but the throne of David was empty and the glory had not come back to the temple. Matthew’s genealogy is arranged in three sets of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile, and from the exile to the Christ (1:17). In other words, the story went up to a king, down into exile, and now up again to the King. The covenant with Abraham, the covenant with David, and the new covenant promised by Jeremiah all meet in this child. At the Last Supper Jesus calls his blood “my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (26:28).

How Matthew Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: Matthew explicitly applies Isaiah 7:14 to the virgin birth (1:22–23) and Micah 5:2 to Bethlehem (2:5–6). These are not clever coincidences found after the fact. Matthew presents them as God keeping his word.
  • Type fulfilled: Jesus relives Israel’s story and gets it right. He comes out of Egypt (2:15, quoting Hosea 11:1), passes through the waters at his baptism, and is tested forty days in the wilderness, where he answers Satan three times from Deuteronomy (4:1–11). Where Israel failed, the true Son obeys.
  • Type fulfilled: Like Moses, Jesus is spared from a king’s slaughter of infants and then gives God’s law from a mountain. But he speaks with his own authority: “You have heard that it was said… But I say to you” (5:21–22). He is not only a new Moses. He is the Lord who gave the law.
  • Promise fulfilled: The risen Jesus says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (28:18). That is the language of Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives dominion so that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin, commenting on Matthew 5:17, wrote that Christ declares “his doctrine is so far from being at variance with the law, that it agrees perfectly with the law and the prophets, and not only so, but brings the complete fulfillment of them.” That is the Reformed way of reading Matthew: the law is not thrown away, it is fulfilled, and Christ is its goal.

The Great Commission is also where Reformed friends read the future differently. Doug Wilson, a postmillennialist, reads Matthew 28 alongside Daniel 7 and expects the gospel to disciple whole nations before Christ returns. In Heaven Misplaced he writes: “We have the task of announcing to the remaining rebels in the hinterlands that their capital city has already fallen, their ruler dethroned, and that resistance is futile.” Grudem, a historic premillennialist, expects the gospel to go to every nation but also expects a time of great tribulation before Christ returns. Both agree that the King already reigns and that our job is to make disciples.

Matthew 28:19 also joins baptism to discipling the nations. Paedobaptists (Calvin, Frame, Wilson, Sproul) see households and children included in the nations being discipled. Baptists (Grudem, the 1689 Confession) see baptism given to those who are made disciples by faith. Both agree that Jesus commands it and that it is done “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (28:19).

For Today

It is Christmas Day. The child in the manger is not a sentimental decoration. He is the Son of David, the Son of Abraham, the Lord of the law, and Immanuel. Everything God promised in the Old Testament was waiting for him, and everything you need is found in him. The same King who was laid in a feeding trough now holds all authority in heaven and on earth, and he has promised to be with his people every day until the end. Whatever this day holds, it holds Christ with us.

Reflect

  1. Which Old Testament promise fulfilled in Matthew strengthens your faith most today, and why?
  2. If Jesus really has all authority, what part of your life are you still treating as outside his rule?

Pray

Father, thank you for keeping your word. You promised a Son of David and a blessing for the nations, and in the fullness of time you sent your Son, born of a virgin in Bethlehem. Thank you that he fulfilled the law I have broken and gave his blood for the forgiveness of my sins. Lord Jesus, you are Immanuel. Be with me today, rule over every part of my life, and use me to make disciples. Amen.

family.scriptureText: But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days… And he shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God. And they shall dwell secure…
family.context: Micah promises a ruler from tiny Bethlehem whose origins are ancient. He shepherds in the Lord’s strength so the flock dwells secure. Greatness hides in littleness; rule looks like shepherding. Bethlehem’s littleness is part of the promise. God often routes salvation through overlooked places. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is born in Bethlehem as that ruler and shepherd. He stands for his flock in the Father’s strength, laying down his life for the sheep. Security is found under his care, not in our size or status. Jesus shepherds in the Lord’s strength; security is relational before it is circumstantial. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: When you feel “too little,” remember Bethlehem. Entrust someone you worry about to Jesus the Shepherd—name them and ask him to keep them secure. Place a worry under his shepherding by name and leave it there tonight. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: How does Jesus shepherding us in the Lord’s strength help us dwell more securely with each other?
family.prayer: Jesus, Shepherd-King from Bethlehem, ancient and near—stand for us in the Father’s strength. Keep our household secure under your care. Amen.

devo.title: The Servant Who Gave His Life as a Ransom
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Mark 1:1–15 — The beginning of the gospel and the voice in the wilderness
  2. Mark 8:27–38 — “You are the Christ,” and the road to the cross
  3. Mark 10:35–45 — “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve”
  4. Mark 15:33–39 — The torn curtain and the centurion’s confession

Old Testament background: Isaiah 40:3–5; Isaiah 52:13–53:12

The Book and Its Themes

Mark is the shortest and fastest of the Gospels. The word “immediately” runs through it like a drumbeat. Early church tradition links it to Peter’s preaching, and it reads like an eyewitness telling the story in a hurry. Mark opens with a title, “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1), and then answers two questions. The first half (chapters 1–8) asks, “Who is this?” Jesus heals, casts out demons, calms the sea, and forgives sins, and people keep wondering. At the turning point Peter answers, “You are the Christ” (8:29). The second half (chapters 8–16) asks what kind of Christ he is. Jesus immediately begins to teach that “the Son of Man must suffer many things” (8:31). From then on the road leads to Jerusalem and the cross. The key verse is 10:45: the Son of Man came “to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45).

Where Mark Stands in the Covenant Story

Mark begins with Isaiah 40, the great chapter of comfort for exiles: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (1:3). Isaiah promised that the LORD himself would come back to his people, lead a new exodus, and bring them home. Mark identifies John the Baptist as that voice and Jesus as the Lord who comes. Then Mark shows that the way home runs through Isaiah 53. The Servant who is “pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5) and who makes “many to be accounted righteous” (Isaiah 53:11) is the King himself. The new exodus is accomplished not by a military victory over Rome but by a substitutionary death. The covenant that Moses sealed with blood at Sinai (Exodus 24:8) is renewed in “my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (14:24).

How Mark Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: Mark joins Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3 to introduce John and Jesus (1:2–3). The messenger prepares the way, and the Lord himself arrives.
  • Promise fulfilled: The Servant of Isaiah 53 gives his life “for many” (Isaiah 53:11–12). Jesus deliberately echoes this when he says he came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). He understood his own death in the light of Isaiah’s Servant.
  • Type fulfilled: When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (15:38). The veil that guarded the Most Holy Place, the heart of the tabernacle and temple system, was opened from God’s side. The way into God’s presence is now through the death of his Son (Hebrews 10:19–20).
  • Echo: Jesus cries the opening words of Psalm 22 from the cross (15:34). The whole psalm moves from forsakenness to praise and to the nations turning to the LORD. The Roman centurion’s confession, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (15:39), is the first sign of it.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin, commenting on the ransom saying, wrote that Jesus declares “his life is the price of our redemption; whence it follows, that we obtain an undeserved reconciliation with God.” That is the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution in a single clause. J. I. Packer spent much of his life defending the same truth. His Tyndale lecture What Did the Cross Achieve? The Logic of Penal Substitution (published in Tyndale Bulletin 25, 1974) argued that the substitution is the heart of the atonement, not one theory among many.

Mark 10:13–16, where Jesus takes children in his arms and blesses them, is another place where Reformed friends read differently. Paedobaptists such as Calvin, Frame, and Wilson see it as support for counting the children of believers within the covenant community. Baptists such as Grudem note that Jesus blesses the children but does not baptize them, and they reserve baptism for those who profess faith. Both sides should bring their children to Jesus, and both should teach them that the kingdom must be received “like a child” (10:15).

For Today

Mark shows you a Christ who is strong enough to command storms and humble enough to wash away your sin with his own blood. He also shows you what following him looks like: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me” (8:34). Greatness in his kingdom is measured by service. Today, look for one ordinary way to serve someone in your home or work without being noticed. You are following a King who knelt.

Reflect

  1. Where are you more like James and John, asking for a seat of honor, than like the Servant who came to serve?
  2. What does it mean to you personally that Jesus paid a ransom for you?

Pray

Lord Jesus, Servant of the Lord, you did not come to be served but to serve and to give your life as a ransom for many. Thank you for the price you paid for me. Thank you that the curtain is torn and I may come near to the Father through you. Make me quick to serve and slow to seek honor. Give me courage to take up my cross and follow you today. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.”
family.context: Aged Simeon holds the infant Jesus and declares his life’s wait complete. Salvation is visible—a child—and it is public: light for the nations, glory for Israel. Peace comes from seeing God’s promise kept. Simeon’s peace is not retirement ease; it is promise-kept rest while holding Jesus. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is God’s salvation prepared for all peoples. To “see” him by faith is to share Simeon’s peace. He is revelation-light for outsiders and glory for God’s people—wide mercy in one person. Light for Gentiles and glory for Israel means Jesus widens mercy without canceling faithfulness. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Ask for Simeon-eyes: where is Jesus already present as salvation that you have treated as ordinary? Name him as light for someone far from faith you care about. Pray for someone outside your usual faith circle to see this light. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: What would it mean for us to “depart in peace” tonight because our eyes have seen God’s salvation in Jesus?
family.prayer: Lord, our eyes look to Jesus, your salvation and light for the nations. Give us Simeon’s peace and a heart for all peoples. Amen.

devo.title: Everything Written About Me Must Be Fulfilled
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Luke 1:67–79 — Zechariah’s song of the covenant remembered
  2. Luke 4:16–21 — “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing”
  3. Luke 15:1–24 — The Father who runs to the lost son
  4. Luke 24:13–35, 44–47 — Christ in Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms

Old Testament background: Genesis 22:16–18; Isaiah 61:1–2

The Book and Its Themes

Luke was a physician and a careful historian. He tells Theophilus that he has “followed all things closely for some time past” (1:3) so that he “may have certainty” (1:3–4). His Gospel is the first of two volumes; Acts is the second. Luke’s great themes are salvation for the lost (“the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,” 19:10), the reversal of human status (the humble are lifted up and the proud brought low), the work of the Holy Spirit, prayer, and joy. Luke gives special attention to people others overlooked: the poor, widows, tax collectors, Samaritans, and women. Only Luke tells the parables of the Good Samaritan, the lost son, and the Pharisee and the tax collector. The book opens and closes in the temple, with praise.

Where Luke Stands in the Covenant Story

Luke begins with faithful Israelites waiting for “the consolation of Israel” (2:25) and “the redemption of Jerusalem” (2:38). Mary and Zechariah sing songs packed with Old Testament language. Zechariah praises God “to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (1:72–73). Luke’s genealogy runs all the way back to “Adam, the son of God” (3:38). Jesus is the true son of Abraham, the son of David, and the last Adam who will undo the ruin of the first. At the end, the risen Jesus opens the minds of his disciples to understand the whole Old Testament as pointing to his suffering, his resurrection, and the preaching of repentance and forgiveness “to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (24:47).

How Luke Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1–2 and announces, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21). He is the anointed one who brings good news to the poor and liberty to the captives, the true Jubilee.
  • Promise fulfilled: Zechariah’s song says God has “raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (1:69) and has remembered the oath sworn to Abraham. The covenants with Abraham and David are kept in Jesus.
  • Type fulfilled: At the transfiguration, Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about his “departure” (9:31). The Greek word is exodus. The cross and resurrection are the new and greater exodus, rescuing God’s people from slavery to sin and death.
  • Promise fulfilled: On the Emmaus road, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (24:27). Later he says that “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (24:44). This is the charter for this whole devotional series.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin, commenting on Luke 24:27, drew the lesson for every Christian reader: “In order that Christ may be made known to us through the Gospel, it is therefore necessary that Moses and the Prophets should go before as guides, to show us the way.” He warned against anyone who would cut off the Old Testament from the gospel. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that the God of Israel and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ are one God, and that the Old Testament is Christian Scripture.

Luke’s parable of the lost son (15:11–32) is a picture of grace. J. I. Packer wrote much about adoption, the truth that God receives sinners not as hired servants but as sons. The father in the parable runs, embraces, and clothes his son before the son can finish his speech. That is the gospel the Reformers recovered: acceptance with God is a gift, not a wage.

For Today

Luke shows a Savior who seeks the lost and a Father who runs to meet them. If you feel far from God today, do not rehearse a speech about how you will earn your way back. Come home. And if you are the older brother, proud of your record and irritated by grace given to others, come into the feast too. Then open your Bible the way Jesus taught the Emmaus disciples, expecting to find him there, and ask him to make your heart burn within you as he opens the Scriptures (24:32).

Reflect

  1. Do you see yourself more in the younger son or the older son right now?
  2. How has reading the Old Testament with Christ at the center changed the way you read your Bible?

Pray

Father, thank you for remembering your holy covenant and the oath you swore to Abraham. Thank you for sending Jesus to seek and to save the lost, and for running to meet me when I was still far off. Open my mind to understand the Scriptures, as Jesus did for his disciples. Let my heart burn as I see him in Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms. In his name, amen.

family.scriptureText: For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.
family.context: John contrasts gifts: Moses mediated law; Jesus Christ brings grace and truth in person. From Jesus’ fullness we receive wave after wave of grace. He makes the unseen God known. Grace upon grace pictures continuous supply from a Person of endless fullness. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time. Take one more breath before moving on: God is speaking through this text to a real household with real needs.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus, at the Father’s side, exeals God. Connection to God is not guessing; it is receiving from Christ’s fullness. Christmas is grace upon grace—God known and God kind in the Son. Jesus makes God known—so Christian knowing is relational revelation, not speculation. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other. Hold onto this: Jesus is not watching from a distance to grade you; he is the Savior who draws near and gives what he commands.
family.application: Instead of measuring whether you have “done enough” this season, receive. Thank Jesus for a specific grace already given today, then ask for grace to show truth with kindness at home. Receive grace for today’s failure before you lecture yourself into next year’s improvement. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance. Choose the next right minute—not the perfect month—and take it together.
family.talk: Where do we need “grace upon grace” from Jesus’ fullness right now?
family.prayer: Jesus Christ, from your fullness we receive grace upon grace. Make the Father known among us. Fill our home with your grace and truth. Amen.

devo.title: The Word Made Flesh Who Tabernacled Among Us
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. John 1:1–18 — The Word who was God became flesh
  2. John 3:1–16 — New birth, the lifted-up serpent, and God’s love for the world
  3. John 6:25–51 — “I am the bread of life”
  4. John 20:24–31 — “My Lord and my God!”

Old Testament background: Genesis 1:1–3; Exodus 40:34–38; Numbers 21:4–9

The Book and Its Themes

John’s Gospel is simple enough for a child and deep enough to drown a theologian. John tells us exactly why he wrote it: “these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (20:31). He opens before creation with the eternal Word who “was with God, and… was God” (1:1). He then structures much of his story around seven signs, from water turned to wine to the raising of Lazarus, and around Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, and the true vine. John’s key words are believe, life, light, truth, love, witness, and glory. The long Upper Room discourse (chapters 13–17) is the most intimate teaching Jesus gives, and his high-priestly prayer in chapter 17 lets us overhear the Son speaking to the Father.

Where John Stands in the Covenant Story

John begins with “In the beginning,” the first words of Genesis. The Word through whom all things were made has now entered his own creation. Then John reaches for the tabernacle: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (1:14). The verb literally means “pitched his tent.” The glory that filled the tabernacle in the wilderness and the temple in Solomon’s day is now seen in the face of Jesus. John also sets much of Jesus’ ministry at Israel’s feasts: Passover, Tabernacles, and Dedication. At each one Jesus fulfills what the feast pictured. And when John the Baptist sees him coming, he says, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (1:29).

How John Shows Us Christ

  • Type fulfilled: Jesus is the true tabernacle and temple. “We have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (1:14). Later he says of his body, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (2:19).
  • Type fulfilled: Jesus tells Nicodemus, “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (3:14). The dying Israelites looked at the bronze serpent and lived (Numbers 21:8–9). Sinners look to the crucified Christ in faith and live.
  • Type fulfilled: The manna in the wilderness fed Israel for a day. Jesus says, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (6:35). Our fathers ate manna and died, but whoever feeds on Christ by faith lives forever (6:49–51).
  • Promise fulfilled: John notes that the soldiers did not break Jesus’ legs, “that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of his bones will be broken’” (19:36). That was a rule for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46). Jesus is the Passover Lamb.
  • Echo: Jesus’ “I am” sayings echo the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14). When he says, “before Abraham was, I am” (8:58), his hearers pick up stones, because they understand the claim.

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed confessions read John 1 with the creeds of the early church. The Westminster Confession says that in Christ “two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion” (WCF 8.2). That is John 1:1 and 1:14 held together.

D. A. Carson, whose commentary on John is widely used, argued in a 1987 article on John 20:31 that “the Fourth Gospel is primarily evangelistic after all.” In other words, John wrote first of all to bring readers to faith, though believers are richly fed by it too. John is an evangelistic book. It is also a deeply Reformed one: no one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws him (6:44), and all that the Father gives to the Son will come to him, and the Son will never cast them out (6:37). Calvin and Grudem, Presbyterian and Baptist, agree on this. Sovereign grace and the free offer of the gospel stand side by side in John.

For Today

John wrote so that you would believe and have life. Do not read today as a spectator. Thomas doubted, and Jesus came to him and showed him his wounds. Thomas answered with the highest confession in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” (20:28). Jesus is the bread you need today, the light for your path, the shepherd who knows your name, and the resurrection and the life. Come to him again, and he will not cast you out.

Reflect

  1. Which of Jesus’ “I am” sayings do you most need to hear today, and why?
  2. How does knowing that the Father draws people to Christ change the way you pray for those who do not yet believe?

Pray

Lord Jesus, eternal Word, you were with God and you are God, and you became flesh and pitched your tent among us. Thank you that I have seen your glory, full of grace and truth, in the gospel. You are the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and the bread of life. Keep me believing, and give me life in your name. My Lord and my God, amen.

family.scriptureText: And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
family.context: The birth arrives in crowded inconvenience. “No place” is not a sentimental detail; it shows the Son of God entering a world that does not rearrange itself for him. Holiness arrives in borrowed space. Crowded inns and full calendars still miss him. The detail stings because it is familiar. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus begins his earthly life as welcome-without-room—anticipating a ministry of rejection and a cross outside the city. Yet he came anyway. Our connection to him starts with his willingness to enter our crowded, unready world. He came anyway—this is gospel stubbornness of love entering unready spaces. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Make room deliberately: clear ten minutes, clear a grievance, clear a seat at your table. Hospitality to Jesus often looks like interrupting your inn-full schedule for what matters. Clear room in the evening: fewer inputs, more attention to the Son who arrived without fanfare. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: Where is there “no room” for Jesus in our current pace—and what will we move to welcome him?
family.prayer: Jesus, you entered a world with no place for you. We make room for you tonight. Be at the center of our Christmas and our home. Amen.

devo.title: The Risen King Pours Out His Spirit to the Ends of the Earth
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Acts 1:1–11 — Witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the end of the earth
  2. Acts 2:14–41 — Peter’s Pentecost sermon and the promise “for you and for your children”
  3. Acts 10:34–48 — The Spirit falls on the Gentiles
  4. Acts 15:12–21 — David’s fallen tent rebuilt

Old Testament background: Joel 2:28–32; Psalm 16:8–11; Amos 9:11–12

The Book and Its Themes

Acts is Luke’s second volume. His Gospel told “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (1:1), and Acts tells what the risen Jesus continues to do by his Spirit through his church. The book follows the pattern of 1:8: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (1:8). Chapters 1–7 are centered in Jerusalem, chapters 8–12 move into Judea and Samaria, and chapters 13–28 follow Paul’s missionary journeys until he preaches in Rome “with all boldness and without hindrance” (28:31). Its themes are the ascension and reign of Christ, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, the preaching of the resurrection, the inclusion of the Gentiles, suffering for the name, and the unstoppable growth of the word of God. Luke keeps reporting that “the word of God continued to increase” (6:7; 12:24; 19:20).

Where Acts Stands in the Covenant Story

At Babel, God scattered the nations and confused their languages (Genesis 11). At Pentecost, the Spirit enables the apostles to declare in the languages of the nations “the mighty works of God” (2:11). At Sinai, the law came with fire and three thousand died after the golden calf (Exodus 32:28). At Pentecost, the Spirit comes with fire, and about three thousand are saved (2:41). The new covenant promise that God would put his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:27; Joel 2:28) is now being kept. Abraham was promised that in his offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed. Peter tells the crowd at the temple that this promise is now being fulfilled through the risen Servant Jesus (3:25–26).

How Acts Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: Peter says Pentecost is what “was uttered through the prophet Joel” (2:16). The Spirit is poured out on all flesh, sons and daughters, young and old, and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.
  • Promise fulfilled: Peter argues from Psalm 16 that David, being a prophet, foresaw the resurrection of the Christ, whose flesh would not see corruption (2:25–31). From Psalm 110 he proves that Jesus is now seated at God’s right hand (2:34–35). The ascended Jesus is the one who “has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing” (2:33).
  • Promise fulfilled: At the Jerusalem Council, James cites Amos 9:11–12. God is rebuilding the fallen tent of David so that the Gentiles may seek the Lord (15:15–17). The Messiah’s kingdom now includes the nations without circumcision.
  • Type fulfilled: Stephen’s speech traces Israel’s history from Abraham to Solomon’s temple and concludes that “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands” (7:48). The temple pointed to a better dwelling place: Christ and the Spirit-filled people of God.

Through Reformed Eyes

Acts is where the Reformed family disagrees most openly, so it is worth being careful and kind.

On baptism, paedobaptists point to Peter’s words in 2:39, “the promise is for you and for your children” (2:39), and to the household baptisms of Lydia and the Philippian jailer (16:15, 33). Calvin, commenting on 2:39, stressed that the promise must be applied personally: “this is the rule of a true faith, when I am thus persuaded that salvation is mine, because that promise appertaineth unto me which offereth the same.” The Westminster Confession concludes that “the infants of one, or both, believing parents, are to be baptized” (WCF 28.4). Baptists note that the same verse continues, “and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself” (2:39), and that in Acts those baptized are those who “received his word” (2:41). Grudem summarizes his own view in his teaching outline: “My position is Baptistic – namely, that baptism is appropriately administered only to those who give a believable profession of faith in Jesus Christ.” The 1689 Confession calls professing believers “the only proper subjects of this ordinance” (29.2).

On spiritual gifts, Grudem reads Acts and 1 Corinthians as continuationist: the miraculous gifts were not limited to the apostles. Many confessional Reformed teachers are cessationist and see the sign gifts as tied to the founding of the church. All agree that the Spirit’s great work is to exalt Christ. J. I. Packer put it memorably: “The Spirit’s message is never, ‘Look at me; listen to me; come to me; get to know me,’ but always ‘Look at him, and see his glory; listen to him, and hear his word; go to him, and have life; get to know him, and taste his gift of joy and peace.’”

For Today

The same ascended Lord who sent his Spirit at Pentecost still reigns, and his word still grows. You are part of the story Acts left open, since it ends with Paul preaching in Rome and no final chapter. Whatever your Jerusalem is today, your home, your workplace, your town, you are a witness there. You do not need to manufacture power. Ask for the Spirit, open your mouth, and point to Jesus.

Reflect

  1. Who in your own “Jerusalem” needs to hear the good news of the risen Christ from you?
  2. Where do you need to rely on the Spirit’s power rather than your own ability?

Pray

Lord Jesus, risen and ascended King, thank you for pouring out your Spirit on your church and keeping the promise you made through Joel. Thank you that the gospel has come from Jerusalem all the way to us. Fill me with your Spirit, make me bold, and let my words point to you and not to me. Let your word increase and multiply in our land. Amen.

family.theme: Glory to God, Peace on Earth
family.scriptureText: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!”
family.context: Heaven’s army appears not for battle but for praise. Glory rises to God; peace is announced toward people as a gift of his favor. Christmas rearranges both worship and human relationships. Heaven’s host praises; earth is offered peace as gift. Christmas is vertical glory and horizontal healing. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Peace on earth arrives because God is pleased to save through his Son. Jesus is our peace (Ephesians 2:14)—reconciling us to God and breaking dividing walls. Glory and peace meet in him. Jesus himself is our peace—with God first, then among people he is joining together. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Practice the double movement: speak glory to God aloud, then take one peacemaking step on earth—gentle words, a repaired tone, a blessing spoken over someone. Make one peacemaking move that matches the song you sing. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: How can our family join heaven’s song—glory to God—and embody peace with someone nearby?
family.prayer: Glory to you, God in the highest. Through Jesus, give us peace on earth in our relationships. Let your favor shape our home. Amen.

devo.title: The Righteousness of God Revealed
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Romans 1:16–17; 3:21–26 — The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ
  2. Romans 4:1–8, 18–25 — Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness
  3. Romans 5:12–21; 6:1–11 — Two Adams, and union with Christ in his death and resurrection
  4. Romans 8:28–39 — No condemnation, no separation

Old Testament background: Genesis 15:1–6; Habakkuk 2:4; Psalm 32:1–2

The Book and Its Themes

Romans is Paul’s fullest explanation of the gospel. He wrote it around AD 57 to a church he had not yet visited, hoping they would help send him on to Spain. The gospel, he says, is “the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (1:16), because in it “the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith” (1:17). The argument moves in great steps. All people, Jews and Gentiles alike, are under sin (1:18–3:20). God justifies sinners freely by his grace through faith in Christ, whom he put forward as a propitiation by his blood (3:21–5:21). Those who are justified are united to Christ and set free to live a new life by the Spirit (6–8). God has not abandoned his promises to Israel (9–11). And the mercies of God call us to present our bodies as living sacrifices in the church and the world (12–16).

Where Romans Stands in the Covenant Story

Romans reads the whole Old Testament story through two heads: Adam and Christ. “Sin came into the world through one man” (5:12), and death reigned from Adam to Moses. Then God made a promise to Abraham, who was counted righteous by faith before he was circumcised, so that he would be “the father of all who believe” (4:11). The law of Moses came in “to increase the trespass” (5:20) and to show sin for what it is. But the law was never God’s way of giving life to sinners. “The law and the Prophets bear witness” (3:21) to a righteousness that comes by faith. Paul quotes Habakkuk: “The righteous shall live by faith” (1:17). In Christ, the last Adam, God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do (8:3).

How Romans Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: The gospel is “promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh” (1:2–3). Romans opens with the Old Testament and the Davidic promise.
  • Type fulfilled: Adam “was a type of the one who was to come” (5:14). One man’s disobedience brought condemnation to all in him; one man’s obedience brings justification and life to all in him (5:18–19). This is the covenant headship we saw in Genesis, now fulfilled.
  • Type fulfilled: God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (3:25). The word recalls the mercy seat on the ark, where the blood of atonement was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Christ is the place where God’s wrath is turned away and his justice is satisfied.
  • Promise fulfilled: Abraham and David are Paul’s two witnesses that justification is by faith apart from works (4:1–8). God’s promise that Abraham would be the father of many nations is being kept as Gentiles believe (4:16–18).

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin loved Romans. In the Argument to his commentary he wrote that “when any one gains a knowledge of this Epistle, he has an entrance opened to him to all the most hidden treasures of Scripture.” The Reformation doctrine of justification came straight out of Romans 3–5. The Westminster Confession states it carefully: “Those whom God effectually calleth, he also freely justifieth: not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous” (WCF 11.1), not for anything done by them, “but for Christ’s sake alone.” The 1647 Shorter Catechism puts it in one sentence: “Justification is an act of God’s free grace, wherein he pardoneth all our sins, and accepteth us as righteous in his sight, only for the righteousness of Christ imputed to us, and received by faith alone” (Q. 33).

Romans 6:3–4 is where baptism enters the argument: “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death” (6:4). Grudem, a Baptist, argues that “the symbolism of union with Christ in his death, burial, and resurrection seems to require baptism by immersion.” The 1689 Confession likewise calls baptism “a sign of his fellowship with him, in his death, and resurrection; of his being engrafted into him” (29.1). Presbyterians agree that baptism signifies union with Christ, but they see it as a sign of the covenant given to believers and their children, and they do not require immersion. Romans 9–11 also divides friends: some Reformed teachers expect a large-scale future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ (11:25–26), and others read “all Israel” as the full number of God’s people. Everyone agrees that God’s word has not failed (9:6).

For Today

Romans 8 begins with “no condemnation” and ends with “no separation.” Everything in between is the work of God for you in Christ. If you are in Christ, the verdict on the last day has already been announced. That is not a license for sin; Paul answers that objection firmly in chapter 6. It is the ground of a free and grateful life. Today, when your conscience accuses you, answer it with Romans 8:1 and 8:34: Christ died, he was raised, and he intercedes for you.

Reflect

  1. Where are you still trying to add your own performance to Christ’s righteousness?
  2. Which of the “no separation” promises in Romans 8:35–39 do you most need to believe today?

Pray

Righteous Father, I confess that I have sinned and fall short of your glory. Thank you for putting forward your Son as a propitiation by his blood, so that you are just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Thank you that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Teach me to walk in newness of life, and keep me sure that nothing in all creation can separate me from your love in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger. And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them. But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
family.context: Shepherds hurry, see, and speak. Crowds wonder. Mary treasures and ponders—holding mystery with care. Faith needs both proclamation and quiet reflection. Haste and pondering both belong to faith. Some run to tell; some treasure quietly; the child is worth both. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing. Take one more breath before moving on: God is speaking through this text to a real household with real needs.
family.jesusConnection: The child in the manger is worth hastening toward and pondering long. Jesus invites both witness and wonder. Knowing him is not only collecting facts; it is treasuring him in the heart. Jesus is not less wondrous after many Decembers. Pondering resists numbness. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love. Hold onto this: Jesus is not watching from a distance to grade you; he is the Savior who draws near and gives what he commands.
family.application: After the noise of the season, take two quiet minutes to ponder one truth about Jesus without fixing or planning. Let wonder catch up to activity. Protect two minutes of quiet after this reading before the next task claims you. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy. Choose the next right minute—not the perfect month—and take it together.
family.talk: What about Jesus do we need to treasure and ponder more slowly, instead of rushing past?
family.prayer: Jesus, like the shepherds we come to you; like Mary we want to treasure you. Settle your truth in our hearts beyond the noise. Amen.

devo.title: Christ Our Passover, Christ the Firstfruits
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 1 Corinthians 1:18–31 — Christ crucified, the power and wisdom of God
  2. 1 Corinthians 5:6–8; 10:1–4, 16–17 — Christ our Passover, the spiritual Rock, one bread
  3. 1 Corinthians 12:4–13 — One Spirit, many gifts, one body
  4. 1 Corinthians 15:1–8, 20–28, 54–58 — Christ raised as the firstfruits

Old Testament background: Exodus 12:1–13; Leviticus 23:9–14; Isaiah 25:6–9

The Book and Its Themes

Corinth was a wealthy port city, proud, divided, and famous for its immorality. The church Paul planted there reflected its city. The believers were splitting into fan clubs around favorite teachers, tolerating sexual sin, suing one another, abusing the Lord’s Supper, competing over spiritual gifts, and doubting the bodily resurrection. Paul answers every problem by bringing them back to the cross and the resurrection. “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” (1:23), but to those who are called, Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1:24). The book also contains the great chapter on love (13) and the fullest New Testament teaching on the resurrection (15). Its message is that the gospel reshapes everything: our pride, our bodies, our marriages, our worship, and our hope.

Where 1 Corinthians Stands in the Covenant Story

Paul reads the exodus as a story for the church. “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (10:1–2). They ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink, “and the Rock was Christ” (10:4). Yet most of them were overthrown in the wilderness. “Now these things took place as examples for us” (10:6). The same God who redeemed Israel from Egypt has redeemed the church through Christ, and the same warnings against idolatry and grumbling apply. At the Lord’s Table Paul quotes Jesus: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (11:25). The church lives in the new-covenant era, between the first coming of Christ and his return, when the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.

How 1 Corinthians Shows Us Christ

  • Type fulfilled: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (5:7). The lamb of Exodus 12, whose blood turned away the destroyer, pointed to Jesus. So Paul tells the church to clean out the old leaven of malice and evil and to keep the feast with sincerity and truth.
  • Type fulfilled: “The Rock was Christ” (10:4). The water that flowed from the rock in the wilderness was a gift of grace through Christ to the old covenant people.
  • Type fulfilled: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (15:20). At the Feast of Firstfruits, the first sheaf of the harvest was waved before the Lord as a pledge of the whole harvest (Leviticus 23:10–11). Christ’s resurrection is the first sheaf, and ours will follow.
  • Promise fulfilled: “Death is swallowed up in victory” (15:54) quotes Isaiah 25:8. “O death, where is your sting?” (15:55) echoes Hosea 13:14. The prophets promised that God would defeat death itself, and the risen Christ has begun to do it.

Through Reformed Eyes

1 Corinthians 12–14 is the classic battleground over spiritual gifts. Wayne Grudem is the best-known Reformed continuationist. His teaching outline defines it this way: “The gift of prophecy in the NT is telling something that God has spontaneously brought to mind.” He argues that such prophecy does not carry the authority of Scripture and must be tested (14:29). Many confessional Reformed teachers are cessationist, holding that revelatory gifts ceased with the apostles and the completion of the canon. Both sides agree that the Bible alone is the final authority, that love is greater than any gift (chapter 13), and that everything must be done “decently and in order” (14:40).
