On the Lord’s Supper (10:16; 11:23–26), Calvin taught that believers truly feed on Christ by faith through the Spirit, not by a change in the bread and not by mere remembrance. Many Reformed Baptists hold the same view; the 1689 Confession closely follows Westminster on the Supper. On 15:24–28, Christ reigns “until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (15:25). Wilson reads this with postmillennial optimism, expecting the gospel to subdue the nations before Christ returns. Amillennial and premillennial Reformed teachers read the same verses as describing Christ’s present heavenly reign and final victory. All agree that “the last enemy to be destroyed is death” (15:26).

For Today

The Corinthians were impressed by status, eloquence, and spiritual show. Paul told them that God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God” (1:29). Christ Jesus is our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption (1:30). Today, let the resurrection steady you. Because Christ is raised, “your labor is not in vain” (15:58). Every act of faithful work, every word of love, and every quiet act of obedience in the Lord counts.

Reflect

  1. In what ways are you tempted to boast in something other than Christ?
  2. How would living in the light of the coming resurrection change one ordinary decision today?

Pray

Lord Jesus, you are our Passover Lamb, sacrificed for us, and the firstfruits of the resurrection. Thank you that you have been raised and that death is swallowed up in victory. Humble my pride, heal the divisions among your people, and make our church a body that loves. Help me to be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in your work, knowing that my labor in you is not in vain. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world. He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.
family.context: Hebrews stacks breathtaking claims: the Son is heir, creator, radiance of glory, exact imprint, upholder of all things—and the one who made purification for sins and sat down. The manger child is this cosmic Son. Hebrews will not let us keep Jesus small. The speaking Son is creator, radiance, and purifier. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Christmas is God speaking by his Son. Jesus connects us to God’s glory and to purified nearness: he sat down because the purifying work is finished. We worship a Lord both cradled and enthroned. He sat down—finished purification—so Christmas worship includes rested confidence, not only sentiment. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Hold two truths together tonight: Jesus is near enough for a manger and mighty enough to uphold all things. Let that steady both affection and reverence in your worship. Let reverence and nearness share the same prayer tonight. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: How does knowing Jesus upholds the universe and also made purification for sins change how we approach him?
family.prayer: Son of God, radiance of glory—thank you for speaking to us, purifying us, and sitting down as Lord. We worship you, manger-born and majesty-crowned. Amen.

devo.title: All the Promises of God Find Their Yes in Him
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 2 Corinthians 1:3–11, 18–22 — The God of all comfort, and every promise Yes in Christ
  2. 2 Corinthians 3:4–18 — Ministers of a new covenant, with unveiled faces
  3. 2 Corinthians 4:1–18; 5:14–21 — Treasure in jars of clay; the new creation and the great exchange
  4. 2 Corinthians 12:1–10 — “My grace is sufficient for you”

Old Testament background: Exodus 34:29–35; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Isaiah 53:4–6

The Book and Its Themes

2 Corinthians is Paul’s most personal letter. After 1 Corinthians, things got worse before they got better. Paul made a painful visit, wrote a severe letter, and faced a group of impressive “super-apostles” (11:5) who mocked his weak presence and unimpressive speech. In reply Paul opens his heart. He describes afflictions so heavy that he “despaired of life itself” (1:8), a thorn in the flesh that God would not remove, and a ministry carried in “jars of clay” (4:7). The theme of the book is power in weakness. God comforts us in all our affliction so that we can comfort others (1:4), and his power is made perfect in weakness (12:9). Along the way Paul gives some of the richest sentences in the Bible about the new covenant, the new creation, reconciliation, and generous giving (chapters 8–9).

Where 2 Corinthians Stands in the Covenant Story

Chapter 3 is one of the clearest New Testament explanations of the difference between the old and new covenants. When Moses came down from Sinai, his face shone so brightly that he put a veil over it (Exodus 34:29–35). Paul says the old covenant had real glory, but it was a “ministry of death, carved in letters on stone” (3:7) because it commanded without giving life. The new covenant, promised in Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36, is a “ministry of the Spirit” (3:8), written “on tablets of human hearts” (3:3). When a person turns to the Lord, “the veil is removed” (3:16), and “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image” (3:18).

How 2 Corinthians Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory” (1:20). This is the thesis of this whole devotional series.
  • Type fulfilled: The shining face of Moses was a fading glory. Christ is the image of God, and God has shone in our hearts “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6).
  • Promise fulfilled: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (5:17). Isaiah promised new heavens and a new earth and told Israel to “remember not the former things” (Isaiah 43:18; 65:17). The new creation has begun in the risen Christ.
  • Type fulfilled: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (5:21). The sin offerings of Leviticus and the Servant of Isaiah 53, who bore the sins of many, meet here in the great exchange.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin, commenting on 1:20, drew out the lesson that “all the promises of God rest upon Christ alone as their support,” and he called that truth one of the main articles of our faith. If you want to know whether a promise of God is for you, look first at Christ. All the promises are yes in him, and if you are in him by faith, they are yes for you.

2 Corinthians 5:21 is a key text for the Reformed doctrine of double imputation: our sin was counted to Christ, and his righteousness is counted to us. Packer, Sproul, and Grudem all teach this, and so do both the Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession. Chapter 3 also shows where Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists emphasize different things. Both see one covenant of grace running through Scripture. Baptists especially stress the newness Paul describes here: the new covenant is a ministry of the Spirit that writes the law on every member’s heart. Presbyterians stress that the same gracious covenant was really present under Moses, though veiled. Paul affirms both: glory then, and greater glory now.

For Today

New Year’s Day is a day for resolutions, and most of them are made in our own strength. 2 Corinthians offers a different start to the year: every promise of God is already Yes in Christ, and his grace is sufficient for you. You do not know what this year will bring. You may face affliction, pressure, and weakness. But “we do not lose heart” (4:16), because the God who raised Jesus will raise you too. Say your Amen to God’s promises today.

Reflect

  1. Which promise of God do you most need to claim in Christ as this year begins?
  2. Where do you need to stop hiding your weakness and let Christ’s power rest on you?

Pray

Father of mercies and God of all comfort, thank you that all your promises find their Yes in Jesus. As this new year begins, I bring you my plans and my fears. Thank you that you made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him I might become your righteousness. Shine in my heart with the light of the knowledge of your glory in his face. Let your grace be sufficient for me and your power be made perfect in my weakness. Through Jesus Christ, amen.

family.scriptureText: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works.
family.context: Paul calls Jesus’ coming an “appearing” of grace that saves and trains. Christmas looks forward to another appearing in glory. Between them, a purified people learn to live differently. Grace appears and trains—salvation that schools a people while they wait for glory. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Grace appears in Jesus our great God and Savior, who gave himself to redeem and purify us. He connects past appearing, present training, and future hope into one story of belonging to him. Jesus gave himself to redeem and purify; Christmas Eve is belonging language, not only candlelight. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: On Christmas Eve, let grace appear in how you treat one another: renounce a worldly passion (irritability, envy of others’ celebrations) and practice one zealous good work of love. Renounce one ungodly reflex and replace it with a zealous kindness before bed. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: How is Jesus’ appearing training us—not only comforting us—as we wait for our blessed hope?
family.prayer: Jesus, grace appeared in you. Redeem and purify us as your people. Teach us to live for you tonight as we wait for your glory. Amen.

devo.title: Sons of Abraham Through Faith
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Galatians 1:6–12 — No other gospel
  2. Galatians 2:15–21 — Justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law
  3. Galatians 3:6–14, 23–29 — The blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles
  4. Galatians 4:1–7 — Sent to redeem, so that we might be adopted as sons

Old Testament background: Genesis 12:1–3; Genesis 15:6; Deuteronomy 21:22–23

The Book and Its Themes

Galatians is Paul’s most urgent letter. He skips his usual thanksgiving and goes straight to the crisis: “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel” (1:6). Teachers had arrived in the churches of Galatia insisting that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be full members of God’s people. Paul saw that this was not a minor addition but a different gospel. If righteousness could be gained through the law, “then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21). The book defends Paul’s apostleship (chapters 1–2), argues from Scripture that justification is by faith (3–4), and shows that freedom in Christ is not license but life in the Spirit, which bears the fruit of love, joy, and peace (5–6). Martin Luther’s great commentary on Galatians (1535) made it a charter of Christian freedom for the Reformation and ever since.

Where Galatians Stands in the Covenant Story

Galatians gives a precise map of the covenants. God made a promise to Abraham and his offspring, and he ratified it before the law existed. “The law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void” (3:17). Why then the law? “It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made” (3:19). The law was a guardian until Christ came, so that we might be justified by faith (3:24). Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian. Paul’s allegory of Hagar and Sarah (4:21–31) contrasts slavery under Sinai with freedom in the Jerusalem above.

How Galatians Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: “The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you shall all the nations be blessed’” (3:8). The promise of Genesis 12:3 is being fulfilled as Gentiles believe in Christ.
  • Promise fulfilled: The promise was made “to Abraham and to his offspring” (3:16), singular, “who is Christ.” All who belong to Christ are therefore “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (3:29).
  • Type fulfilled: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (3:13). The curse of Deuteronomy 21:23 fell on him so that the blessing of Abraham might come to us.
  • Promise fulfilled: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (4:4–5). The seed of the woman of Genesis 3:15 has come.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin, commenting on 3:24, described the law as a schoolmaster for childhood. He wrote that “the law was the grammar of theology, which, after carrying its scholars a short way, handed them over to faith to be completed.” The law is good, but it was always meant to lead us to Christ. J. I. Packer drew out the warmth of 4:4–7: God sent his Son and his Spirit so that we would call him “Abba! Father!” Packer wrote, “If you want to judge how well a person understands Christianity, find out how much he makes of the thought of being God’s child, and having God as his Father.”

Galatians also shows how Reformed Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists frame the covenants. Westminster sees one covenant of grace administered first under the law and then under the gospel. The 1689 Confession says the covenant of grace was revealed “first of all to Adam in the promise of salvation by the seed of the woman, and afterwards by farther steps, until the full discovery thereof was completed in the New Testament” (7.3). Many Reformed Baptists read Sinai as a distinct covenant that served the promise until Christ. Both views reject the idea that anyone was ever saved by keeping the law, and both affirm that all believers, Jew and Gentile, are Abraham’s offspring in Christ.

For Today

The Galatians were tempted to add something to Christ. We are tempted the same way, adding our performance, our spiritual disciplines, or our church credentials as if they made us more acceptable to God. Paul says that in Christ “you are all sons of God, through faith” (3:26). You are not a slave trying to earn your keep. You are an heir. Today, go to God as a child goes to a father, and then walk by the Spirit, serving others in love with the freedom Christ has won.

Reflect

  1. What are you tempted to add to Christ as the basis of your acceptance with God?
  2. How does knowing you are an adopted son or daughter change how you pray?

Pray

Abba, Father, thank you for sending your Son, born of a woman and born under the law, to redeem me and adopt me into your family. Thank you that he became a curse for me so that the blessing of Abraham might come to me. Guard me from every false gospel and every attempt to earn what you have freely given. Let the fruit of your Spirit grow in me: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. In Jesus’ name, amen.

family.scriptureText: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
family.context: John defines love by God’s initiative. Love is not first our feeling upward; it is God sending his Son so we might live, and giving him as the atoning sacrifice for sins. Christmas and the cross interpret each other. John dismantles pride: love is defined by God’s sending, not by our spiritual temperature. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the manifest love of God—sent that we might live through him, and given as propitiation. Connecting to Jesus means receiving life we did not invent and mercy we did not deserve. Living through Jesus and being covered by his propitiation is the Christmas gift beneath every other gift. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: On Christmas Day, receive before you perform. Thank God that love started with him. Then let received love become given love in one concrete kindness under your roof. Receive first. Then give one kindness that looks like love already received. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: How does “not that we have loved God but that he loved us” free our Christmas from pressure and fill it with Jesus?
family.prayer: Father, you loved us first and sent your Son that we might live through him. Thank you for Jesus, the propitiation for our sins. We receive your love today. Amen.

devo.title: One New Man, One Temple, One Bride
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Ephesians 1:3–14 — Every spiritual blessing in Christ, chosen before the foundation of the world
  2. Ephesians 2:1–22 — Saved by grace; Jew and Gentile one new man and one holy temple
  3. Ephesians 4:1–16 — One body, gifts from the ascended Christ
  4. Ephesians 5:22–33; 6:10–18 — Christ and the church; the armor of God

Old Testament background: Genesis 2:18–24; Psalm 68:18; Isaiah 59:15–17

The Book and Its Themes

Ephesians soars. Its first half (chapters 1–3) is doctrine sung as praise. Paul blesses God for choosing us in Christ before the foundation of the world, for redemption through his blood, for the sealing of the Holy Spirit, and for God’s plan “to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him” (1:10). He reminds the Ephesians that they were “dead in the trespasses and sins” (2:1), but God, being rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ. “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (2:8). The second half (chapters 4–6) shows how this grace is lived out: walking in unity, putting off the old self, speaking the truth in love, submitting to one another in marriage, family, and work, and standing firm in the armor of God. The phrase “in Christ” or “in him” runs through the whole letter.

Where Ephesians Stands in the Covenant Story

Ephesians tells the Gentile believers what they once were: “separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world” (2:12). In Christ they have been “brought near by the blood of Christ” (2:13). The dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile has been broken down, and God has created “one new man in place of the two” (2:15). Together they are “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (2:19). The temple, where Gentiles were kept at a distance, is replaced by a living temple built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone (2:20–22). The promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed in his offspring has become a single family.

How Ephesians Shows Us Christ

  • Type fulfilled: Marriage itself was a picture from the beginning. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24, “the two shall become one flesh” (5:31), and then says, “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (5:31–32). Adam and Eve were a living sign of Christ and his bride.
  • Type fulfilled: The Jerusalem temple is fulfilled in the church, “a holy temple in the Lord… a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (2:21–22), with Christ as cornerstone (Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22).
  • Promise fulfilled: Paul applies Psalm 68:18 to the ascension: “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men” (4:8). The victorious divine warrior of the psalm is Christ, who gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers to build his church.
  • Echo: The armor of God (6:14–17) is drawn from Isaiah 59:17, where the LORD himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation. The armor we wear is the Lord’s own armor, and Christ is the one who first wore it into battle.

Through Reformed Eyes

Ephesians 1 is a fountain of Reformed teaching on election. Calvin, commenting on 1:4, wrote: “The foundation and first cause, both of our calling and of all the benefits which we receive from God, is here declared to be his eternal election.” The Reformed have always insisted that election is “in Christ.” We do not look for our election in some secret decree apart from him. We look to Christ, and in him we find the Father’s love.

Ephesians 2 also shapes the Reformed doctrine of the church. The Westminster Confession says that “the visible church, which is also catholic or universal under the gospel (not confined to one nation, as before under the law), consists of all those throughout the world that profess the true religion; and of their children” (WCF 25.2). The 1689 Baptist Confession instead describes those who profess the faith of the gospel as “visible saints,” of whom local churches ought to be made up (26.2), and it has no “and of their children.” That one phrase is the whole baptism debate in miniature. Doug Wilson’s emphasis on the visible, objective covenant community comes from Ephesians-like texts. Grudem emphasizes that the church is the community of all true believers. All agree with Paul that there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (4:5–6).

For Today

Ephesians begins in the heavenly places and ends in the kitchen, the bedroom, the workplace, and the battlefield. The grace that chose you before the world began is meant to shape how you speak to your wife, raise your children, treat your employees, and resist temptation. Today, pray Paul’s prayer for yourself and your family: that you would “comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (3:18–19).

Reflect

  1. Do you think of your election as something to argue about or as a reason for praise, as Paul does in 1:3–14?
  2. In which relationship (marriage, family, work, church) do you most need to live out the grace you have received?

Pray

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing. Thank you for choosing me in him before the foundation of the world, and for making me alive when I was dead in sin. Thank you for breaking down the wall of hostility and making us one family in Christ. Strengthen me with power through your Spirit, root me in love, and clothe me in your armor today. To you be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus forever. Amen.

family.scriptureText: In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it… The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.
family.context: After celebration, John reminds us: life is in the Word, light keeps shining, darkness does not win—even when the world fails to recognize its Maker. Recognition is not automatic; revelation continues. Unrecognized light still shines. The world’s failure to know him does not extinguish him. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the true light and the world’s Maker walking unrecognized. Union with him means living by his life-light when post-holiday gray returns. Darkness cannot overcome him—so it cannot finally overcome those who are in him. Life in Jesus means darkness is real but not ultimate for those who belong to the true light. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: When the season’s sparkle fades, do not assume Jesus fades. Open his Word tomorrow as deliberately as you opened gifts. Ask him to shine on one dark corner you have been avoiding. Open Scripture tomorrow as deliberately as you opened gifts—let ordinary days stay lit. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: Where do we need Jesus’ light to keep shining after the Christmas moments pass?
family.prayer: Jesus, in you is life and light. Darkness has not overcome you. Shine in us and make yourself known in our ordinary days. Amen.

devo.title: Every Knee Shall Bow
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Philippians 1:3–11, 19–26 — “To live is Christ, and to die is gain”
  2. Philippians 2:1–11 — The mind of Christ, who emptied himself and was exalted
  3. Philippians 3:4–14 — Counting all things loss to gain Christ and his righteousness
  4. Philippians 4:4–13 — Rejoice, pray, think, and be content in him

Old Testament background: Isaiah 45:22–25; Isaiah 52:13–53:12

The Book and Its Themes

Philippians is a thank-you letter written from prison. The church at Philippi, the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16), had supported him faithfully and sent a gift by Epaphroditus. Paul writes back with warmth and joy. The words “joy” and “rejoice” appear again and again, though Paul is in chains and facing possible execution. His secret is Christ. “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21). The letter’s themes are partnership in the gospel, humble unity in the church, the example of Christ’s humility and exaltation, the surpassing worth of knowing Christ, pressing on toward the goal, and contentment in every circumstance. At its center is one of the earliest and most magnificent hymns to Christ in the New Testament (2:6–11).

Where Philippians Stands in the Covenant Story

In chapter 3 Paul lists his old covenant credentials: “circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee” (3:5). He was blameless as to the righteousness under the law. But he now counts it all loss, even rubbish, “in order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (3:8–9). The privileges of Israel were real gifts from God, but they were never meant to be a ladder to climb. They were meant to point to the Messiah. Paul also calls believers “the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh” (3:3). The true people of God are those who are in Christ.

How Philippians Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: In Isaiah 45:23 the LORD swears, “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance” (Isaiah 45:23). Paul applies this oath to Jesus: at the name of Jesus “every knee should bow… and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (2:10–11). Words spoken by Israel’s God about himself are spoken about Jesus.
  • Type fulfilled: The pattern of humiliation and exaltation runs through Isaiah’s Servant, who is “high and lifted up” (Isaiah 52:13) after being despised and rejected (Isaiah 52:13–53:12). Christ “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him” (2:8–9).
  • Echo: Adam grasped at equality with God and fell. Christ, “though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (2:6). The last Adam reverses the first Adam’s grasping with self-giving obedience.

Through Reformed Eyes

John Frame built much of his theology around the confession that Jesus is Lord. In a short piece on the lordship of Christ, he notes that the Old Testament’s central confession is that the LORD is God, and he concludes, “so the confession ‘Jesus is Lord’ (Rom. 10: 9; 1 Cor. 12: 3; Phil. 2: 11; cf. John 20: 28; Acts 2: 36) summarizes the message of the New Testament.” Philippians 2 is the high point of that confession.

Philippians 3:9 is also one of the clearest texts on imputed righteousness. Paul does not want “a righteousness of my own” (3:9), but “the righteousness from God that depends on faith” (3:9). Calvin, Packer, Sproul, and Grudem all appeal to this verse. Philippians 2:12–13 shows the Reformed balance of grace and effort: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (2:12–13). We work because God works, never in order to make him work.

Doug Wilson has long made joyful Christian living a theme of his teaching, and Philippians shows why joy is not optional decoration. Paul commands it: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice” (4:4). Paul says this from a prison cell, which shows that joy is rooted in Christ, not in circumstances.

For Today

Paul learned contentment “in any and every circumstance” (4:12), not by gritting his teeth but by knowing Christ. “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (4:13) is not a promise of athletic success. It is a promise that Christ will strengthen you to be content in plenty and in want. Today, bring your anxieties to God with thanksgiving, and the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your heart and mind in Christ Jesus (4:6–7).

Reflect

  1. What would you have to count as loss in order to treasure Christ above everything?
  2. Where is God calling you to have the mind of Christ by humbling yourself for the good of others?

Pray

Lord Jesus Christ, though you were in the form of God, you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted you. I confess with every tongue that you are Lord. Teach me to count everything as loss compared to knowing you. Give me your mind, your humility, and your joy. Let your peace guard my heart today. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him… And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.
family.context: Luke sketches Jesus’ hidden years with growth language: strength, wisdom, favor. The eternal Son truly shared human development. Holiness can look like patient becoming. Jesus’ growth sanctifies the long middle of life—learning, stature, favor—not only crisis moments. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing. Take one more breath before moving on: God is speaking through this text to a real household with real needs.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus sanctifies ordinary growth. He connects us to God not only in miracles but in faithful maturing. Following him includes increasing in wisdom—learning, listening, and living under the Father’s favor. Following a Savior who increased in wisdom frees families to value formation over image. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love. Hold onto this: Jesus is not watching from a distance to grade you; he is the Savior who draws near and gives what he commands.
family.application: Choose one area to grow in wisdom this week as a family: slower speech, better listening, learning a truth from Scripture you have skimmed. Growth is a discipleship path, not a childhood-only theme. Pick a wisdom goal small enough to practice daily for a week. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy. Choose the next right minute—not the perfect month—and take it together.
family.talk: Where do we want to “increase in wisdom” together in the days ahead?
family.prayer: Jesus, you grew in wisdom and favor. Teach us to grow under the Father’s care—strong in grace, wise in love. Amen.

devo.title: The Substance Belongs to Christ
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Colossians 1:13–23 — The image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation, head of the church
  2. Colossians 2:6–15 — Fullness in Christ; circumcised and buried with him
  3. Colossians 2:16–23 — A shadow of the things to come
  4. Colossians 3:1–17 — Seek the things above; put on the new self

Old Testament background: Genesis 1:26–28; Proverbs 8:22–31; Leviticus 23:1–8

The Book and Its Themes

Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, and the church there had been planted by Epaphras, not by Paul himself. A troubling teaching had appeared, a mixture of Jewish food and festival rules, worship of angels, visions, and harsh treatment of the body (2:16–23). It promised spiritual fullness through extra rituals and experiences. Paul answers with Christ. The Son is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. For by him all things were created” (1:15–16). “In him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell” (1:19), and “you have been filled in him” (2:10). You do not need anything added to Christ. The letter then turns to the practical life of those who have been raised with Christ: setting minds on things above, putting off sin, putting on compassion and forgiveness, letting the word of Christ dwell richly, and living faithfully in the household.

Where Colossians Stands in the Covenant Story

Colossians reaches back to creation and forward to new creation. Christ is the one through whom all things were made and for whom all things exist (1:16). He is also “the firstborn from the dead” (1:18), the beginning of the new creation. Through his blood on the cross, God reconciles all things to himself (1:20). Paul then explains the old covenant ceremonies. Food laws, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths were “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (2:17). They were real and good in their time, like a shadow cast by someone approaching. Now the person has arrived. The new self is “being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (3:10), restoring what Adam lost.

How Colossians Shows Us Christ

  • Type fulfilled: Adam was made in the image of God to rule the world (Genesis 1:26–28). Christ is “the image of the invisible God” (1:15), the true image-bearer, and in him we are renewed in that image (3:10).
  • Echo: The language of 1:15–17 echoes Proverbs 8, where Wisdom was present at creation. Paul presents Christ as the personal Wisdom of God, in whom “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (2:3).
  • Type fulfilled: The feasts and Sabbaths of the law were shadows, and “the substance belongs to Christ” (2:17). Passover, Firstfruits, the Day of Atonement, and the Sabbath rest all find their reality in him.
  • Type fulfilled: Believers have received “a circumcision made without hands… by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism” (2:11–12). Physical circumcision pointed to the cutting away of the sinful nature, which Christ accomplishes.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin’s comment on 2:17 is vivid: “Those, therefore, who still adhere to those shadows, act like one who should judge of a man’s appearance from his shadow, while in the mean time he had himself personally before his eyes.” In the Institutes he made the same point about the whole Christian life. Since “the whole sum of our salvation, and every single part of it, are comprehended in Christ,” we must not look for even the smallest part of it anywhere else (2.16.19).

Colossians 2:11–12 is one of the key texts in the baptism debate. Paedobaptists (Calvin, Westminster, Frame, Wilson, Sproul) see here a direct link between circumcision and baptism: as the sign of the covenant was given to the children of Abraham, so it should be given to the children of believers. Baptists (Grudem, the 1689 Confession) answer that the circumcision Paul describes is spiritual, “made without hands,” and that the passage ties baptism to faith: “raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God” (2:12). Both agree that what matters most is the circumcision of the heart, which only Christ can give.

For Today

The false teachers in Colossae offered a “Christ plus” religion: Christ plus special experiences, Christ plus rules, Christ plus spiritual elitism. Every generation has its version. Paul’s answer is that you already have everything in Christ. You do not need to climb higher. You need to set your mind on things above, “where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (3:1). Today, let the word of Christ dwell in you richly. Sing to God with thankfulness, and do everything, in word or deed, in the name of the Lord Jesus (3:16–17).

Reflect

  1. What “Christ plus” message are you most tempted by?
  2. What would it look like for you to set your mind on things above today in a specific area of life?

Pray

Lord Jesus, you are the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, and the head of the church. All the fullness of God dwells in you bodily, and I am complete in you. Forgive me for looking for life in shadows when the substance is yours. Set my mind on things above, put to death what is earthly in me, and clothe me with compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, and love. Let your word dwell in me richly today. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened… If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!”
family.context: Jesus encourages persistent prayer with a Father comparison: even flawed parents give good gifts; how much more the heavenly Father. Asking, seeking, and knocking describe a relationship of trust, not a vending machine. Jesus normalizes persistent prayer with a Father who loves to give good gifts. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: We pray to the Father through the Son who taught us this confidence. Jesus reveals the Father’s heart and opens the way by his own mediation. Good gifts climax in the gift of himself and the Spirit. We ask through the Son who reveals the Father’s heart and secures our access. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: As the year ends, ask openly: what do we need to ask, seek, and knock for—wisdom, healing of a relationship, courage for a next step? Pray it simply together. Write the ask in one sentence and pray it without decorating it. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: What good gift from the Father are we being invited to ask for through Jesus as this year closes?
family.prayer: Father in heaven, through Jesus we ask, seek, and knock. Give good gifts according to your wisdom, and teach us to trust your heart. Amen.

devo.title: Waiting for His Son from Heaven
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 1 Thessalonians 1:2–10 — Turned to God from idols, waiting for his Son
  2. 1 Thessalonians 2:13; 4:1–8 — The word of God at work; called to holiness
  3. 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 — The Lord himself will descend; we will always be with the Lord
  4. 1 Thessalonians 5:1–11, 16–24 — Children of the day; rejoice, pray, give thanks

Old Testament background: Daniel 7:13–14; Daniel 12:1–3; Zephaniah 1:14–16

The Book and Its Themes

1 Thessalonians is one of Paul’s earliest letters, written around AD 50 to a young church he had been forced to leave after only a few weeks (Acts 17:1–10). He had been anxious for them, and when Timothy brought back good news of their faith and love, Paul wrote with relief and affection. He remembers how they “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven” (1:9–10). The letter has three great themes: thankfulness for the word of God at work in them, a call to holiness, especially sexual purity, and hope in the return of Christ. Every chapter ends with a reference to the Lord’s coming. The young believers were grieving over church members who had died, and Paul comforts them: the dead in Christ will rise first, and together we will meet the Lord.

Where 1 Thessalonians Stands in the Covenant Story

The Old Testament prophets spoke often of the day of the LORD, a day of judgment on the wicked and deliverance for God’s people (Joel 2; Amos 5; Zephaniah 1). Daniel saw one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14), and he foresaw a resurrection in which “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2). Paul tells the Thessalonians that this day is bound up with the return of Jesus. “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (5:2). For unbelievers it will bring sudden destruction. For believers it will bring salvation, “for God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us” (5:9–10).

How 1 Thessalonians Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: The day of the LORD in the prophets becomes the day of the Lord Jesus (5:2). The divine Judge and Deliverer of the Old Testament is the returning Christ.
  • Promise fulfilled: Daniel’s promise of resurrection is anchored in the resurrection of Jesus: “since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep” (4:14).
  • Echo: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God” (4:16). The trumpet and cloud recall Sinai, where the LORD came down in a thick cloud with a very loud trumpet blast (Exodus 19:16). The God who came down at Sinai will come again in his Son.

Through Reformed Eyes

Paul’s promise that “we who are alive… will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air” (4:17) is the main text for the rapture, and Reformed teachers read it differently from popular dispensational teaching. Wayne Grudem, a historic premillennialist, argues for a single return of Christ after the great tribulation. His teaching outline concludes: “It seems best to conclude that the church will go through the time of tribulation predicted by Jesus.” Amillennial and postmillennial Reformed teachers, including Calvin and Wilson, also see one visible return of Christ at the end, not a secret rapture followed by a second coming. Many point out that the word for “meet” was used for citizens going out to welcome a visiting ruler and then escorting him back into their city. On that reading, we rise to meet the King and return with him to the renewed earth.

On holiness, the Reformed tradition reads the words “this is the will of God, your sanctification” (4:3) as a call grounded in grace. The God who called us is the God who will sanctify us completely: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it” (5:24).

For Today

The Thessalonians were waiting, and waiting well. They worked with their hands, loved one another, grieved with hope, and lived as children of the day. Today you may be grieving someone who died in Christ. Paul does not tell you not to grieve. He tells you not to grieve “as others do who have no hope” (4:13). We will always be with the Lord. “Therefore encourage one another with these words” (4:18). Then, as you wait, “rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances” (5:16–18).

Reflect

  1. Does the return of Christ shape your daily life, or is it mostly a topic for debate?
  2. Who in your life needs to be encouraged today with the hope of the resurrection?

Pray

Lord Jesus, I wait for you from heaven, the Son who rescues us from the wrath to come. Thank you that you died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we will live with you. Comfort all who grieve with the hope of the resurrection. Sanctify me completely, spirit, soul, and body, and keep me blameless until your coming. You who call me are faithful, and you will surely do it. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
family.context: The Christian life is a race of endurance, not a sprint of vibes. Weights and clinging sin slow us. The key strategy is directional: looking to Jesus, who pioneered and completes faith and now sits enthroned. Endurance races need a focal point. Weights drop when eyes stay on Jesus. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus connects start and finish of faith. He endured the cross for joy—our redemption and his exaltation. Fixing our eyes on him means interpreting the year’s gains and losses through his finished work and present reign. He perfected faith by enduring the cross for joy; we run in his wake, not in parallel self-salvation. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Name one weight to lay aside before a new year—resentment, comparison, a habit that drains love. Then literally “look to Jesus”: read this passage again slowly as your closing focus. Lay aside the weight you named with a concrete next step—confession, deletion, apology. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: What weight or clinging sin do we need to lay aside so we can run looking to Jesus?
family.prayer: Jesus, founder and perfecter of our faith—we fix our eyes on you. You endured the cross for joy. Give us endurance and freedom to run with you. Amen.

devo.title: Stand Firm Until the Day of the Lord
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 2 Thessalonians 1:3–12 — Relief for the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed
  2. 2 Thessalonians 2:1–12 — The man of lawlessness and the breath of the Lord’s mouth
  3. 2 Thessalonians 2:13–17 — Chosen, called, and established
  4. 2 Thessalonians 3:1–13 — Pray for the word; do not grow weary in doing good

Old Testament background: Isaiah 11:1–5; Isaiah 66:15–16; Daniel 11:36–37

The Book and Its Themes

2 Thessalonians was written only a few months after the first letter. The persecution of the church had grown worse, and some had been shaken by a report, perhaps a forged letter, claiming that “the day of the Lord has come” (2:2). Some believers had stopped working, perhaps because they thought the end was so near that daily labor no longer mattered. Paul writes to steady them. He assures them that God is just and will repay those who afflict them (chapter 1). He corrects their confusion about the end by telling them what must happen first (chapter 2). And he commands the idle to work quietly and earn their own living, because “if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (3:10). The book’s themes are God’s justice, Christ’s final victory over evil, the security of the elect, and faithful, ordinary work while we wait.

Where 2 Thessalonians Stands in the Covenant Story

Paul’s description of Christ’s return draws heavily on the Old Testament. The Lord Jesus will be revealed “from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire” (1:7–8), echoing Isaiah 66:15, where the LORD comes in fire to render his anger. The man of lawlessness who “exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship” (2:4) recalls the arrogant king of Daniel 11:36. And his defeat echoes Isaiah 11:4, where the shoot from the stump of Jesse “shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked” (Isaiah 11:4). Paul says, “the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” (2:8). The messianic King of Isaiah 11 is the returning Jesus.

How 2 Thessalonians Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: The Branch from Jesse slays the wicked with the breath of his lips (Isaiah 11:4). Paul applies this directly to the Lord Jesus at his coming (2:8).
  • Promise fulfilled: The LORD’s fiery coming in judgment (Isaiah 66:15) is the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven (1:7). Again, what the prophets said of Israel’s God, the apostles say of Jesus.
  • Echo: Christ will come “to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed” (1:10). Isaiah foresaw the nations seeing the glory of the LORD (Isaiah 66:18–19). On that day, Christ’s glory will be reflected in his people.

Through Reformed Eyes

Chapter 2 is one of the hardest passages in the New Testament, and Reformed teachers handle it differently. Futurist readers, including Grudem, see the man of lawlessness as a final individual Antichrist who will appear before Christ returns. Many older Reformed writers, following the Reformers, identified him with the papacy as a long-running institution; the original Westminster Confession calls the Pope of Rome “that Antichrist, that man of sin” (WCF 25.6, 1646 text), and the 1689 Baptist Confession kept the same identification (26.4). American Presbyterian revisions later dropped it; the Orthodox Presbyterian text of 25.6 still denies that the pope is head of the church but no longer calls him the man of sin. Partial preterists such as Doug Wilson and R. C. Sproul have argued that many of the New Testament’s end-time warnings, especially Jesus’ Olivet Discourse, were fulfilled in the Jewish war and the destruction of the temple in AD 70; some apply this passage the same way. Paul himself said the Thessalonians already knew what was restraining (2:6), which we do not. Humility is in order.

What is clear is more important than what is debated. Paul gives thanks that “God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth” (2:13). Election does not make believers passive. It gives them courage to “stand firm and hold to the traditions” (2:15) they were taught. And it sends them back to ordinary work. Calvin and the Reformers taught that every lawful calling is a place to serve God. Doug Wilson has built much of his ministry on the same conviction: the hope of Christ’s reign should make Christians more diligent in this world, not less.

For Today

Speculation about the end can make Christians anxious or idle. Paul’s answer is neither panic nor withdrawal, but steady faithfulness. The Lord is faithful, and he will establish you and guard you against the evil one (3:3). Today, do the work in front of you well, and “do not grow weary in doing good” (3:13). The King is coming, and the best way to be ready is to be found faithful.

Reflect

  1. Do your thoughts about the end times make you more faithful in daily life, or more anxious and distracted?
  2. Where do you need to recommit to steady, diligent work as a way of serving Christ?

Pray

Lord Jesus, you will come in glory to be marveled at among all who have believed, and you will destroy every enemy with the breath of your mouth. Thank you that the Father chose us to be saved through the sanctifying work of the Spirit and belief in the truth. Keep me from fear and from idleness. Establish my heart in every good work and word. Direct my heart to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ. Amen.

family.scriptureText: So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom… Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days… Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!
family.context: Moses’ psalm faces human frailty honestly, then asks for wisdom that numbers days, joy rooted in steadfast love, and God’s establishing of ordinary work. Time becomes meaningful under mercy. Numbering days is wisdom, not morbidity. Moses asks for love-satisfied joy and established work. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: In Jesus, steadfast love is satisfied fully—morning mercies with a cross-shaped proof. He establishes work that seems small by joining it to his kingdom. Wisdom numbering days leads us to invest life in him. In Jesus, steadfast love has a face and established work joins kingdom purpose. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Review the year briefly without cruelty: where did you see God’s steadfast love? Offer tomorrow’s work to him to establish—school, job, home care—as kingdom-connected labor. Offer tomorrow’s ordinary labor to God as something he can establish. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: If we number our days with wisdom, what deserves more of our attention in Jesus’ name next year?
family.prayer: Lord, teach us to number our days. Satisfy us with your steadfast love in Jesus. Establish the work of our hands for your glory. Amen.

devo.title: One Mediator, One Household of God
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 1 Timothy 1:12–17 — “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners”
  2. 1 Timothy 2:1–7 — One God and one mediator, the man Christ Jesus
  3. 1 Timothy 3:1–16 — Overseers, deacons, and the mystery of godliness
  4. 1 Timothy 6:6–16 — Contentment, the good fight, and the King of kings

Old Testament background: Deuteronomy 6:4; Job 9:32–33; Psalm 110:1–4

The Book and Its Themes

1 Timothy is a letter from an older pastor to his younger colleague. Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus to deal with false teachers who were obsessed with myths, genealogies, and speculative uses of the law (1:3–7). Paul writes so that Timothy will know “how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth” (3:15). The letter covers prayer for all people and for rulers, the conduct of men and women in worship, the qualifications for elders and deacons, care for widows, the honor due to faithful elders, and warnings against the love of money. Running through it all is sound doctrine that produces godliness. The gospel is summed up in a “trustworthy saying”: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1:15).

Where 1 Timothy Stands in the Covenant Story

The Old Testament confessed that “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). It also showed the need for someone to stand between this holy God and sinful people. Job longed for an arbiter “who might lay his hand on us both” (Job 9:33). Moses stood in the gap for Israel, and the priests offered sacrifices on the people’s behalf. Psalm 110 promised a King who would also be “a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). In 1 Timothy Paul brings these threads together: “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (2:5–6). The household of God, the church, now carries forward the role Israel had: to hold out the truth to the nations.

How 1 Timothy Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: Job’s cry for an arbiter is answered. Christ Jesus is the one mediator, fully God and fully man, who can lay his hand on both God and us (2:5).
  • Type fulfilled: Moses and the priests stood between God and the people, but they were sinners who needed mediation themselves. Christ “gave himself as a ransom for all” (2:6), offering not an animal but himself.
  • Promise fulfilled: The “mystery of godliness” (3:16) is a hymn to Christ: “He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (3:16). The promised Son of David has been revealed, raised, preached to the nations, and enthroned.
  • Echo: Christ is “the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords” (6:15). Old Testament titles for the LORD over all earthly kings now belong to the one who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate (6:13).

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed tradition has always loved 1 Timothy 2:5. The Westminster Confession says, “It pleased God, in his eternal purpose, to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus, his only begotten Son, to be the Mediator between God and man, the Prophet, Priest, and King” (WCF 8.1). Calvin taught that “the office which he received from the Father consists of three parts,” prophet, king, and priest (Institutes 2.15.1). The 1647 Shorter Catechism, which we have been learning, says it the same way: “Christ, as our redeemer, executeth the offices of a prophet, of a priest, and of a king, both in his estate of humiliation and exaltation” (Q. 23).

1 Timothy 3 is also where Reformed churches organize their government differently. Presbyterians (Calvin, Westminster, Frame, Sproul, Wilson) see a plurality of elders in each church joined to wider assemblies such as presbyteries. Reformed Baptists such as Grudem also favor a plurality of elders but generally govern each congregation independently, with fellowship between churches. Both agree that elders must be “above reproach” (3:2), able to teach, and men of proven character in their homes.

For Today

Paul never got over being saved. He called himself the foremost of sinners, a former blasphemer and persecutor, and he said Christ saved him as an example of perfect patience for everyone who would believe (1:16). If Christ can save Paul, he can save you and anyone you are praying for. Today, take Paul’s instruction seriously and pray “for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions” (2:1–2), including our own leaders, since God “desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2:4).

Reflect

  1. Do you approach God through Christ the one mediator, or do you sometimes try to approach him on your own merits?
  2. Who in authority over you (in government, work, or church) do you need to pray for this week?

Pray

Immortal, invisible God, the King of the ages, thank you that there is one mediator between you and us, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom. Thank you that he came into the world to save sinners like me. Keep your church a pillar and buttress of the truth. Give our leaders wisdom, and let us live peaceful, quiet, godly lives. To you be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

family.scriptureText: But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness. “The Lord is my portion,” says my soul, “therefore I will hope in him.”
family.context: In a book of grief, hope rises by deliberate remembering: steadfast love, endless mercies, morning renewal, great faithfulness. The soul chooses the Lord as portion when circumstances feel empty. Hope in Lamentations is remembered, not mood-based. Mercy is morning-new because God is faithful. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the Lord’s portion made personal—Emmanuel whose mercies meet us each morning through finished redemption and living intercession. New Year hope is not optimism; it is faithfulness proven in Christ. Jesus is the portion that does not shrink when years change. New Year courage is his faithfulness. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: On New Year’s Eve, call mercy to mind out loud. Refuse both despair and self-hype. Say together: “The Lord is our portion”—and name Jesus as the reason that sentence holds. Speak “great is your faithfulness” over both regrets and hopes before midnight habits take over. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What mercy from God through Jesus do we need to call to mind so hope rises for the year ahead?
family.prayer: Faithful Lord, your mercies are new every morning. Jesus is our portion and our hope. We enter what comes next trusting your steadfast love. Amen.

devo.title: All Scripture Is Breathed Out by God
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 2 Timothy 1:8–14 — Grace given before the ages began; guard the good deposit
  2. 2 Timothy 2:1–13 — Be strong in grace; remember Jesus Christ, risen and the offspring of David
  3. 2 Timothy 3:10–4:5 — The sacred writings that make wise for salvation; preach the word
  4. 2 Timothy 4:6–18 — “I have fought the good fight”

Old Testament background: Numbers 16:5; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 19:7–11

The Book and Its Themes

2 Timothy is Paul’s last letter. He is in a Roman prison again, this time in chains like a criminal, and he knows that his death is near: “the time of my departure has come” (4:6). Many have deserted him. Only Luke is with him. He writes to Timothy, his “beloved child” (1:2), to pass on the baton. The letter’s themes are suffering for the gospel without shame, guarding the good deposit of sound teaching, entrusting it to faithful men who will teach others also (2:2), enduring like a soldier, an athlete, and a farmer, resisting false teachers, and above all, preaching the word in season and out of season. It ends with Paul asking for his cloak and his books, and with unshaken confidence: “The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom” (4:18).

Where 2 Timothy Stands in the Covenant Story

2 Timothy shows how the faith passes from one generation to the next. Timothy learned the Scriptures from childhood from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (1:5; 3:15). “The sacred writings” Timothy knew from childhood were the Old Testament, and Paul says they “are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (3:15). That is the claim of this whole devotional: the Old Testament leads to Christ. Paul also roots the gospel in the Davidic covenant: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel” (2:8). The promised son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16) is the risen Lord.

How 2 Timothy Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: Jesus is “risen from the dead, the offspring of David” (2:8). God promised David a son whose throne would be established forever, and the resurrection is how that promise is kept.
  • Promise fulfilled: God’s purpose and grace, “which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (1:9–10). What God purposed in eternity and promised in history has appeared in Christ.
  • Echo: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2:19) is taken from Numbers 16:5, where God distinguished his true people from Korah’s rebellion. In a time of false teaching, Christ the Lord still knows and keeps his own.

Through Reformed Eyes

2 Timothy 3:16 is the classic text on the inspiration of Scripture: “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (3:16). Calvin wrote on this verse that what distinguishes our religion from all others is that “we know that God hath spoken to us, and are fully convinced that the prophets did not speak at their own suggestion, but that, being organs of the Holy Spirit, they only uttered what they had been commissioned from heaven to declare.” J. I. Packer defended the same truth in “Fundamentalism” and the Word of God (1958) and was a leading framer of the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978). John Frame’s The Doctrine of the Word of God (2010) presents Scripture as the personal word of the covenant Lord. Grudem’s Systematic Theology opens with Scripture for the same reason. On this point all of our teachers stand together.

2 Timothy 2:2 also shows why the Reformed tradition prizes a trained, faithful ministry and teaching the next generation. Doug Wilson’s work in classical Christian education grows out of the conviction that children should be taught the sacred writings from childhood, as Timothy was. Families do the same work every time they open the Bible together at the table.

For Today

Paul at the end of his life did not boast about his achievements. He said he had fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith, and that a crown of righteousness was waiting for him and “to all who have loved his appearing” (4:8). Today, open the Scriptures with confidence that they are God’s own breath. Let them teach, reprove, correct, and train you. And think about who you are passing the faith on to, in your family, your church, or your work. That is how the gospel travels through the generations.

Reflect

  1. Who taught you the Scriptures, and who are you teaching them to now?
  2. Where are you tempted to be ashamed of the gospel or to avoid suffering for it?

Pray

Lord God, thank you that all Scripture is breathed out by you and is able to make me wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. Thank you for those who taught me your word. Help me to guard the good deposit, to be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and to pass the faith to others who will teach others also. Give me courage to finish my race and keep the faith, longing for the appearing of Jesus. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Pray then like this: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.”
family.context: Jesus teaches prayer that starts with God—Father, holy name, kingdom, will—before daily bread and personal need. The year’s first posture is worship and surrender, not self-launch. Jesus’ model prayer prioritizes God’s name and will before our list. That order is mercy for anxious planners. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: We pray “Father” because Jesus brings us home as siblings with him. Kingdom and will center on the King’s agenda. Starting the year with this prayer aligns a household with Jesus’ own priorities before the Father. Because Jesus brings us to the Father, “our” Father is a shared family address for the year. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: Pray the first lines slowly as a family dedication of the year. Then ask what “your will be done” might mean in one practical arena—speech, calendar, generosity. Dedicate the year with those first lines, then attach one practical “will be done” to your calendar. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: What would it look like for God’s name to be hallowed and his will sought first in our home this year?
family.prayer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done—in our family on earth as in heaven—through Jesus our Lord. Amen.

devo.title: The Grace of God Has Appeared
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Titus 1:1–9 — The hope of eternal life promised before the ages began; elders for every town
  2. Titus 2:1–10 — Sound doctrine for every age and station
  3. Titus 2:11–15 — Grace has appeared, training us, as we wait for our great God and Savior
  4. Titus 3:3–8 — The washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit

Old Testament background: Exodus 19:5–6; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Deuteronomy 14:2

The Book and Its Themes

Paul had left Titus on the island of Crete to “put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town” (1:5). The Cretans had a reputation for dishonesty and laziness, and Paul even quotes one of their own poets on the subject (1:12). False teachers were upsetting whole families for shameful gain. Paul’s answer is that sound doctrine must produce good works. The word “good works” appears again and again (1:16; 2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14). The short letter has two of the most beautiful summaries of the gospel in the New Testament (2:11–14 and 3:4–7), and each one is followed by practical instructions for older men, older women, young women, young men, and servants, and for believers living under governing authorities. Titus teaches that grace does not only pardon. It trains.

Where Titus Stands in the Covenant Story

At Sinai God told Israel, “you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples” (Exodus 19:5). Titus 2:14 echoes this directly: Christ “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (2:14). The redemption from Egypt has become redemption from lawlessness, and the treasured people now includes Cretans. Titus 3:5 also echoes the new covenant promise of Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises to sprinkle clean water on his people, give them a new heart, and put his Spirit within them. Paul says God “saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior” (3:5–6).

How Titus Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: The hope of eternal life was promised by “God, who never lies… before the ages began” (1:2), and has now been revealed in the preaching of the gospel (1:3).
  • Type fulfilled: Israel was God’s treasured possession, redeemed from Egypt. The church is “a people for his own possession” (2:14), redeemed by Christ, who gave himself for us.
  • Promise fulfilled: Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing water and a new Spirit is fulfilled in “the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (3:5), poured out through Jesus Christ.
  • Echo: Christians wait for “the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:13). Like the shining glory of the LORD in the tabernacle, Christ’s glory will be revealed. This verse is one of the clearest New Testament statements that Jesus is God.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin, commenting on 2:13, drew a straight line from hope to holiness: “if that hope be deeply seated in our mind, it is impossible that it should not lead us to devote ourselves wholly to God.” That is why Titus moves so easily from the second coming to self-control and good works. Grace that has appeared trains us to renounce ungodliness, and grace that will appear keeps us looking up.

Titus 3:5 is another place where the Reformed family reads differently. Many Presbyterian interpreters see “the washing of regeneration” (3:5) as connected to baptism, the outward sign of the inward washing the Spirit gives. Baptists, including Grudem, emphasize that the washing is the Spirit’s work of new birth, not the water itself. The Westminster Confession is careful here as well: grace and salvation are not so inseparably annexed to baptism “as that no person can be regenerated, or saved, without it; or, that all that are baptized are undoubtedly regenerated” (WCF 28.5). Both sides agree on the main point Paul is making: we are saved “not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (3:5).

For Today

Titus shows that sound doctrine is not cold. It produces older men who are sober-minded, older women who teach what is good, young people who are self-controlled, and workers who are trustworthy, “so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (2:10). Your faithfulness in ordinary work and family life adorns the gospel, like a frame around a painting. Today, ask how your conduct at work and at home can make the teaching about Christ more attractive to those who watch you.

Reflect

  1. How is the grace of God training you right now to say no to something and yes to something better?
  2. In what ordinary area of life could you “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (2:10) this week?

Pray

God our Savior, thank you that your grace has appeared, bringing salvation for all people. Thank you that you saved me not because of works I have done, but according to your own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Train me to renounce ungodliness and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly in this present age, as I wait for the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. Amen.

family.scriptureText: We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.
family.context: Paul grounds ethics in union: buried with Christ, raised to walk new. Newness is not a calendar trick; it is resurrection life shared with Jesus. Death to the old self is the doorway. Baptismal union language makes newness theological: buried and raised with Christ. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Union with Jesus’ death and resurrection is the Christian’s deepest “new year.” We walk new because we are joined to the risen Christ by the Father’s glory—not because January magic resets us. Walking new is possible because resurrection life is shared, not because willpower reinvented you on January 1. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Identify one old pattern to bury with Christ again—bitterness, secrecy, harsh humor—and one newness to practice as risen people: honesty, blessing, Sabbath rest. Name the pattern to bury and the practice to walk—then ask for the Spirit’s power. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: What does walking in newness of life with Jesus look like for us in January, concretely?
family.prayer: Father of glory, we are united with Christ in death and resurrection. Help us walk in newness of life together by your power. Amen.

devo.title: Receive Him as You Would Receive Me
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Philemon 1–7 — Thanksgiving for Philemon’s love and faith
  2. Philemon 8–16 — Onesimus, once useless, now useful, a beloved brother
  3. Philemon 17–25 — “Charge that to my account”

Old Testament background: Exodus 21:1–6; Deuteronomy 23:15–16; Isaiah 53:4–6, 12

The Book and Its Themes

Philemon is the shortest of Paul’s letters, a single page, and the most personal. Philemon was a believer in Colossae, probably wealthy, who hosted a church in his house. His slave Onesimus had run away, perhaps after stealing from him (18), and somehow ended up with Paul in prison. There Onesimus became a Christian. Now Paul sends him back with this letter, appealing to Philemon to receive him “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (16). The name Onesimus means “useful,” and Paul plays on it: “Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me” (11). The letter’s themes are reconciliation, the power of the gospel to change relationships, love that appeals rather than commands, and the new family created in Christ.

Where Philemon Stands in the Covenant Story

The law of Moses regulated servanthood in Israel and placed limits on it. A Hebrew servant was to go free in the seventh year (Exodus 21:2). Kidnapping a person and selling him was a capital crime (Exodus 21:16). And Israel was told not to return a runaway slave to his master, but to let him live among them wherever he chose (Deuteronomy 23:15–16). These laws reminded Israel that they themselves had been slaves in Egypt and that the LORD had redeemed them. In Philemon, Paul does not issue a new civil law. Instead, he places a slave and a master in the same family of God, at the same table, under the same Lord. The gospel goes to the root.

How Philemon Shows Us Christ

  • Type fulfilled: Paul tells Philemon, “If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account” (18). This is a picture of substitution. The Servant of Isaiah 53 bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12). Christ took our debt on his account so that we could be received by the Father.
  • Echo: Paul says, “receive him as you would receive me” (17). In the same way, the Father receives us as he receives his Son, because we are in Christ (Ephesians 1:6).
  • Echo: The exodus pattern of redemption, from slavery to sonship, plays out in miniature. Onesimus, a slave, becomes “a beloved brother… both in the flesh and in the Lord” (16).

Through Reformed Eyes

Philemon raises hard questions. Why didn’t Paul simply condemn slavery outright? Christians have answered in different ways. Many Reformed teachers point out that the gospel works from the inside out. It did not start an armed revolt, but it planted principles (every person in God’s image, masters and slaves as brothers under one Master, Ephesians 6:9) that eventually undermined slavery in Christian lands. John Frame has written that Christians have greatly influenced Western culture, including in the abolition of slavery, and he urges believers to bring Christ’s lordship into all of public life: “In the general society as well as in the church, Christians should settle for nothing less than the comprehensive lordship of Jesus Christ.” At the same time, Christians must be honest that believers in history have also defended evil practices. The gospel judges us too.
