Philemon also shows the Reformed understanding of the church as a new family. In the house church at Colossae, a master and his former slave would now share the Lord’s Supper side by side. Grudem, Frame, and Wilson all stress that the church is meant to display a reconciled humanity. Whatever our station, we are “all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

For Today

Philemon asks you to do something hard: to receive someone who wronged you, not grudgingly but as a brother. You can do it because Christ said to the Father about you, “Charge that to my account.” Is there someone who owes you, someone who hurt you, someone you have written off as useless? Ask God to help you see that person as Paul saw Onesimus, as someone Christ may make useful. And if you are the one who has wronged someone, take courage. In Christ there is a way home.

Reflect

  1. Is there someone you need to receive as a brother or sister in Christ, despite a past wrong?
  2. How does knowing that Christ has taken your debt on his account change the way you treat those who owe you?

Pray

Lord Jesus, you took my debt and said to the Father, “Charge that to my account.” Thank you that I am received for your sake as a beloved child. Give me a heart like Paul’s, quick to reconcile and slow to command. Help me to receive those who have wronged me, to forgive as I have been forgiven, and to treat every brother and sister as one for whom you died. Make your church a family where all are one in you. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
family.context: Paul refuses both complacency and paralysis. He presses on because Christ already seized him. The past is neither erased nor enthroned; the upward call in Christ defines direction. Paul’s press-on energy is response to being already Christ’s possession. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Christ Jesus has made us his own—that is the engine. We pursue him because we are possessed by him. The prize is God’s upward call in Christ, not self-made achievement. Forgetting what lies behind is not amnesia; it is refusing to let the past be lord. Jesus is Lord. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Name one thing behind you to stop rehearsing, and one forward step of faithfulness in Jesus—reconciliation, a habit of Scripture, serving someone. Press on without pretending perfection. Choose one forward faithfulness and take it within three days. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: How does “Christ Jesus has made me his own” change the way we press on this year?
family.prayer: Christ Jesus, you have made us your own. We press on toward the upward call in you—forgetting what enslaves us behind, straining forward in grace. Amen.

devo.title: The Better Priest, the Better Sacrifice, the Better Covenant
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Hebrews 1:1–4; 2:14–18 — God has spoken by his Son; made like his brothers
  2. Hebrews 4:14–5:10 — A great high priest after the order of Melchizedek
  3. Hebrews 8:6–13; 9:11–14 — The new covenant and the blood that purifies the conscience
  4. Hebrews 10:11–25; 12:1–2 — One sacrifice for all time; looking to Jesus

Old Testament background: Genesis 14:17–20; Psalm 110:1–4; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Leviticus 16

The Book and Its Themes

Hebrews is a sermon written to Jewish Christians who were under pressure to go back. They had suffered for their faith, and now the old ways of temple, priesthood, and sacrifice looked safer and more solid than an invisible Christ. The author’s answer is one word: better. Jesus is better than the angels (chapters 1–2), better than Moses (3), better than Joshua’s rest (4), better than Aaron’s priesthood (5–7), and the mediator of a better covenant with better promises (8), a better sanctuary (9), and a better sacrifice (10). Then come the great chapter of faith (11), the call to run the race looking to Jesus (12), and practical exhortations (13). Woven through the argument are five solemn warnings against drifting away. The book’s thesis is in its first sentences: “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (1:1–2).

Where Hebrews Stands in the Covenant Story

No book in the Bible explains the relationship between the Old and New Testaments more fully. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34 at length, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, and concludes, “In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away” (8:13). The tabernacle was “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (8:5), and the law had “but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities” (10:1). The animal sacrifices had to be repeated, which proved they could never take away sins. Christ “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (9:26).

How Hebrews Shows Us Christ

  • Type fulfilled: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blessed Abraham and received his tithe (Genesis 14:18–20). Psalm 110:4 promised a priest forever after his order. Hebrews 7 shows that Jesus is that priest: king and priest in one, without beginning or end, superior to Levi.
  • Type fulfilled: On the Day of Atonement the high priest entered the Most Holy Place once a year with blood (Leviticus 16). Christ “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (9:12).
  • Promise fulfilled: The new covenant of Jeremiah 31 is now in force. God writes his laws on our hearts and “will remember their sins no more” (8:12), because Christ’s single offering “has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (10:14).
  • Type fulfilled: Joshua gave Israel the land but not final rest (4:8). Jesus brings God’s people into the true Sabbath rest (4:9–10).

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin said in the Argument to his commentary that Hebrews “so fully explains that Christ is the end of the Law.” On the first verse he noted that the author sets before us one God in both Testaments, “that no one might think that the Law militates against the Gospel, or that the author of one is not the author of the other.”

Hebrews is also where Presbyterian and Baptist covenant theology show their differences most clearly. Reformed Baptists point to Hebrews 8:10–11: in the new covenant “they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (8:11). They take this to mean that the new covenant community is made up of those who truly know the Lord, which is one reason they baptize professing believers. Presbyterians such as Calvin, Frame, Sproul, and Wilson read the same chapter as describing the fuller blessing of the one covenant of grace, which still includes believers and their children in its outward administration. The warning passages (6:4–8; 10:26–31) are another point of discussion. Wilson’s emphasis on the objective covenant leads him to say that real members of the visible covenant can fall away and be cut off, though he holds that God’s elect will persevere. Other Reformed teachers read the warnings as describing those who were never truly regenerate, and as God’s appointed means of keeping the elect persevering. Calvinists of every kind agree that those truly born again will persevere to the end.

For Today

Hebrews was written to tired Christians tempted to drift. If that is you, the cure is not trying harder. It is “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith” (12:2). You have a great high priest who sympathizes with your weaknesses and who was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (4:15). “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (4:16).

Reflect

  1. What “old ways” are you tempted to fall back on instead of resting in Christ’s finished work?
  2. How does knowing that Jesus sympathizes with your weakness change the way you pray?

Pray

Great High Priest, Lord Jesus, you entered the holy places once for all with your own blood and secured an eternal redemption. Thank you that your one sacrifice has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Thank you for the new covenant in which you remember our sins no more. When I am weary and tempted to drift, turn my eyes to you, the founder and perfecter of my faith. Help me to draw near to the throne of grace with confidence today. Amen.

family.theme: Wise and Foolish Builders at Work
family.scriptureText: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror and then goes away and at once forgets what he was like. But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.
family.context: James warns that hearing without doing is self-deception—like forgetting your face after a mirror glance. Blessing rests on persevering action shaped by the liberating word. The mirror metaphor exposes religious consumption without transformation. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: The Word we hear is fulfilled in Jesus, and he sends the Spirit so we can act. Doing the word is life in liberty under the Lord who first acted for us—not earning love, but embodying received truth. Doing the word is liberty under Jesus, because he fulfilled the law and empowers obedience by the Spirit. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Pick one truth from this 60-day journey you have heard and not yet practiced. Do it in the next 48 hours. Let the mirror become a path. Convert one heard truth from this series into a 48-hour action. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: What word from Jesus are we in danger of hearing only—and what is one doing step we will take?
family.prayer: Lord Jesus, free us from hearing-only faith. Make us doers of your word who persevere, blessed in the doing by your grace. Amen.

devo.title: Faith That Works and Wisdom from Above
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. James 1:2–8, 17–27 — Trials, wisdom, every good gift, doers of the word
  2. James 2:1–13 — No partiality; the royal law
  3. James 2:14–26 — Faith without works is dead
  4. James 3:13–18; 5:7–11 — Wisdom from above; the patience of Job and the coming of the Lord

Old Testament background: Genesis 22:1–18; Leviticus 19:15–18; Proverbs 2:1–11

The Book and Its Themes

James, the brother of the Lord and a leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19), wrote to Jewish believers “in the Dispersion” (1:1). His letter reads like the Wisdom literature of the Old Testament, especially Proverbs, and it is full of echoes of Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount. It moves quickly from topic to topic: joy in trials, asking God for wisdom, doing the word and not only hearing it, refusing favoritism to the rich, showing faith by works, taming the tongue, humility before God, the folly of boasting about tomorrow, warnings to the oppressive rich, patience until the Lord comes, and prayer for the sick. The book has about fifty commands in five chapters. James is not interested in a faith that only talks. He wants faith that does what God says.

Where James Stands in the Covenant Story

James stands in the line of the prophets and the wise men of Israel. Like Amos, he denounces the rich who oppress workers (5:1–6). Like Proverbs, he prizes wisdom that comes from God and shows itself in a good life (3:13–18). Like Leviticus 19, he commands love of neighbor without partiality (2:8–9). James calls this “the royal law” (2:8), the law of the King. He also speaks of “the perfect law, the law of liberty” (1:25). For James, the law is not a ladder to earn salvation. It is the shape of the new life God gives when he brings us forth “by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures” (1:18). This is new covenant language: the word implanted in the heart (1:21).

How James Shows Us Christ

  • Echo: James mentions Jesus by name only twice (1:1; 2:1), but his letter is saturated with Jesus’ teaching. “Let your ‘yes’ be yes and your ‘no’ be no” (5:12) echoes Matthew 5:37. The blessing on the poor (2:5) echoes Luke 6:20. James is the Sermon on the Mount put into practice.
  • Promise fulfilled: James calls Jesus “the Lord of glory” (2:1). The glory that filled the tabernacle and temple belongs to the risen Christ.
  • Type fulfilled: Abraham’s offering of Isaac (Genesis 22) showed that his faith was real (2:21–23). The ram provided in Isaac’s place, as we saw in Volume 1, points to the Lamb God provided. True faith rests on God’s provision and then obeys.
  • Echo: “You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful” (5:11). Job’s suffering and restoration point forward to the greater Sufferer whose patience ended in glory.

Through Reformed Eyes

James wrote that “a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (2:24), and the Council of Trent used those words against the Reformers. R. C. Sproul explains that there is no real conflict with Paul. Paul is talking about how a sinner is declared righteous before God. James is talking about how a claim to faith is shown to be genuine. As Sproul puts it, “True faith will absolutely and necessarily yield the fruits of obedience and the works of righteousness.” Calvin had made the same point in his commentary: in James 2 “the dispute here is not respecting the cause of justification, but only what avails a profession of faith without works.”

The Westminster Confession says that good works are “the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith” (WCF 16.2). That is exactly what James is saying. Grudem, Packer, Frame, and Wilson all agree. The Reformed slogan, often traced back to the Reformers, says it well: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

For Today

James is the most practical book in the New Testament. It will not let you hide behind correct doctrine. Today, choose one command from James and do it. Ask God for wisdom in a decision you are facing (1:5). Bridle your tongue in a conversation where you are tempted to speak in anger (1:19–20). Visit someone who is lonely or in need (1:27). Show no partiality to the rich or important (2:1). Faith that is alive will show itself in some small, concrete way today.

Reflect

  1. Is there a gap between what you believe and what you do in one specific area of life?
  2. Which of James’s commands is the Spirit pressing on you today?

Pray

Father of lights, every good gift and every perfect gift comes down from you. Thank you for bringing me forth by the word of truth. Give me wisdom from above, which is pure, peaceable, gentle, and full of mercy. Make me a doer of the word and not a hearer only. Tame my tongue, humble my pride, and let my faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, show itself in love and good works. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.”… And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh.
family.context: Foreign sages travel far to find a child-king. They ask, journey, rejoice, fall down, and give. Worship is costly seeking that ends in glad surrender of treasure. Epiphany wise men show that seeking Jesus may cross cultures and cost treasure. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is King of the Jews and Lord of the nations—worthy of Gentile worship from the start. Epiphany reveals him to outsiders. We connect to Jesus the way they did: seek, bow, give him our best. Falling down to worship a child declares his kingship; gifts answer his worth. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Offer Jesus a “treasure” tomorrow: time, praise, resources, or a skill used for someone’s good. Let January begin with worship gifts, not only resolutions. Decide the treasure you will open for him this week and follow through. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What treasure can we open for Jesus—the born King—as this season of revealing continues?
family.prayer: Born King Jesus, like the wise men we seek you and worship you. Receive the treasures of our hearts and hands. Lead us by your light. Amen.

devo.title: A Chosen Race, a Royal Priesthood
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 1 Peter 1:3–12 — Born again to a living hope; the prophets searched and inquired
  2. 1 Peter 1:17–25; 2:4–10 — Ransomed by precious blood; living stones and a holy nation
  3. 1 Peter 2:21–25; 3:18–22 — By his wounds you have been healed; Noah, baptism, and the risen Christ
  4. 1 Peter 4:12–19; 5:6–11 — Fiery trials and the God of all grace

Old Testament background: Exodus 19:5–6; Isaiah 53:4–9; Genesis 6:9–8:19

The Book and Its Themes

Peter writes to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey, calling them “elect exiles of the dispersion” (1:1). They were suffering slander and hostility for their faith, and Peter wants them to stand firm in “the true grace of God” (5:12). His themes are the living hope of the resurrection, the joy of salvation in the middle of trials, holiness because God is holy, the identity of the church as God’s people, submission and good conduct in a hostile world, Christ’s suffering as both our substitute and our example, and humble trust in the God who will restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish us after we have suffered a little while (5:10). Peter, who once denied Jesus to avoid suffering, now teaches others how to suffer well.

Where 1 Peter Stands in the Covenant Story

1 Peter takes the titles given to Israel at Sinai and gives them to the church. God told Israel, “you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). Peter tells believers, Jew and Gentile alike, “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (2:9). He quotes Hosea: “Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people” (2:10; Hosea 1:10; 2:23). The temple is now made of “living stones” built on Christ, the cornerstone of Isaiah 28:16 (2:4–6). And like Israel in Babylon, believers are “sojourners and exiles” (2:11) in this world, seeking its good while they wait for their true home.

How 1 Peter Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: The prophets “searched and inquired carefully” (1:10) about this salvation, asking what time “the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (1:11). The Old Testament prophets were preaching Christ, and they knew they were serving a later generation (1:12).
  • Promise fulfilled: 1 Peter 2:22–25 quotes and echoes Isaiah 53 more fully than any other New Testament passage: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth.... He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.... By his wounds you have been healed” (2:22, 24).
  • Type fulfilled: Christians are ransomed “with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1:19). The Passover lamb and the spotless sacrifices of the law point to him.
  • Type fulfilled: Noah and his family were “brought safely through water” (3:20) in the ark. Peter says, “Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (3:21).

Through Reformed Eyes

1 Peter 3:21 is a text every tradition must handle carefully. Peter says baptism saves, and then he immediately explains: not by washing the body, but as “an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.” Reformed Baptists such as Grudem stress that the baptism that saves is tied to the believer’s appeal to God, which fits their practice of baptizing those who profess faith. Presbyterians such as Calvin, Frame, Sproul, and Wilson stress that baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant whose saving power lies in Christ’s resurrection, not in the water. Both reject the idea that the water itself regenerates.

1 Peter 2:9 is the foundation of the Reformation doctrine of the priesthood of all believers. Every Christian, not only clergy, may come to God through Christ and offer “spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (2:5). And 1 Peter 2:24 and 3:18 (“Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God,” 3:18) are central texts for the penal substitution that Packer, Sproul, and Grudem defended.

For Today

Peter calls you an exile. That is not a sad word. It means you belong somewhere better. Your citizenship, inheritance, and hope are kept in heaven for you, “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1:4). So when you suffer for doing good, do not be surprised. Entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good (4:19). Today, take Peter’s counsel: “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (5:7).

Reflect

  1. Where do you feel most like an exile in your culture, and how does 1 Peter help you respond?
  2. How does knowing you are part of a royal priesthood shape the way you pray for others?

Pray

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus from the dead. Thank you for ransoming me with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless Lamb. Thank you that he bore my sins in his body on the tree, and by his wounds I am healed. Make me a living stone in your house and a faithful exile in this world. I cast all my anxieties on you, because you care for me. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
family.context: The risen Jesus claims total authority, then sends his people on a disciple-making mission with a Trinitarian baptismal name and a teaching task—and promises his presence to the age’s end. The Great Commission rests on Jesus’ all-authority and ends with his always-presence—courage with company. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Our sixty days end where Christian life always aims: under Jesus’ authority, with Jesus’ mission, in Jesus’ presence. He connects heaven’s authority to earth’s going. We are never sent alone. Making disciples is the natural overflow of sixty days spent knowing him: baptizing belonging, teaching obedience. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: Ask how your household can take one disciple-making step: pray for someone far from Jesus, share what you have learned, invite, serve, or encourage baptismal faithfulness in your church family. Pick one relational next step—pray, invite, share, encourage—and treat his “I am with you” as enough. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: As Jesus sends us with “I am with you always,” what is one next step of making disciples we can take together?
family.prayer: Risen Jesus, all authority is yours. Send our family under your word. Teach us to make disciples, and keep your promise—be with us always. Amen.

devo.title: The Prophetic Word Made More Sure
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 2 Peter 1:3–11 — Everything for life and godliness; partakers of the divine nature
  2. 2 Peter 1:16–21 — Eyewitnesses of his majesty; men carried along by the Holy Spirit
  3. 2 Peter 2:1–10 — False teachers, and the Lord who rescued Noah and Lot
  4. 2 Peter 3:1–18 — The day of the Lord and new heavens and a new earth

Old Testament background: Genesis 6–8; Genesis 19:1–29; Psalm 90:4; Isaiah 65:17–25

The Book and Its Themes

2 Peter is Peter’s farewell. He knows that “the putting off of my body will be soon” (1:14), and he wants to leave his readers a reminder they can hold on to after he is gone. The letter has three movements. First, grow in grace: God’s divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness, so we must add virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection, and love to our faith (chapter 1). Second, beware of false teachers who deny the Master who bought them, twist Scripture, and promise freedom while they are slaves of corruption (chapter 2). Third, do not doubt the Lord’s return. Scoffers will ask, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (3:4), but the Lord is not slow; he is patient, “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (3:9). The letter ends where it began: “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).

Where 2 Peter Stands in the Covenant Story

2 Peter reads history as a series of judgments and rescues. God did not spare the ancient world but preserved Noah, “a herald of righteousness” (2:5). He turned Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes but rescued righteous Lot (2:6–7). These are patterns: “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment” (2:9). The flood shows that God has judged the world before and will judge it again, this time by fire (3:5–7). But the end is not destruction for its own sake. “According to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (3:13). That promise comes from Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. The story that began with creation will end with new creation.

How 2 Peter Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: On the mount of transfiguration, Peter heard the Father’s voice: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (1:17). These words echo Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1, where God speaks of his royal Son and his chosen Servant.
  • Promise fulfilled: Peter says, “we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed” (1:19). The Old Testament prophecies are confirmed by the coming of Christ, and they shine “as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (1:19).
  • Type fulfilled: Noah’s ark and Lot’s rescue picture the salvation Christ brings. Judgment falls on the world, and God brings his people safely through it.
  • Promise fulfilled: The new heavens and new earth promised by Isaiah will come with the day of the Lord (3:10–13). Jesus is the Lord whose coming the scoffers deny.

Through Reformed Eyes

2 Peter 1:20–21 is, with 2 Timothy 3:16, a foundation for the Reformed doctrine of Scripture: “no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21). The Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession both open with a chapter on Holy Scripture for this reason. John Frame describes Scripture as God’s own personal word to his people, carrying the authority of the covenant Lord. Packer and Grudem agree that because God is its author, Scripture is fully trustworthy.

2 Peter 3:9 has been debated between Calvinists and Arminians. Some Reformed interpreters read “any” and “all” as referring to God’s people, the “you” to whom Peter writes. Calvin took a different route. He wrote, “So wonderful is his love towards mankind, that he would have them all to be saved, and is of his own self prepared to bestow salvation on the lost.” He then explained that “no mention is here made of the hidden purpose of God… but only of his will as made known to us in the gospel.” In other words, the gospel offer is sincere and free to all, while God effectually draws those he has chosen. On the end of the world, Reformed readers also differ on whether 3:10 describes the destruction of the present creation or its purifying renewal. Many Reformed teachers, including Wilson with his strong emphasis on this world’s future, favor renewal.

For Today

Peter wrote to people who were tempted to think God’s promises were stale. Every generation faces the same temptation. But a thousand years with the Lord are as one day (3:8, echoing Psalm 90:4). His delay is mercy. Today, use the time God gives. Add to your faith one of the virtues of 1:5–7, and pay attention to the word of God as to a lamp in a dark place. The day is coming, and the morning star will rise.

Reflect

  1. Do you think of God’s patience as slowness, or as mercy?
  2. Which of the virtues in 2 Peter 1:5–7 most needs to grow in your life?

Pray

Lord God, your divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness through the knowledge of Jesus Christ. Thank you for the prophetic word, made more sure, which shines like a lamp in a dark place. Guard me from false teaching and from doubting your promises. Thank you for your patience with me. Help me to wait for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells, and to grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and forever. Amen.

devo.title: The Propitiation for Our Sins
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 1 John 1:1–2:2 — The Word of life; walking in the light; an advocate with the Father
  2. 1 John 3:1–10 — See what kind of love: we are children of God
  3. 1 John 4:7–19 — God is love; he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins
  4. 1 John 5:1–13 — Overcoming faith, and the testimony that God gave us eternal life

Old Testament background: Leviticus 16:15–22; Deuteronomy 6:4–6; Jeremiah 31:33–34

The Book and Its Themes

1 John was written by the apostle John, probably late in the first century, to churches that had been shaken by a split. Some had left the fellowship (2:19), denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh and claiming a superior spiritual knowledge that did not require obedience or love. John writes to reassure the faithful: “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). He gives three tests of genuine faith that keep circling through the letter: right belief about Jesus (the doctrinal test), obedience to God’s commands (the moral test), and love for the brothers (the social test). The letter’s great themes are light and darkness, truth and lies, love and hate, life and death, and the astonishing love of the Father who calls us his children.

Where 1 John Stands in the Covenant Story

1 John is full of new covenant realities. Jeremiah promised that in the new covenant, “they shall all know me” and “I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). John writes, “I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake” (2:12), and “you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge” (2:20). The commandment to love is “an old commandment that you had from the beginning” (2:7), rooted in the law of Moses, yet it is also new, because it is now seen in Christ who laid down his life for us. The Day of Atonement, when the high priest offered blood to cover the sins of the people (Leviticus 16), is fulfilled in Jesus, “the propitiation for our sins” (2:2).

How 1 John Shows Us Christ

  • Type fulfilled: “He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world” (2:2). Like the mercy seat, where atoning blood turned away God’s wrath, Christ is the one in whom God’s justice is satisfied and his love poured out.
  • Type fulfilled: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (2:1). The high priest bore the names of the tribes on his breastpiece before the LORD (Exodus 28:29). Jesus pleads for his people in heaven on the basis of his own finished sacrifice.
  • Promise fulfilled: “The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil” (3:8). The promise of Genesis 3:15 that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent is being kept.
  • Echo: John opens with “That which was from the beginning” (1:1), echoing both Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1. The eternal Word of life was heard, seen, and touched.

Through Reformed Eyes

J. I. Packer’s chapter “The Heart of the Gospel” in Knowing God is built on 1 John 4:10. He asked, “Has the word propitiation any place in your Christianity? In the faith of the New Testament it is central.” He argued that without propitiation, the gospel is not the gospel. The love of God, as John defines it, is not God overlooking sin but God sending his own Son to bear its penalty: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (4:10).

1 John 2:2 (“for the sins of the whole world”) is also discussed in the debate over the extent of the atonement. Reformed teachers who hold to particular redemption, including many in both the Westminster and 1689 traditions, read “the whole world” as people from every nation, not only Jews, or as the worldwide scope of the gospel offer. Grudem also holds to particular redemption in his Systematic Theology, while urging care and charity in how the doctrine is stated. Everyone agrees that Christ’s death is sufficient for all and freely offered to all.

For Today

John wrote so that you may know you have eternal life. He did not write to make you anxious but to make you sure. If you believe in the Son, if you are walking in the light, and if you love your brothers and sisters, even imperfectly, these are evidences of new birth. And when you sin, “we have an advocate with the Father” (2:1). Today, stop and consider John’s words: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (3:1).

Reflect

  1. What assurance does 1 John give you, and what areas of your life does it call you to examine?
  2. How does knowing that Christ is the propitiation for your sins change the way you understand God’s love?

Pray

Father, see what kind of love you have given us, that we should be called your children, and so we are. Thank you for sending your Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Thank you that when I sin, I have an advocate with you, Jesus Christ the righteous. Keep me walking in the light, believing in your Son, and loving my brothers and sisters, because you first loved us. Keep me from idols. Amen.

devo.title: Walking in Truth and Love
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 2 John 1–3 — Loved in the truth, for the sake of the truth
  2. 2 John 4–6 — Walking in the truth; the commandment from the beginning
  3. 2 John 7–13 — Deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh; abide in the teaching

Old Testament background: Deuteronomy 6:4–9; Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Isaiah 54:1–8

The Book and Its Themes

2 John is a short note, small enough to fit on a single sheet of papyrus. “The elder,” almost certainly the apostle John, writes “to the elect lady and her children” (1). Many interpreters take this as a way of addressing a local church and its members, though some think it refers to an actual Christian woman and her family. Either way, the message is clear. John rejoices that some of her children are “walking in the truth” (4). He reminds them of the old commandment to love one another (5). And he warns them about traveling teachers who deny “the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” (7). Such teachers must not be welcomed and given a platform, because that would be taking part in their wicked works (10–11). The two great words of the letter are truth (five times) and love (four times). John will not let them be separated.

Where 2 John Stands in the Covenant Story

The Old Testament joined love and truth from the beginning. Israel was to love the LORD with all their heart and to keep his words on their hearts and teach them to their children (Deuteronomy 6:4–7). They were also to reject any prophet who led them after other gods, however impressive his signs (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). 2 John brings both commands into the new covenant. Love for God and one another is the old commandment we have had “from the beginning” (6). And faithfulness to the truth about Christ is the test of every teacher. The covenant community is to be a household of love and a guardian of truth. The prophets often pictured God’s people as a woman and her children (Isaiah 54:1–8), so it is fitting that John may be addressing the church as “the elect lady.”

How 2 John Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: Grace, mercy, and peace come “from God the Father and from Jesus Christ the Father’s Son” (3). The Son promised in Psalm 2 and Isaiah 9 is named as the source of covenant blessing with the Father.
  • Promise fulfilled: The heart of John’s warning is the incarnation. Jesus Christ has come “in the flesh” (7). The God who promised to dwell with his people (Exodus 29:45) has done it in the person of his Son.
  • Echo: Whoever “abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son” (9). The covenant promise “I will be your God” (Exodus 6:7) is fulfilled only through the Son. To deny the Son is to lose the Father.

Through Reformed Eyes

The confession that Jesus Christ came in the flesh was the battle line in the early church, and it is still the center of Christian orthodoxy. The Westminster Confession states it carefully: in Christ “two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion” (WCF 8.2). The 1647 Shorter Catechism says Christ, “being the eternal Son of God, became man, and so was, and continueth to be, God and man in two distinct natures, and one person, forever” (Q. 21). Grudem’s Systematic Theology defends both the full humanity and the full deity of Christ in its treatment of the person of Christ. Calvin’s commentaries do not cover 2 John, but his treatment of the two natures in the Institutes (2.12–14) is a classic.

2 John also guides how churches handle false teaching. John does not tell the elect lady to be rude to unbelievers, but to refuse to give a platform or support to those who deny Christ. Reformed teachers of every kind agree that truth and love are not opposites. Genuine love is willing to say hard things, and truth must always be spoken in love (Ephesians 4:15).

For Today

We live in a time that values love without truth, and some Christians answer with truth without love. John holds both. Today, examine whether you are walking in the truth and walking in love. If you tend to be soft on truth, ask God for courage. If you tend to be hard in your manner, ask God for tenderness. And thank God that the Son came in real flesh, so that real people like us can be saved.

Reflect

  1. Do you lean more toward truth without love or love without truth? What would balance look like for you?
  2. How can you encourage someone in your family or church who is “walking in the truth”?

Pray

Father, thank you for the grace, mercy, and peace that come from you and from Jesus Christ your Son, in truth and love. Thank you that the eternal Son came in the flesh to save us. Keep me abiding in the teaching of Christ, so that I have both the Father and the Son. Give me courage to hold the truth and tenderness to speak it in love. Let our family and our church walk in the truth together. Amen.

devo.title: Fellow Workers for the Truth
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. 3 John 1–4 — Walking in the truth, the elder’s greatest joy
  2. 3 John 5–8 — Supporting those who go out for the sake of the name
  3. 3 John 9–15 — Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, and Demetrius, who has a good testimony

Old Testament background: Genesis 18:1–8; Deuteronomy 10:17–19; Numbers 16:1–3

The Book and Its Themes

3 John is the shortest book in the Bible by word count in Greek, and it is the most personal of John’s letters. It is addressed to “the beloved Gaius” (1), a faithful believer who had shown generous hospitality to traveling missionaries. John praises him, encourages him to keep supporting these brothers “in a manner worthy of God” (6), and warns about a church leader named Diotrephes, “who likes to put himself first” (9). Diotrephes refused to receive John’s letter, spread wicked talk about him, refused to welcome the missionaries, and even put out of the church those who wanted to help them. John contrasts him with Demetrius, who “has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself” (12). The letter’s themes are walking in the truth, hospitality for the sake of the gospel, partnership in mission, and the danger of proud leadership.

Where 3 John Stands in the Covenant Story

Hospitality runs all through the Old Testament. Abraham ran to welcome three strangers and served them a meal, not knowing at first that the LORD was among them (Genesis 18:1–8; compare Hebrews 13:2). Israel was commanded to love the sojourner, “for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19). The missionaries John mentions had gone out “for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (7). They were carrying the promise to Abraham, that all nations would be blessed, out to the nations. Diotrephes, on the other hand, recalls Korah, who rose up against Moses and Aaron because he wanted their place (Numbers 16). God’s people have always been troubled by leaders who love to be first.

How 3 John Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: The missionaries went out “for the sake of the name” (7). The name of the LORD, which Israel was to make known among the nations, is now the name of Jesus Christ, at which every knee will bow.
  • Type fulfilled: Abraham’s hospitality to the LORD and his messengers is fulfilled when believers welcome Christ’s servants. Jesus said, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40).
  • Echo: Diotrephes loves to be first. Jesus, the true leader, “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). Christ’s way of leadership is the opposite of the self-promotion of Korah and Diotrephes.

Through Reformed Eyes

3 John gives a small window into the life of the early church: local congregations, traveling missionaries, and the need for faithful leadership. The Westminster Confession says that “unto this catholic visible church Christ hath given the ministry, oracles, and ordinances of God, for the gathering and perfecting of the saints, in this life, to the end of the world” (WCF 25.3). Both Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist churches look to the New Testament for how elders should lead: not “domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). Calvin’s commentaries do not cover 3 John, but his teaching on church order and the office of pastor in the Institutes (Book 4) has shaped Reformed churches ever since.

3 John also commends financial and practical support for missionaries. Supporting “people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (8) is a way every believer can share in the Great Commission. Wilson, Frame, and Grudem all teach that ordinary work and generous giving are part of serving Christ’s kingdom.

For Today

You may never go out as a missionary, but you can be a Gaius. You can open your home, support those who go, and refresh the saints. You can also check your heart for any trace of Diotrephes, any love of being first, any resentment when others get the attention. Today, “do not imitate evil but imitate good” (11). Think of one gospel worker you can encourage, support, or pray for this week.

Reflect

  1. How could your home or your giving help send the gospel out “for the sake of the name”?
  2. Where do you see a desire to be first in your own heart?

Pray

Lord Jesus, you came not to be served but to serve. Forgive me for every desire to put myself first. Thank you for faithful believers like Gaius who walk in the truth and open their homes. Make me generous and hospitable, a fellow worker for the truth. Bless those who have gone out for the sake of your name, and let them lack nothing. Let my life have a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. Amen.

devo.title: Kept for Jesus Christ
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Jude 1–4 — Called, beloved, and kept; contend for the faith once for all delivered
  2. Jude 5–16 — Warnings from Israel in the wilderness, fallen angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, and Korah
  3. Jude 17–25 — Build yourselves up, keep yourselves in God’s love, and the God who is able to keep you

Old Testament background: Numbers 14:26–35; Numbers 16:1–35; Genesis 4:1–8

The Book and Its Themes

Jude, “a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (1), and so a half-brother of the Lord himself, had planned to write a warm letter about “our common salvation” (3). Instead, he felt compelled to write urgently, because false teachers had crept into the church unnoticed. They were “ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (4). Jude calls believers to “contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (3). Most of the letter is a vivid catalogue of Old Testament warnings, but it is framed at both ends by the security of God’s people. They are “called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ” (1), and the letter ends with one of the greatest doxologies in Scripture, praising the God “who is able to keep you from stumbling” (24).

Where Jude Stands in the Covenant Story

Jude reads the Old Testament as a warning to the church. He reminds them that “Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (5). That is a striking verse: Jude, like Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:4, sees Christ active in the exodus. Jude then points to angels who abandoned their proper dwelling, to Sodom and Gomorrah, and to three Old Testament rebels: Cain, who murdered his brother, Balaam, who sold his gift for money, and Korah, who rebelled against Moses (11). He even cites a prophecy of Enoch, the seventh from Adam (14–15). The lesson is that God’s judgment on unbelief and rebellion in the old covenant is a real warning for those who claim his name in the new.

How Jude Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: Jesus is “our only Master and Lord” (4). Jude gives Jesus the titles that belong to the LORD of Israel.
  • Type fulfilled: The exodus deliverance is attributed to Jesus (5), which shows the unity of the covenant of grace. The Lord who redeemed Israel from Egypt is the same Lord who redeems his church.
  • Echo: Korah’s rebellion against God’s appointed mediators (Numbers 16) foreshadows every rebellion against Christ, the final Prophet, Priest, and King. Those who reject his authority share Korah’s end.
  • Promise fulfilled: The God who kept Israel in the wilderness, carrying them “as a man carries his son” (Deuteronomy 1:31), now keeps believers for Jesus Christ and will “present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (24).

Through Reformed Eyes

Jude holds two truths together that the Reformed tradition has always taught. Believers are “kept for Jesus Christ” (1) by God, and believers must “keep yourselves in the love of God” (21). Calvin, commenting on the closing doxology, wrote that Jude shows “our exhortations and labors can do nothing except through the power of God accompanying them.” This is the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints: God keeps his people, and he does so by means of their own watchfulness, prayer, and faith.

Jude’s command to “contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (3) shapes the Reformed commitment to sound doctrine and to the finished canon of Scripture. The faith is not being added to; it is to be guarded and handed on. Doug Wilson’s ministry is known for robust, sometimes combative, defense of the faith in public, and Frame and Grudem have both written at length on why doctrine matters for life. All of them would add Jude’s balance: “have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire” (22–23). Contending for the faith is never an excuse for cruelty.

For Today

You live in a time of confusion about truth and morality, much like Jude’s. You are called to contend for the faith. But notice how Jude says to do it: build yourselves up in your most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, and show mercy to others (20–23). And then rest in the God who is able to keep you from stumbling. Your perseverance does not finally depend on your grip on him, but on his grip on you.

Reflect

  1. Where are you being called to contend for the faith, and how can you do it with mercy?
  2. How does the doxology in verses 24–25 give you confidence today?

Pray

Now to him who is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Keep me in your love, Father. Build me up in the faith, help me pray in the Spirit, and give me mercy for those who doubt. Thank you that I am called, beloved, and kept for Jesus Christ. Amen.

devo.title: Behold, I Am Making All Things New
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Revelation 1:4–8, 12–18 — The faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, the one like a son of man
  2. Revelation 5:1–14 — The Lion of the tribe of Judah is a Lamb who was slain
  3. Revelation 19:6–16; 20:1–6 — The marriage supper of the Lamb; the King of kings; the thousand years
  4. Revelation 21:1–7; 22:1–5, 16–21 — New heavens and new earth; the river of life; “Come, Lord Jesus!”

Old Testament background: Genesis 2:8–10; Daniel 7:9–14; Isaiah 65:17–19; Ezekiel 47:1–12

The Book and Its Themes

Revelation is the last book of the Bible and the capstone of the whole story. It was given to the apostle John in exile on the island of Patmos, to be sent to seven churches in Asia Minor that were facing persecution, compromise, and complacency (chapters 2–3). It is written in apocalyptic style, full of symbols drawn from the Old Testament: lampstands, seals, trumpets, bowls, beasts, a dragon, a harlot, and a bride. Its message is not hidden. Jesus Christ is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth (1:5). He has conquered by his blood, he walks among his churches, and he will come again to judge the world, defeat every enemy, and make all things new. Revelation calls believers to faithful endurance, to worship the Lamb and refuse the beast, and to lift up their heads, because the Lord God Almighty reigns.

Where Revelation Stands in the Covenant Story

Revelation gathers up the whole Bible. Its imagery comes from Genesis, Exodus, the Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Zechariah more than from any other source; scholars count hundreds of allusions to the Old Testament, though John never formally quotes it. The plagues on the persecuting world recall the plagues on Egypt, and the redeemed sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (15:3). The final chapters return to Eden. There is a river of the water of life, and the tree of life with leaves “for the healing of the nations” (22:2). “No longer will there be anything accursed” (22:3), because the curse of Genesis 3 has been borne by the Lamb. The covenant promise that runs through Scripture is finally fulfilled: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (21:3).

How Revelation Shows Us Christ

  • Promise fulfilled: John sees “one like a son of man” (1:13), the figure of Daniel 7:13, now risen and glorified. He holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18).
  • Type fulfilled: John is told to look at “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” (5:5), the messianic King of Genesis 49:9–10 and Isaiah 11. When he turns, he sees “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (5:6). The Passover lamb and the Lamb of Isaiah 53 are the conquering King. He wins by being slain.
  • Promise fulfilled: The rider on the white horse is called “Faithful and True,” and on his robe is written “King of kings and Lord of lords” (19:11, 16). Psalm 2’s promise that the Son will rule the nations with a rod of iron is fulfilled in him (19:15).
  • Type fulfilled: The new Jerusalem is shaped like a perfect cube (21:16), like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:20). John sees “no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (21:22). The whole new creation has become the holy of holies.

Through Reformed Eyes

Revelation 20 and the “thousand years” is where our teachers differ most, and it is good to say so plainly. Wayne Grudem is a historic premillennialist. He believes Christ will return after a time of great tribulation and then reign on earth for a thousand years before the final judgment. His teaching outline concludes, “It seems best to conclude that the church will go through the time of tribulation predicted by Jesus.” Doug Wilson is a postmillennialist and a partial preterist. He reads much of Revelation as fulfilled in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, and he expects the gospel to triumph across the world before Christ returns. He writes, “Virtually all the books of the New Testament have an expectant air about them.” R. C. Sproul also argued for a partial-preterist reading of the Olivet Discourse in The Last Days According to Jesus. Calvin, who wrote no commentary on Revelation, rejected the earthly millennium of the chiliasts in the Institutes: “This fiction is too puerile to need or to deserve refutation” (3.25.5). His view is closest to what is now called amillennialism, which sees the thousand years as the present reign of Christ and his saints. John Frame says simply, “I am not a premillennialist,” and he insists that Christ’s lordship must be pursued in every area of life now.

These differences are real, but they sit inside a deep agreement. The Westminster Confession says, “God hath appointed a day, wherein he will judge the world, in righteousness, by Jesus Christ, to whom all power and judgment is given of the Father” (WCF 33.1). Christ will return bodily and visibly, the dead will be raised, the wicked will be judged, and God’s people will dwell with him forever in a renewed creation. Every Reformed teacher can pray with John, “Come, Lord Jesus!”

For Today

This is the last day of the series. Over three volumes you have walked from “In the beginning” to “Come, Lord Jesus.” You have seen the seed promised in Eden, the covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David, the prophets’ longing, and the coming of the Son who fulfilled it all. Revelation shows you the end of the story: a Lamb on the throne, a bride made ready, and a city where God dwells with his people. Whatever you face today, you know how the story ends. “Behold, I am making all things new” (21:5).

Reflect

  1. Which picture of Christ in Revelation (the Son of Man, the Lamb, the Rider, the Bridegroom) most strengthens you today?
  2. Looking back over all three volumes, how has seeing Christ in all the Scriptures changed the way you read your Bible?

Pray

Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come, worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing. Thank you that by his blood he ransomed people for you from every tribe and language and people and nation. Thank you for showing us Christ in all the Scriptures, from Genesis to Revelation. Keep us faithful until he comes. Make all things new. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

quote.author: R. C. Sproul
quote.text: If we stagger at the wrath of God, let us stagger at the Cross. Here is where our astonishment should be focused.
quote.comment: When we struggle with God’s justice, Sproul points us to the one place where wrath and grace meet, where the innocent Son took what we deserved.

read.title: The Faithfulness of God
read.author: Samuel Saldivar
read.note: Walks through the main Old and New Testament words and pictures for God’s faithfulness, and how God keeps his covenant promises in Christ even when his people are unfaithful (2 Timothy 2:13).

quote.author: Charles H. Spurgeon
quote.text: …he believes him to be too wise to err and too good to be unkind; he trusts him where he cannot trace him, looks up to him in the darkest hour, and believes that all is well.
quote.comment: When we can’t see what God is doing, we can still rest in who he is, perfectly wise and perfectly good.

read.title: The Wisdom of God
read.author: Daniel J. Ebert IV
read.note: Biblical wisdom as living in step with God’s created order and saving work, centred on Christ, God’s wisdom in person.
